Figure 5: Diagram of the partial lifting of the n=2 degeneracy by the linear Stark effect.











NoteThe Stark effect





Johannes Stark observed the splitting of spectral lines in an electric field in 1913. In quantum mechanics, the splitting follows from the dipole interaction and the degeneracy of the unperturbed levels.





4.4 Near-degeneracy
Two levels are not always exactly degenerate, but their separation can be comparable to the coupling. If
\[
|E_1^{(0)}-E_2^{(0)}|\lesssim2|\lambda W_{12}|,
\]
the denominators of the nondegenerate method become small and the expansion loses its hierarchy. We must then diagonalize exactly the small block containing these levels, as in Equation 24, while treating their coupling to the rest of the spectrum perturbatively. This strategy is called near-degenerate perturbation theory.

title: Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics
text:
5 Time-dependent perturbations
A time-dependent perturbation does more than change an eigenstate: it can transfer energy and cause transitions. Consider
\[
\widehat H(t)=\widehat H_0+\lambda\widehat W(t),
\tag{30}\]
with \(\widehat H_0|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle\). Expand the exact state in the stationary basis of \(\widehat H_0\):
\[
|\Psi(t)\rangle
=\sum_n c_n(t)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}|n\rangle.
\tag{31}\]
The free phases have been factored out; every transition is contained in the coefficients \(c_n(t)\).

5.1 Evolution equations for the amplitudes
Differentiate Equation 31:
\[
i\hbar\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}|\Psi(t)\rangle
=\sum_n
\left(i\hbar\dot c_n(t)+E_nc_n(t)\right)
e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}|n\rangle.
\]
The term in \(E_n\) is exactly reproduced by \(\widehat H_0|\Psi\rangle\) and cancels on both sides of the Schrödinger equation. This leaves
\[
\sum_n i\hbar\dot c_n e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}|n\rangle
=\lambda\sum_n c_n e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\widehat W(t)|n\rangle.
\]
Project onto \(\langle f|\) and then multiply by \(e^{iE_ft/\hbar}\). We obtain the exact system
\[
i\hbar\dot c_f(t)
=\lambda\sum_n W_{fn}(t)e^{i\omega_{fn}t}c_n(t),
\tag{32}\]
with
\[
W_{fn}(t)=\langle f|\widehat W(t)|n\rangle,
\qquad
\omega_{fn}=\frac{E_f-E_n}{\hbar}.
\]
The same construction can be written with the evolution operator in the interaction picture. Defining
\[
\widehat W_I(t)
=e^{i\widehat H_0t/\hbar}\widehat W(t)
e^{-i\widehat H_0t/\hbar},
\]
the integral equation is
\[
\widehat U_I(t)
=\widehat I-\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar}
\int_0^t\widehat W_I(t_1)\widehat U_I(t_1)\,\mathrm dt_1.
\]
Substituting this equation back into itself gives the Dyson series:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat U_I(t)
&=\widehat I
-\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar}\int_0^t\widehat W_I(t_1)\,\mathrm dt_1\\
&\quad+\left(-\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar}\right)^2
\int_0^t\mathrm dt_1\int_0^{t_1}\mathrm dt_2\,
\widehat W_I(t_1)\widehat W_I(t_2)+\cdots.
\end{aligned}
\tag{33}\]
The bound \(t_2<t_1\) places the later operator on the left. Their order matters because operators at different times need not commute.
Suppose that the system is initially in \(|i\rangle\):
\[
c_n(0)=\delta_{ni}.
\]
At first order, replace \(c_n(t)\) on the right-hand side by its zeroth-order value \(\delta_{ni}\). For \(f\ne i\),
\[
i\hbar\dot c_f^{(1)}(t)
=\lambda W_{fi}(t)e^{i\omega_{fi}t}.
\]
Integrating from \(0\) to \(t\),
\[
c_{f\leftarrow i}^{(1)}(t)
=-\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar}
\int_0^t W_{fi}(t')e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}\,\mathrm dt'.
\tag{34}\]
Here, the superscript \((1)\) denotes the amplitude truncated at first order; the factor \(\lambda\) is therefore already included.
The transition probability at the first nonzero order is then
\[
P_{i\to f}(t)
=|c_{f\leftarrow i}^{(1)}(t)|^2+O(\lambda^3).
\tag{35}\]
The integral selects the part of the excitation near the transition frequency \(\omega_{fi}\). The matrix element must also be nonzero.
Replacing the initial amplitude by one is valid while its depletion is small:
\[
\sum_{f\ne i}P_{i\to f}(t)\ll1.
\tag{36}\]
At longer times, a resonant two-level system requires the Rabi solution derived below.


5.2 Rectangular pulse and spectral width
Take a constant coupling \(W_{fi}\) applied between \(0\) and \(\tau\), and then switched off. For \(t\ge\tau\),
\[
c_{f\leftarrow i}^{(1)}
=-\frac{i\lambda W_{fi}}{\hbar}
\int_0^\tau e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}\,\mathrm dt'.
\]
Centering the exponential around \(\tau/2\),
\[
\int_0^\tau e^{i\omega t'}\,\mathrm dt'
=e^{i\omega\tau/2}
\frac{2\sin(\omega\tau/2)}{\omega}.
\]
The probability becomes
\[
P_{i\to f}
=\frac{\lambda^2|W_{fi}|^2\tau^2}{\hbar^2}
\operatorname{sinc}^2\!\left(\frac{\omega_{fi}\tau}{2}\right),
\tag{37}\]
where \(\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin u/u\) and \(\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1\). The first zeros occur at \(|\omega_{fi}|=2\pi/\tau\): a longer pulse has a narrower frequency width. The time-dependent external source can exchange energy with the system.


Show the Python code
t = np.linspace(-1, 13, 1200)
detuning = np.linspace(-12, 12, 1600)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.1))
for tau, couleur in [(1.0, ORANGE), (4.0, BLEU), (9.0, VIOLET)]:
    pulse = ((t >= 0) & (t <= tau)).astype(float)
    # np.sinc(z) = sin(pi*z)/(pi*z)
    spectre = np.sinc(detuning * tau / (2*np.pi))**2
    axes[0].plot(t, pulse + 0.08*(tau-1), color=couleur, lw=2,
                 label=fr"$\tau={tau:g}$")
    axes[1].plot(detuning, spectre, color=couleur, lw=2,
                 label=fr"$\tau={tau:g}$")

axes[0].set(xlabel="$t$", ylabel="$W(t)$ (shifted)",
            title="Rectangular excitations", ylim=(-0.1, 1.8))
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"detuning $\omega_{fi}$", ylabel="normalized profile",
            title=r"$\mathrm{sinc}^2(\omega_{fi}\tau/2)$")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: A longer pulse has a narrower transition spectrum.







5.3 Sinusoidal excitation and resonance
Consider
\[
\widehat W(t)=\widehat A F_0\cos(\omega t)
=\frac{F_0\widehat A}{2}
\left(e^{i\omega t}+e^{-i\omega t}\right).
\tag{38}\]
The amplitude Equation 34 then contains two integrals oscillating at angular frequencies \(\omega_{fi}+\omega\) and \(\omega_{fi}-\omega\), respectively. If \(E_f>E_i\) and \(\omega\simeq\omega_{fi}\), the second term varies slowly and builds up coherently: this is absorption resonance. The term at \(\omega_{fi}+\omega\) oscillates rapidly and averages almost to zero.
The spatial factor
\[
A_{fi}=\langle f|\widehat A|i\rangle
\]
determines the selection rules. For example, an electric dipole interaction is proportional to \(\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{E}}\) and couples only states whose symmetries make this matrix element nonzero.


5.4 Fermi’s golden rule
For an exactly resonant discrete final state, first-order theory initially predicts growth proportional to \(t^2\). In a continuum, we must sum over many final states. The peak of width \(1/t\) becomes narrower while its height grows as \(t^2\); its area therefore grows as \(t\).
If \(\rho(E_f)\) is the density of final states and \(V_{fi}\) is the matrix element of the resonant component of the perturbation, we obtain a constant transition rate
\[
\Gamma_{i\to f}
=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}|V_{fi}|^2\rho(E_f)
\bigg|_{E_f=E_i+\hbar\omega}.
\tag{39}\]
Here \(V_{fi}\) includes the physical coupling strength; for absorption from \(\lambda F_0 A\cos(\omega t)\), \(V_{fi}=\lambda F_0 A_{fi}/2\). The rate is larger when the coupling is stronger or when more final states are available.
The energy selection follows from the distributional limit
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t
\left|\int_0^t e^{i\nu t'}\,dt'\right|^2
=2\pi\delta(\nu),
\qquad \nu=\frac{E_f-E_i}{\hbar}-\omega.
\]
Integrating over \(\rho(E_f)\,dE_f\) gives the rate above. The observation time must resolve a smooth group of final states, while the transition probability remains small. This is the interval in which \(P(t)\simeq\Gamma t\) applies.


5.5 Two-level system and Rabi oscillations
When the system has only two relevant levels, the resonant transition can be treated beyond first order. Let \(|g\rangle\) be the ground state, \(|e\rangle\) the excited state, and
\[
E_e-E_g=\hbar\omega_0.
\]
In the ordered basis \((|g\rangle,|e\rangle)\), take a sinusoidal coupling with a real positive amplitude:
\[
H(t)=\frac{\hbar}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\omega_0&2\Omega\cos(\omega t)\\
2\Omega\cos(\omega t)&\omega_0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For the excitation used above, \(\Omega=|\lambda F_0 A_{eg}|/\hbar\). Write \(|\Psi\rangle=R(t)|\chi\rangle\), with
\[
R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{i\omega t/2}&0\\0&e^{-i\omega t/2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Schrödinger equation for \(|\chi\rangle\) contains
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_{\mathrm{rot}}
&=R^\dagger H R-i\hbar R^\dagger\dot R\\
&=\frac{\hbar}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\Delta&\Omega(1+e^{-2i\omega t})\\
\Omega(1+e^{2i\omega t})&\Delta
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \Delta=\omega_0-\omega.
\end{aligned}
\]
Near resonance, with \(|\Delta|,\Omega\ll\omega_0\), the terms at \(2\omega\) oscillate much faster than the amplitudes change. Dropping them gives the rotating-wave approximation (RWA):
\[
\widehat H_{\mathrm{RWA}}
=\frac{\hbar}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}
-\Delta&\Omega\\
\Omega&\Delta
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Delta=\omega_0-\omega.
\tag{40}\]
The frequency \(\Omega\) is the Rabi angular frequency at resonance. The approximation keeps coherent transitions but neglects the rapidly oscillating terms. The eigenvalues of the constant matrix are
\[
\varepsilon_\pm
=\pm\frac{\hbar}{2}\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}.
\]
Define \(\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\). Since
\[
\widehat H_{\mathrm{RWA}}^2
=\frac{\hbar^2\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}{4}\widehat I,
\]
the even and odd powers of the Hamiltonian group together in the evolution exponential:
\[
e^{-i\widehat H_{\mathrm{RWA}}t/\hbar}
=\widehat I\cos\left(\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}t}{2}\right)
-\frac{2i\widehat H_{\mathrm{RWA}}}{\hbar\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}}
\sin\left(\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}t}{2}\right).
\]
Applying this operator to \(|g\rangle\), the component along \(|e\rangle\) is
\[
\langle e|\Psi(t)\rangle
=-i\frac{\Omega}{\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}}
\sin\left(\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}t}{2}\right).
\]
If the system starts in \(|g\rangle\), the probability of occupying the excited state is
\[
P_e(t)=
\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}
\sin^2\!\left(
\frac{t}{2}\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}
\right).
\tag{41}\]
At resonance, \(\Delta=0\),
\[
P_e(t)=\sin^2\left(\frac{\Omega t}{2}\right).
\]
A pulse of duration \(t_\pi=\pi/\Omega\) completely inverts the population: this is a \(\pi\) pulse. A pulse of duration \(t_{\pi/2}=\pi/(2\Omega)\) creates an equal superposition.
Off resonance, two changes happen at the same time: the oscillation becomes faster, at the generalized angular frequency \(\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\), but its maximum amplitude decreases to
\[
P_e^{\max}=\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}.
\tag{42}\]


Show the Python code

t = np.linspace(0, 8*np.pi, 1200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.2))
for Delta, couleur in [(0.0, BLEU), (0.6, ORANGE), (1.5, VIOLET)]:
    Omega_eff = np.sqrt(Omega**2 + Delta**2)
    Pe = Omega**2 / Omega_eff**2 * np.sin(Omega_eff*t/2)**2
    axes[0].plot(t/np.pi, Pe, color=couleur, lw=2,
                 label=fr"$\Delta/\Omega={Delta:g}$")

dets = np.linspace(-4, 4, 1000)
for duree, couleur in [(np.pi, BLEU), (3*np.pi, ORANGE), (7*np.pi, VIOLET)]:
    Om_eff = np.sqrt(Omega**2 + dets**2)
    Pe_fin = Omega**2 / Om_eff**2 * np.sin(Om_eff*duree/2)**2
    axes[1].plot(dets/Omega, Pe_fin, color=couleur, lw=2,
                 label=fr"$t={duree/np.pi:g}\pi/\Omega$")

axes[0].set(xlabel=r"time $\Omega t/\pi$", ylabel=r"$P_e(t)$",
            title="Coherent population exchange", ylim=(-0.03, 1.03))
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"detuning $\Delta/\Omega$", ylabel=r"$P_e(t_{\rm fin})$",
            title="Frequency selectivity", ylim=(-0.03, 1.03))
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7: Rabi oscillations: time evolution and the resonance profile of a pulse.







5.6 The Bloch sphere
A pure two-level state can be written as
\[
|\psi\rangle
=\cos\frac{\vartheta}{2}|g\rangle
+e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\vartheta}{2}|e\rangle.
\]
It is associated with the Bloch vector
\[
\mathbf r=
(\sin\vartheta\cos\varphi,
\sin\vartheta\sin\varphi,
\cos\vartheta).
\]
The Hamiltonian Equation 40 corresponds to an effective field proportional to
\[
\boldsymbol\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}=(\Omega,0,-\Delta).
\]
In this rotating frame, its evolution is \(\dot{\mathbf r}=\boldsymbol\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}\times\mathbf r\). It rotates about this axis at angular frequency \(\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\). The north pole represents \(|g\rangle\) and the south pole represents \(|e\rangle\), so \(P_e=(1-r_z)/2\).
At resonance, the axis is horizontal and a state starting at the north pole can reach the south pole. Away from resonance, the axis tilts and complete inversion is no longer possible.


5.7 Sudden and slow changes
If the Hamiltonian changes over a time \(\tau\) much shorter than the relevant internal times \(\hbar/|E_m-E_n|\), the state changes very little during the switch. To find the later evolution, expand this same state in the eigenbasis of the new Hamiltonian.
For a smooth, slow change, an isolated eigenstate can follow the instantaneous eigenstate up to a phase. Differentiating \(H(t)|n(t)\rangle=E_n(t)|n(t)\rangle\) and projecting onto \(\langle m(t)|\) gives
\[
\langle m|\dot n\rangle
=\frac{\langle m|\dot H|n\rangle}{E_n-E_m},
\qquad m\ne n.
\]
Comparing this mixing rate with \(|E_n-E_m|/\hbar\) gives the usual local estimate for adiabatic evolution:
\[
\hbar\frac{|\langle m(t)|\dot H(t)|n(t)\rangle|}
{|E_n(t)-E_m(t)|^2}\ll1.
\tag{43}\]
A small gap makes this condition harder to satisfy. The estimate must hold throughout the change; over long times, accumulated transitions may also need to be checked.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
1 From free fields to interactions
A free quantum field describes particles which propagate without scattering or decaying. Its Hamiltonian is diagonal in the occupation-number basis,
\[
H_0=\sum_a\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
E_{a,\mathbf p}\,a_a^\dagger(\mathbf p)a_a(\mathbf p),
\]
where \(a\) labels the species, spin or polarization. The time evolution changes only the phase of a multiparticle state. Its momenta and particle content remain unchanged.
An interacting theory is written as
\[
\mathcal L=\mathcal L_0+\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}},
\qquad
H=H_0+H_{\mathrm{int}}.
\tag{1}\]
The interaction contains products of fields and therefore products of creation and annihilation operators. A term proportional to \(\phi^4\), for example, contains terms such as \(a^\dagger a^\dagger aa\), which can change the momenta of two particles, as well as terms which change the number of particles when energy and momentum conservation allow it.
In four space-time dimensions,
\[
[\phi]=1,
\qquad
[\psi]=\frac32,
\qquad
[A_\mu]=1,
\qquad
[\mathcal L]=4.
\]
Two simple examples are
\[
\mathcal L_{\phi^4}
=\frac12(\partial\phi)^2-\frac12m^2\phi^2
-\frac{\lambda}{4!}\phi^4,
\tag{2}\]
and the Yukawa theory
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm Y}
=\frac12(\partial\phi)^2-\frac12\mu^2\phi^2
+\bar\psi(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi
-g\bar\psi\psi\phi.
\tag{3}\]
Both \(\lambda\) and \(g\) are dimensionless. The factor \(1/4!\) in Equation 2 cancels the \(4!\) equivalent ways of attaching four identical scalar fields to a vertex.
We use natural units, \(\hbar=c=1\), and
\[
\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
\]
One-particle states have the relativistic normalization
\[
\langle\mathbf q|\mathbf p\rangle
=2E_{\mathbf p}(2\pi)^3\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\tag{4}\]

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
2 The S-matrix

2.1 Asymptotic states
In a scattering experiment, particles are far apart before the collision and again far apart after it. Stable particles can then be described by free states with their physical masses. We denote them by
\[
|i,\mathrm{in}\rangle
\quad\text{at}\quad t\to-\infty,
\]
and
\[
|f,\mathrm{out}\rangle
\quad\text{at}\quad t\to+\infty.
\]
The scattering matrix connects the two descriptions:
\[
|i,\mathrm{out}\rangle=S|i,\mathrm{in}\rangle.
\]
The transition amplitude is
\[
S_{fi}=\langle f,\mathrm{out}|i,\mathrm{in}\rangle.
\]
Writing
\[
S=\mathbf1+iT
\]
separates the trivial case in which nothing happens from the interaction. Translation invariance gives an overall momentum-conserving delta function. The invariant amplitude \(\mathcal M\) is defined by
\[
\boxed{
\langle f|iT|i\rangle
=i(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}(P_f-P_i)\mathcal M_{i\to f}.}
\tag{5}\]
The delta function is not part of \(\mathcal M\). It expresses a symmetry of space-time, while \(\mathcal M\) contains the dynamics.
Unitarity,
\[
S^\dagger S=1,
\]
implies
\[
-i(T-T^\dagger)=T^\dagger T.
\tag{6}\]
Taking a forward matrix element produces the optical theorem. It relates the imaginary part of a forward amplitude to a sum over all possible intermediate final states. This relation is an important test of perturbative calculations.


2.2 The interaction picture
The Schrödinger picture puts time dependence in the states. The Heisenberg picture puts it in the operators. Perturbation theory is easier in the interaction picture, where the free Hamiltonian controls the operators and the interaction Hamiltonian controls the states.
For a Schrödinger operator \(O_S\),
\[
O_I(t)=e^{iH_0t}O_Se^{-iH_0t}.
\]
The interaction-picture state is
\[
|\Psi(t)\rangle_I=e^{iH_0t}|\Psi(t)\rangle_S.
\]
Differentiating and using the Schrödinger equation gives
\[
i\frac{d}{dt}|\Psi(t)\rangle_I
=H_I(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle_I,
\tag{7}\]
where
\[
H_I(t)=e^{iH_0t}H_{\mathrm{int}}e^{-iH_0t}.
\]
The fields inside \(H_I\) are therefore free fields. This is why free propagators appear in perturbation theory even though the full theory is interacting.
Let \(U_I(t,t_0)\) be the evolution operator,
\[
|\Psi(t)\rangle_I=U_I(t,t_0)|\Psi(t_0)\rangle_I.
\]
It obeys
\[
i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}U_I(t,t_0)
=H_I(t)U_I(t,t_0),
\qquad
U_I(t_0,t_0)=1.
\tag{8}\]
Integrating once gives
\[
U_I(t,t_0)
=1-i\int_{t_0}^{t}dt_1\,H_I(t_1)U_I(t_1,t_0).
\]
Repeated substitution produces the perturbative expansion.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
3 Dyson series and time ordering

3.1 Derivation of the series
The first terms of the iterative solution are
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_I(t,t_0)
={}&1-i\int_{t_0}^{t}dt_1\,H_I(t_1)\\
&+(-i)^2\int_{t_0}^{t}dt_1
\int_{t_0}^{t_1}dt_2\,H_I(t_1)H_I(t_2)+\cdots.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second integral covers only the region \(t_1>t_2\). We may extend it to the full square if we introduce the time-ordering operator,
\[
T\{H_I(t_1)H_I(t_2)\}
=\theta(t_1-t_2)H_I(t_1)H_I(t_2)
+\theta(t_2-t_1)H_I(t_2)H_I(t_1).
\]
Then
\[
\int_{t_0}^{t}dt_1\int_{t_0}^{t_1}dt_2
\,H_I(t_1)H_I(t_2)
=\frac1{2!}\int_{t_0}^{t}dt_1dt_2
\,T\{H_I(t_1)H_I(t_2)\}.
\]
The general result is the Dyson series
\[
\boxed{
U_I(t,t_0)
=T\exp\left[-i\int_{t_0}^{t}dt'\,H_I(t')\right].}
\tag{9}\]
Taking the asymptotic limits gives
\[
\boxed{
S=T\exp\left[-i\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dt\,H_I(t)\right].}
\tag{10}\]
For interactions without derivative subtleties, \(H_I(t)=-\int d^3\mathbf x\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}\), so
\[
S=T\exp\left[i\int d^4x\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}(x)\right].
\tag{11}\]
This last form must be used with care for derivative interactions, constrained systems and gauge theories, where the relation between the interaction Hamiltonian and Lagrangian is more delicate.






NoteDyson’s organisation of perturbation theory





In 1949, Freeman Dyson showed how the operator and diagrammatic approaches to quantum electrodynamics fit into a single perturbative expansion. Time ordering is the step that turns the evolution equation into the diagrams now associated with Feynman’s name.





3.2 Correlation functions
Scattering amplitudes are obtained from time-ordered correlation functions. For an interacting scalar field,
\[
G_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=\langle\Omega|T\{\phi_H(x_1)\cdots\phi_H(x_n)\}|\Omega\rangle,
\]
where \(|\Omega\rangle\) is the interacting vacuum. In terms of interaction-picture fields,
\[
\boxed{
G_n
=\frac{
\langle0|T\left\{
\phi_I(x_1)\cdots\phi_I(x_n)
\exp\left[i\int d^4x\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}(x)\right]
\right\}|0\rangle
}{
\langle0|T\exp\left[i\int d^4x\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}(x)\right]|0\rangle
}.}
\tag{12}\]
The denominator cancels vacuum bubbles: diagrams that contain no external point and are disconnected from the process.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
4 Wick’s theorem

4.1 Normal ordering and contractions
Normal ordering, denoted by colons, places all creation operators to the left of annihilation operators. Its vacuum expectation value vanishes unless the expression contains no operators:
\[
\langle0|:\!\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)\!:|0\rangle=0.
\]
For two free scalar fields, define the contraction by
\[
\big[\phi(x)\phi(y)\big]_{\mathrm c}
\equiv
T\{\phi(x)\phi(y)\}-:\!\phi(x)\phi(y)\!:.
\]
Its vacuum expectation value is the Feynman propagator,
\[
\big[\phi(x)\phi(y)\big]_{\mathrm c}
=\langle0|T\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle
=\Delta_F(x-y),
\]
with
\[
\Delta_F(x-y)
=\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}
\frac{i\,e^{-ip\cdot(x-y)}}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}.
\tag{13}\]
Wick’s theorem states that a time-ordered product of free fields equals the normal-ordered product plus all possible single contractions, all possible double contractions, and so on. For four scalar fields,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T\{\phi_1\phi_2\phi_3\phi_4\}
={}&:\!\phi_1\phi_2\phi_3\phi_4\!:
+\text{all single contractions}\\
&+\Delta_{12}\Delta_{34}
+\Delta_{13}\Delta_{24}
+\Delta_{14}\Delta_{23}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Only complete contractions survive between vacuum states. This is the origin of diagrammatic perturbation theory: every contraction becomes a propagator line, and every factor from \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}\) becomes a vertex.
For fermions, exchanging two fields produces a minus sign. A closed fermion loop therefore contributes an extra factor \(-1\). The sign follows from the operator ordering, not from the shape of the drawing.


4.2 Connected diagrams and loop number
A diagram may be connected or disconnected. Only connected diagrams contribute to the connected part of a correlation function. Vacuum bubbles cancel through the denominator of Equation 12. Disconnected pieces describing several independent scatterings must also be separated when one defines a single connected amplitude.
For a connected diagram with \(I\) internal lines and \(V\) vertices, the number of independent loop momenta is
\[
\boxed{L=I-V+1.}
\tag{14}\]
Tree diagrams have \(L=0\). Each loop introduces an unconstrained four-momentum integration. The word “loop” refers to the topology and the momentum integral; it does not mean that a particle follows a classical closed path.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
5 Momentum-space Feynman rules
The rules are a compact form of the Dyson expansion and Wick’s theorem. They depend on the sign conventions in the Lagrangian and propagators, so one consistent convention must be used from beginning to end.
At every vertex, space-time integration gives
\[
\int d^4x\,e^{-i(p_1+\cdots+p_n)\cdot x}
=(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}(p_1+\cdots+p_n).
\]
It is convenient to take every momentum as incoming at a vertex. Momentum conservation is then
\[
p_1+\cdots+p_n=0.
\]
After using the vertex delta functions, one overall delta function remains. It is removed according to Equation 5, leaving \(i\mathcal M\).

5.1 Scalar \(\phi^4\) theory
For
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}=-\frac{\lambda}{4!}\phi^4,
\]
the momentum-space rules are:
Each internal scalar line of momentum \(p\) contributes
\[
\frac{i}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}.
\]
Each four-scalar vertex contributes
\[
-i\lambda.
\]
Each independent loop momentum is integrated with
\[
\int\frac{d^4\ell}{(2\pi)^4}.
\]
The diagram is divided by its symmetry factor when identical contractions produce the same graph.
For the tree-level process
\[
\phi(p_1)+\phi(p_2)\to\phi(p_3)+\phi(p_4),
\]
there is one contact vertex. Thus
\[
i\mathcal M=-i\lambda,
\qquad
\boxed{\mathcal M=-\lambda.}
\tag{15}\]
At the next order, the \(s\)-channel bubble contains two vertices and two internal lines:
\[
i\mathcal M_s^{(1)}
=\frac12(-i\lambda)^2
\int\frac{d^4\ell}{(2\pi)^4}
\frac{i}{\ell^2-m^2+i\epsilon}
\frac{i}{(\ell+p_1+p_2)^2-m^2+i\epsilon}.
\tag{16}\]
The factor \(1/2\) is its symmetry factor. The \(t\)- and \(u\)-channel diagrams have the same form with different external momentum combinations. The integral is ultraviolet divergent; its treatment belongs to renormalization.


5.2 Yukawa theory
For
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}=-g\bar\psi\psi\phi,
\]
the scalar propagator is
\[
\frac{i}{p^2-\mu^2+i\epsilon},
\]
the fermion propagator is
\[
\frac{i(\not\!p+m)}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon},
\tag{17}\]
and each Yukawa vertex contributes
\[
-ig.
\]
An incoming fermion contributes \(u_s(p)\), an outgoing fermion contributes \(\bar u_s(p)\), an incoming antifermion contributes \(\bar v_s(p)\), and an outgoing antifermion contributes \(v_s(p)\). The order of spinors and gamma matrices must follow the fermion line.
For elastic fermion-fermion scattering through scalar exchange,
\[
\psi(p_1)+\psi(p_2)\to\psi(p_3)+\psi(p_4),
\]
one contribution is
\[
i\mathcal M_t
=(-ig)^2
\left[\bar u(p_3)u(p_1)\right]
\frac{i}{(p_1-p_3)^2-\mu^2+i\epsilon}
\left[\bar u(p_4)u(p_2)\right].
\tag{18}\]
Because the external fermions are identical, the exchanged diagram must also be included with the relative minus sign required by Fermi statistics.
The scalar decay \(\phi\to\psi\bar\psi\) has
\[
i\mathcal M=(-ig)\bar u(p)v(q),
\]
so
\[
\mathcal M=-g\bar u(p)v(q).
\]

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
6 From correlation functions to amplitudes

6.1 LSZ reduction
A correlation function includes external propagators between the interaction region and the points \(x_i\). A scattering amplitude should describe the interaction of on-shell particles, without these external propagators. The Lehmann–Symanzik–Zimmermann reduction formula performs this removal.
For a scalar field with wave-function factor \(Z\), the schematic form is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle p_1',\ldots,p_m',\mathrm{out}
|p_1,\ldots,p_n,\mathrm{in}\rangle_{\mathrm{conn}}
={}&
\left(\frac{i}{\sqrt Z}\right)^{m+n}
\prod_{a=1}^{m}\int d^4x_a\,e^{ip_a'\cdot x_a}
(\Box_{x_a}+m^2)\\
&\times
\prod_{b=1}^{n}\int d^4y_b\,e^{-ip_b\cdot y_b}
(\Box_{y_b}+m^2)
G_{m+n}^{\mathrm{conn}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}\]
The operators \((\Box+m^2)\) cancel the poles of the external propagators. The external momenta are then placed on shell. In diagram language, one calculates connected amputated diagrams and attaches the appropriate external wave functions.
For fermions, the amputation operators are first order, and external spinors remain. This explains why a fermionic amplitude contains factors such as \(\bar u\Gamma u\).
A field is not a particle. A field is a local operator which can create or destroy particle states. The residue \(Z\) measures the overlap between the chosen field and the one-particle state.


6.2 Tree level and loops
The order in the coupling can often be read from the number of vertices. In \(\phi^4\) theory a graph with \(V\) vertices is proportional to \(\lambda^V\). In Yukawa theory it is proportional to \(g^V\).
Tree level means the lowest loop order, not necessarily low energy. A tree amplitude can be used at high energy when perturbation theory remains valid. Conversely, loops can matter at low energy when a tree contribution is forbidden or strongly suppressed.
Internal lines are off shell in general. They are integration variables inside a correlation function and do not satisfy the classical mass-shell relation at every point. Only external asymptotic particles are required to be on shell.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
7 From amplitudes to observables

7.1 Lorentz-invariant phase space
For a final state containing \(n\) particles, define
\[
d\Phi_n(P;p_1,\ldots,p_n)
=(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}\left(P-\sum_{f=1}^{n}p_f\right)
\prod_{f=1}^{n}
\frac{d^3\mathbf p_f}{(2\pi)^3,2E_f}.
\tag{20}\]
This measure is Lorentz invariant. It combines momentum conservation with the on-shell measure of every final particle.
For a decay of a particle of mass \(M\),
\[
\boxed{d\Gamma=\frac1{2M}|\mathcal M|^2d\Phi_n.}
\tag{21}\]
For a two-body decay in the rest frame,
\[
d\Gamma
=\frac{|\mathbf p^*|}{32\pi^2M^2}
|\mathcal M|^2d\Omega,
\]
and after angular integration, when the amplitude is angle-independent,
\[
\Gamma
=\frac{|\mathbf p^*|}{8\pi M^2}|\mathcal M|^2.
\tag{22}\]
For a scattering process \(1+2\to f\),
\[
d\sigma
=\frac{|mathcal M|^2}{4\sqrt{(p_1\cdot p_2)^2-m_1^2m_2^2}}
d\Phi_n.
\tag{23}\]
For \(2\to2\) scattering in the centre-of-mass frame,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}
=\frac1{64\pi^2s}
\frac{|\mathbf p_f^*|}{|\mathbf p_i^*|}
\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.}
\tag{24}\]
The bar means that initial spins are averaged and final spins are summed. If identical particles occur in the final state, phase space must be divided by the appropriate factorial to avoid counting the same physical configuration more than once.


7.2 Mandelstam variables
For \(1+2\to3+4\),
\[
s=(p_1+p_2)^2,
\qquad
t=(p_1-p_3)^2,
\qquad
u=(p_1-p_4)^2.
\tag{25}\]
On shell,
\[
s+t+u=m_1^2+m_2^2+m_3^2+m_4^2.
\]
\(s\) is the squared centre-of-mass energy. The variables \(t\) and \(u\) measure momentum transfer in the two exchange arrangements. They allow amplitudes to be written in a Lorentz-invariant form.
Crossing symmetry relates processes obtained by moving an external particle from the final state to the initial state and replacing it by the corresponding antiparticle with reversed four-momentum. It is a relation between analytic amplitudes, not simply a rotation of a diagram.


7.3 Spin sums and traces
Unpolarized observables require sums over final spins and averages over initial spins. The completeness relations are
\[
\sum_su_s(p)\bar u_s(p)=\not\!p+m,
\]
\[
\sum_sv_s(p)\bar v_s(p)=\not\!p-m.
\tag{26}\]
They turn products of spinor bilinears into gamma-matrix traces. Useful identities include
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu)=4\eta^{\mu\nu},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Tr}
(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma)
=4\left(
\eta^{\mu\nu}\eta^{\rho\sigma}
-\eta^{\mu\rho}\eta^{\nu\sigma}
+\eta^{\mu\sigma}\eta^{\nu\rho}
\right),
\]
and the trace of an odd number of ordinary gamma matrices vanishes.
For example, if
\[
\mathcal M=g\bar u(p)v(q),
\]
then
\[
\sum_{r,s}|\mathcal M|^2
=g^2\operatorname{Tr}
\left[(\not\!p+m)(\not\!q-m)\right].
\]
The trace can then be reduced to scalar products of four-momenta.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
8 Path-integral formulation

8.1 Generating functional for a scalar field
The same perturbative expansion can be obtained from a functional integral. For a real scalar field,
\[
Z[J]
=\int\mathcal D\phi\,
\exp\!\left\{i\int d^4x
\left[\mathcal L(\phi)+J(x)\phi(x)\right]\right\}.
\tag{27}\]
Correlation functions are generated by functional differentiation:
\[
\langle\Omega|T\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)|\Omega\rangle
=\left.
\frac{1}{i^nZ[0]}
\frac{\delta^nZ[J]}
{\delta J(x_1)\cdots\delta J(x_n)}
\right|_{J=0}.
\tag{28}\]
For the free theory,
\[
Z_0[J]
=Z_0[0]\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2}\int d^4x\,d^4y\,
J(x)\Delta_F(x-y)J(y)
\right],
\tag{29}\]
where \(\Delta_F\) includes the factor \(i\) as in Equation 13. Differentiating twice with respect to \(J\) produces the free two-point function. The inverse of the quadratic kinetic operator is therefore the propagator.
For \(\phi^4\) theory,
\[
Z[J]
=\exp\left[
-i\frac{\lambda}{4!}
\int d^4x
\left(\frac1i\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}\right)^4
\right]Z_0[J].
\tag{30}\]
Expanding the exponential in powers of \(\lambda\) and differentiating reproduces the same vertices, propagators and combinatorial factors as the operator method.


8.2 Fermionic fields
Fermionic path integrals use anticommuting Grassmann variables. With sources \(\eta\) and \(\bar\eta\),
\[
Z_0[\eta,\bar\eta]
=\int\mathcal D\psi\mathcal D\bar\psi\,
\exp\!\left\{i\int d^4x
\left(\bar\psi(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi
+\bar\eta\psi+\bar\psi\eta\right)\right\}.
\]
The Gaussian integral gives
\[
Z_0[\eta,\bar\eta]
=Z_0[0]\exp\left[
-\int d^4x\,d^4y\,
\bar\eta(x)S_F(x-y)\eta(y)
\right].
\]
The order of Grassmann derivatives matters and produces the fermionic signs. Integrating out a fermion also gives a determinant rather than the inverse square root found for an ordinary bosonic Gaussian integral. This is another way to understand the minus sign associated with a closed fermion loop.


8.3 Wick rotation
The Minkowski weight \(e^{iS}\) is oscillatory. Many formal and numerical calculations become easier after the change
\[
t=-i\tau,
\qquad
p^0=ip_E^0.
\]
For a scalar field,
\[
\frac{i}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}
\longrightarrow
\frac{1}{p_E^2+m^2}.
\]
The functional weight becomes approximately \(e^{-S_E}\), similar to a statistical Boltzmann factor. The \(i\epsilon\) prescription tells us how the integration contour is rotated without crossing the poles.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
9 A practical calculation
For a tree-level process, begin by writing the interaction Lagrangian and fixing the sign conventions. Draw all connected diagrams at the required order. Label the external and internal momenta, with momentum conserved at each vertex. Translate each diagram into factors for vertices, propagators and external states, while keeping the order of fermion matrices and spinors. Add diagrams coherently before taking the modulus squared.
The result of this step is \(i\mathcal M\) after the overall delta function has been removed. Then calculate \(\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}\), including spin sums, spin averages and interference terms. Finally insert the invariant phase space and flux factor, and include any factorial required for identical final particles.
Several distinctions prevent common mistakes. External particles are on shell, while internal momenta are generally off shell. A virtual line is a factor in a perturbative correlation function, not a directly observable particle. A symmetry factor belongs to the combinatorics of a diagram, while the factorial for identical final particles belongs to phase space. Diagrams must be added before squaring because their interference is physical.
The full chain is therefore
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}
\longrightarrow S
\longrightarrow\text{Dyson expansion}
\longrightarrow\text{Wick contractions}
\longrightarrow i\mathcal M
\longrightarrow\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}
\longrightarrow d\sigma\ \text{or}\ d\Gamma.
\]
Feynman diagrams are useful because they compress this chain without replacing it. Their rules come from the action, time ordering and field contractions; their physical predictions come only after the amplitude is combined with the correct external states and phase-space factors.

title: Interactions, the S-matrix and Feynman diagrams
text:
10 Further reading
A first treatment can be found in D. Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles. More complete derivations are given in M. Schwartz, Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model, M. Srednicki, Quantum Field Theory, and M. Peskin and D. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory.

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
A mass on a spring keeps moving after it first reaches its equilibrium position. The spring pulls it back, but its velocity carries it past that position. This repeated motion is an oscillation.
We start with this simple model, then add friction, an external force and a second mass. The pendulum will show what changes when the restoring force is no longer proportional to the displacement. Throughout these notes, a dot means a derivative with respect to time: \(\dot x\) is velocity and \(\ddot x\) is acceleration.

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
1 The harmonic oscillator

1.1 From the force to the equation
Consider a mass \(m\) moving horizontally on a frictionless surface, attached to a spring with positive stiffness \(k\). We measure its displacement \(x\) from equilibrium. Within the range where Hooke’s law applies, the spring force is \(F=-kx\). The minus sign means that the force points towards equilibrium. The weight and the normal force cancel vertically, so Newton’s second law gives
\[
m\ddot x=-kx,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
m\ddot x+kx=0.
\tag{1}\]
A similar equation describes many other systems near a stable equilibrium. To see why, consider a force that comes from a potential energy \(V(q)\):
\[
m\ddot q=-\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dq}.
\tag{2}\]
At equilibrium, \(q=q_e\) and \(V'(q_e)=0\). With \(x=q-q_e\), a Taylor expansion gives
\[
V(q_e+x)=V(q_e)+V'(q_e)x
+\frac12V''(q_e)x^2+\frac{1}{3!}V^{(3)}(q_e)x^3+\cdots.
\tag{3}\]
Suppose that \(V''(q_e)>0\). The equilibrium is then a local minimum. For small enough \(x\), we can neglect the higher powers and set \(k_{\mathrm{eff}}=V''(q_e)\):
\[
V(q_e+x)\simeq V(q_e)+\frac12k_{\mathrm{eff}}x^2,
\qquad
F(q_e+x)\simeq-k_{\mathrm{eff}}x.
\tag{4}\]
Thus,
\[
m\ddot x+k_{\mathrm{eff}}x=0.
\tag{5}\]
The effective stiffness measures the curvature of the potential near equilibrium. If \(V''(q_e)=0\), the higher powers must be kept, even for small motion. If \(V''(q_e)<0\), the force pushes the system away from equilibrium and this position is unstable. Below, we write the positive stiffness simply as \(k\).


1.2 Solution and initial conditions
Dividing by \(m\) gives
\[
\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=0,
\qquad
\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}.
\tag{6}\]
The quantity \(\omega_0\) is the natural angular frequency, in radians per second. We look for a solution proportional to \(e^{rt}\). Substitution gives
\[
(r^2+\omega_0^2)e^{rt}=0.
\]
Since the exponential does not vanish, \(r=\pm i\omega_0\). The real solution is therefore
\[
x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0t)+B\sin(\omega_0t).
\]
For \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\dot x(0)=v_0\), we have \(A=x_0\) and \(B=v_0/\omega_0\), hence
\[
x(t)=x_0\cos(\omega_0t)
+\frac{v_0}{\omega_0}\sin(\omega_0t).
\tag{7}\]
We can also write \(x(t)=R\cos(\omega_0t-\varphi)\). Expanding this cosine and comparing the coefficients gives
\[
R=\sqrt{x_0^2+\left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_0}\right)^2},
\qquad
\varphi=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_0},x_0\right).
\tag{8}\]
Here \(\operatorname{atan2}\) chooses the angle in the correct quadrant. The period and the frequency are
\[
T_0=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}},
\qquad
f_0=\frac{1}{T_0}.
\]
A larger mass gives slower motion; a stiffer spring gives faster motion. The period does not depend on the amplitude \(R\). This is called isochronism.


1.3 Energy and phase portrait
Multiplying \(m\ddot x+kx=0\) by \(\dot x\) gives
\[
m\ddot x\dot x+kx\dot x=0.
\]
Each term is a time derivative:
\[
m\ddot x\dot x=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac12m\dot x^2\right),
\qquad
kx\dot x=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac12kx^2\right).
\]
It follows that the mechanical energy is constant:
\[
\frac{\mathrm dE}{\mathrm dt}=0,
\qquad
E=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2.
\tag{9}\]
At the turning points \(x=\pm R\), the velocity is zero and the energy is entirely potential. At equilibrium, the speed is greatest and the energy is entirely kinetic.
A phase portrait plots velocity against position, rather than against time. Since \(E=kR^2/2\), energy conservation gives, for \(R>0\),
\[
\frac{x^2}{R^2}+\frac{\dot x^2}{\omega_0^2R^2}=1.
\tag{10}\]
The trajectory is an ellipse in the \((x,\dot x)\) plane. It runs clockwise: at \((R,0)\), the acceleration is negative, so the velocity becomes negative. When \(R=0\), the mass stays at the origin.






NoteHooke’s law





Hooke published his law of elasticity in 1678. It relates the force exerted by a spring to its extension. Real springs follow this law only over a limited range; the harmonic oscillator is the model obtained within that range.





1.4 Numerical solution
To solve the equation numerically, set \(v=\dot x\). One second-order equation becomes two first-order equations:
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\v\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}v\\-\omega_0^2x\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{11}\]
The function below applies the same method to any equation of the form \(\ddot x=a(t,x,v)\).


Python — general solver
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.figsize": (9, 4.8),
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.25,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "font.size": 11,
})

def resoudre_oscillateur(acceleration, y0, temps, *, args=(), methode="DOP853"):
    """Solve x'' = acceleration(t, x, v, *args)."""
    def systeme(t, y):
        x, v = y
        return (v, acceleration(t, x, v, *args))

    solution = solve_ivp(
        systeme,
        (temps[0], temps[-1]),
        y0,
        t_eval=temps,
        method=methode,
        rtol=1e-10,
        atol=1e-12,
    )
    if not solution.success:
        raise RuntimeError(solution.message)
    return solution.y[0], solution.y[1]


For the harmonic oscillator, we can compare the result with the exact solution. The last graph shows the relative change in energy, \((E-E_0)/E_0\), which would be zero in an exact calculation.


Python code
m, k = 1.5, 6.0
omega0 = np.sqrt(k / m)
x0, v0 = 1.0, 0.65
temps = np.linspace(0.0, 8.0 * 2.0 * np.pi / omega0, 2500)

def acceleration_harmonique(t, x, v, m, k):
    return -(k / m) * x

x, v = resoudre_oscillateur(
    acceleration_harmonique, (x0, v0), temps, args=(m, k)
)
x_exact = x0 * np.cos(omega0 * temps) + (v0 / omega0) * np.sin(omega0 * temps)
energie = 0.5 * m * v**2 + 0.5 * k * x**2
erreur_energie = (energie - energie[0]) / energie[0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6))

axes[0].plot(temps, x, label="numerical solution")
axes[0].plot(temps, x_exact, "--", lw=1.3, label="analytical solution")
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$t$ (s)", ylabel=r"$x(t)$ (m)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)

axes[1].plot(x, v, color="tab:orange")
axes[1].scatter([x[0]], [v[0]], s=35, color="black", zorder=3)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$x$ (m)", ylabel=r"$\dot x$ (m s$^{-1}$)")
axes[1].set_aspect("equal", adjustable="datalim")

axes[2].plot(temps, erreur_energie, color="tab:green")
axes[2].set(xlabel=r"$t$ (s)", ylabel=r"$(E-E_0)/E_0$")
axes[2].ticklabel_format(axis="y", style="sci", scilimits=(0, 0))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Harmonic oscillator: position, phase portrait, and energy check.

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
2 Damping and driving
A real oscillator loses energy through friction. We model this by \(F_f=-b\dot x\), with \(b\geq0\). This force opposes the motion and is proportional to speed. It describes viscous damping; dry sliding friction would require a different model.
We can also apply a periodic force, for example through a motor. With amplitude \(F_0\) and angular frequency \(\Omega\), Newton’s law becomes
\[
m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=F_0\cos(\Omega t).
\tag{12}\]
The frequency \(\Omega\) belongs to the external force; \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) belongs to the mass and spring.

2.1 Free damped motion
First set \(F_0=0\). Introduce the damping rate \(\gamma=b/(2m)\) and the damping ratio \(\zeta=\gamma/\omega_0\). The equation is
\[
\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0.
\tag{13}\]
Trying \(x=e^{rt}\) gives
\[
r^2+2\gamma r+\omega_0^2=0,
\qquad
r_\pm=-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-\omega_0^2}.
\tag{14}\]
For \(0<\gamma<\omega_0\), the roots are complex. This is the underdamped regime. With
\[
\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}
=\omega_0\sqrt{1-\zeta^2},
\tag{15}\]
we obtain \(x=e^{-\gamma t}[A\cos(\omega_dt)+B\sin(\omega_dt)]\). The initial conditions give \(A=x_0\) and \(v_0=-\gamma A+\omega_dB\), so
\[
x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}
\left[
x_0\cos(\omega_dt)
+\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega_d}\sin(\omega_dt)
\right].
\tag{16}\]
The mass still oscillates, but its amplitude decreases with the envelope \(e^{-\gamma t}\). Multiplying the equation by \(m\dot x\) gives
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}
\left(\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2\right)
=-b\dot x^2\leq0.
\tag{17}\]
This is the energy lost to friction per unit time. The phase trajectory spirals towards the origin.
At \(\gamma=\omega_0\), the two roots are equal. This is critical damping, with \(b_c=2\sqrt{km}\). The two independent solutions are \(e^{-\omega_0t}\) and \(te^{-\omega_0t}\). Applying the initial conditions gives
\[
x(t)=e^{-\omega_0t}
\left[x_0+(v_0+\omega_0x_0)t\right].
\tag{18}\]
For \(\gamma>\omega_0\), both roots are real and negative. This is the overdamped regime. With \(\Delta=\sqrt{\gamma^2-\omega_0^2}\) and \(r_\pm=-\gamma\pm\Delta\),
\[
x(t)=C_+e^{r_+t}+C_-e^{r_-t},
\]
where \(C_++C_-=x_0\) and \(r_+C_++r_-C_-=v_0\). Solving these two equations gives
\[
C_+=\frac{v_0-r_-x_0}{r_+-r_-},
\qquad
C_-=\frac{r_+x_0-v_0}{r_+-r_-}.
\tag{19}\]
For a mass released from rest, critical damping gives a faster return than overdamping, without crossing equilibrium. Very strong friction makes the return slow: for \(\gamma\gg\omega_0\), the slow root is \(r_+\simeq-\omega_0^2/(2\gamma)\). With a nonzero initial velocity, even a critically damped mass can cross equilibrium once.


Python code
m, k = 1.0, 1.0
omega0 = np.sqrt(k / m)
temps = np.linspace(0, 18, 2500)
regimes = [(0.20, "underdamped"), (1.00, "critical"), (1.60, "overdamped")]
couleurs = ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))

for (zeta, nom), couleur in zip(regimes, couleurs):
    b = 2 * zeta * np.sqrt(k * m)

    def acceleration_amortie(t, x, v, m, k, b):
        return -(b * v + k * x) / m

    x, v = resoudre_oscillateur(
        acceleration_amortie, (1.0, 0.0), temps, args=(m, k, b)
    )
    axes[0].plot(temps, x, color=couleur, label=rf"{nom}, $\zeta={zeta:.1f}$")
    axes[1].plot(x, v, color=couleur, label=nom)

axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$t$ (s)", ylabel=r"$x(t)/x_0$")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)

axes[1].scatter([1], [0], color="black", s=30, zorder=3)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$x/x_0$", ylabel=r"$\dot x/(\omega_0x_0)$")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: The three regimes of a free damped oscillator and their phase portraits.







2.2 Sinusoidal force
For \(b>0\), the full solution is the sum of a free damped solution and a particular solution:
\[
x(t)=x_{\mathrm{trans}}(t)+x_{\mathrm{perm}}(t).
\]
The first term depends on the initial conditions and tends to zero. The second is the steady response to the force. In the underdamped case, the transient has an envelope \(e^{-\gamma t}\); in the other regimes, its decay follows the real roots found above.
To find the steady response, write the force as the real part of \(F_0e^{i\Omega t}\) and try \(\widetilde x=Xe^{i\Omega t}\). Then
\[
\dot{\widetilde x}=i\Omega Xe^{i\Omega t},
\qquad
\ddot{\widetilde x}=-\Omega^2Xe^{i\Omega t}.
\]
Substitution gives
\[
(k-m\Omega^2+ib\Omega)Xe^{i\Omega t}=F_0e^{i\Omega t},
\]
and therefore
\[
X=\frac{F_0}{k-m\Omega^2+ib\Omega}.
\tag{20}\]
Writing \(X=Ae^{-i\delta}\) and taking the real part gives
\[
x_{\mathrm{perm}}(t)=A(\Omega)\cos(\Omega t-\delta),
\]
with
\[
A(\Omega)=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+(b\Omega)^2}},
\tag{21}\]
and
\[
\delta(\Omega)=\operatorname{atan2}(b\Omega,k-m\Omega^2).
\tag{22}\]
At low frequency, \(A\simeq F_0/k\) and \(\delta\simeq0\): the spring follows the force almost as if it were static. At high frequency, \(A\simeq F_0/(m\Omega^2)\) and \(\delta\simeq\pi\). At \(\Omega=\omega_0\), the displacement lags the force by a quarter of a cycle, \(\delta=\pi/2\).


2.3 Resonance and energy transfer
For \(F_0>0\), the amplitude is largest when the denominator of Equation 21 is smallest. Let
\[
D(\Omega)=(k-m\Omega^2)^2+b^2\Omega^2.
\]
Differentiating,
\[
D'(\Omega)=2\Omega\left[-2m(k-m\Omega^2)+b^2\right].
\]
A peak at a nonzero frequency therefore occurs at
\[
\Omega_r=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2}
=\omega_0\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2},
\tag{23}\]
provided \(0<\zeta<1/\sqrt2\). For larger damping, the displacement amplitude decreases from its value at \(\Omega=0\), with no nonzero-frequency peak. The free oscillation frequency \(\omega_d\), the displacement resonance frequency \(\Omega_r\) and the natural frequency \(\omega_0\) are distinct. They are close when damping is weak.
For the graphs, use \(r=\Omega/\omega_0\) and divide the amplitude by \(F_0/k\):
\[
\frac{A}{F_0/k}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}.
\tag{24}\]


Python code
r = np.linspace(0.0, 2.5, 1600)
zetas = [0.05, 0.20, 0.70]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))

for zeta in zetas:
    gain = 1.0 / np.sqrt((1.0 - r**2)**2 + (2.0 * zeta * r)**2)
    phase = np.arctan2(2.0 * zeta * r, 1.0 - r**2)
    axes[0].plot(r, gain, label=rf"$\zeta={zeta}$")
    axes[1].plot(r, np.degrees(phase), label=rf"$\zeta={zeta}$")

axes[0].set(
    xlabel=r"$r=\Omega/\omega_0$",
    ylabel=r"$A/(F_0/k)$",
    ylim=(0, 11),
)
axes[1].set(
    xlabel=r"$r=\Omega/\omega_0$",
    ylabel=r"phase shift $\delta$ (degrees)",
    yticks=[0, 45, 90, 135, 180],
)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(1.0, color="black", ls="--", lw=0.9, alpha=0.7)
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: Amplitude and phase shift of the driven response for several damping values.





Multiplying Equation 12 by \(\dot x\) gives the power balance \(\dot E=-b\dot x^2+F(t)\dot x\). In steady motion with \(\Omega>0\), the average of \(\dot E\) over one period is zero. Since the average of \(\sin^2(\Omega t-\delta)\) is \(1/2\),
\[
\langle P_{\mathrm{diss}}\rangle
=b\langle\dot x^2\rangle
=\frac12b\Omega^2A^2.
\tag{25}\]
The average power supplied by the force is
\[
\langle P_{\mathrm{ext}}\rangle
=\frac12F_0A\Omega\sin\delta
=\langle P_{\mathrm{diss}}\rangle.
\]
For fixed \(F_0\) and \(b>0\), this power is greatest at \(\Omega=\omega_0\), which differs from the frequency of maximum displacement. The quality factor is
\[
Q=\frac{m\omega_0}{b}=\frac{1}{2\zeta}.
\tag{26}\]
A large \(Q\) means weak damping and a narrow resonance peak. When \(Q\gg1\), the frequency width between the two half-power points is approximately \(\Delta\Omega\simeq\omega_0/Q\). For free weakly damped motion, the energy decreases over many oscillations.


2.4 Without damping: beats and resonance
If \(b=0\), the free part does not decay. For a mass initially at rest at equilibrium and \(\Omega\neq\omega_0\), the solution is
\[
x(t)=\frac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^2-\Omega^2}
\left[\cos(\Omega t)-\cos(\omega_0t)\right].
\]
The difference of cosines can be written as
\[
\cos(\Omega t)-\cos(\omega_0t)
=-2\sin\left(\frac{\Omega+\omega_0}{2}t\right)
\sin\left(\frac{\Omega-\omega_0}{2}t\right).
\]
When the two frequencies are close, the first factor oscillates rapidly and the second varies slowly. The resulting changes in amplitude are called beats. Taking the limit \(\Omega\to\omega_0\) gives
\[
x(t)=\frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0}\,t\sin(\omega_0t).
\]
At exact resonance, the amplitude grows linearly with time in this ideal model. There is no finite steady amplitude.

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
3 Coupled and parametric oscillators

3.1 Two coupled masses
Consider two identical masses \(m\). Each is connected to a fixed support by a spring of stiffness \(k\), and a spring of stiffness \(\kappa\) connects the two masses. Their displacements from equilibrium are \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
The extension of the middle spring is \(x_2-x_1\). It exerts a force \(\kappa(x_2-x_1)\) on the first mass and the opposite force on the second. Newton’s equations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
m\ddot x_1+(k+\kappa)x_1-\kappa x_2&=0,\\
m\ddot x_2+(k+\kappa)x_2-\kappa x_1&=0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}\]
In matrix form,
\[
\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf x}+\mathbf K\mathbf x=0,
\quad
\mathbf M=m\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf K=\begin{pmatrix}k+\kappa&-\kappa\\-\kappa&k+\kappa\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{28}\]
A normal mode is a motion in which the two masses oscillate at one frequency with a fixed ratio of amplitudes. Set \(\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf u\cos(\omega t+\phi)\). We obtain
\[
(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)\mathbf u=0.
\tag{29}\]
For a nonzero vector \(\mathbf u\), the determinant must vanish:
\[
\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)
=(k+\kappa-m\omega^2)^2-\kappa^2=0.
\]
This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_+&=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},
&\mathbf u_+&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\\
\omega_-&=\sqrt{\frac{k+2\kappa}{m}},
&\mathbf u_-&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{30}\]
In the symmetric mode, the masses move together and the middle spring does not stretch. In the antisymmetric mode, they move in opposite directions. The middle spring then adds a restoring force, giving the higher frequency \(\omega_-\).
The normal coordinates are
\[
Q_+=\frac{x_1+x_2}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
Q_-=\frac{x_1-x_2}{\sqrt2}.
\tag{31}\]
Adding and subtracting Newton’s equations gives two independent equations:
\[
\ddot Q_++\omega_+^2Q_+=0,
\qquad
\ddot Q_-+\omega_-^2Q_-=0.
\tag{32}\]
For example, displace only the first mass by \(A\) and release both from rest. Then \(Q_+(0)=Q_-(0)=A/\sqrt2\). Returning to \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1(t)&=\frac A2\left[\cos(\omega_+t)+\cos(\omega_-t)\right],\\
x_2(t)&=\frac A2\left[\cos(\omega_+t)-\cos(\omega_-t)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]


Python code
m, k, kappa = 1.0, 1.0, 0.12
omega_plus = np.sqrt(k / m)
omega_moins = np.sqrt((k + 2 * kappa) / m)
A = 1.0
temps = np.linspace(0, 180, 5000)

# Initial conditions: only the first mass is displaced.
x1 = 0.5 * A * (np.cos(omega_plus * temps) + np.cos(omega_moins * temps))
x2 = 0.5 * A * (np.cos(omega_plus * temps) - np.cos(omega_moins * temps))
Q_plus = (x1 + x2) / np.sqrt(2)
Q_moins = (x1 - x2) / np.sqrt(2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))

axes[0].plot(temps, x1, label=r"$x_1$")
axes[0].plot(temps, x2, label=r"$x_2$", alpha=0.85)
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$t$ (s)", ylabel="displacement")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(temps, Q_plus, label=r"$Q_+$")
axes[1].plot(temps, Q_moins, label=r"$Q_-$")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$t$ (s)", ylabel="normal coordinate")
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4: Exchange of amplitude between two coupled oscillators and decomposition into normal modes.





For weak coupling, the two frequencies are close and beats appear. Energy passes back and forth between the masses through the middle spring. The total energy, including the energy in that spring, remains constant.
For several masses, the same calculation leads to \(\mathbf K\mathbf u_n=\omega_n^2\mathbf M\mathbf u_n\). Each normal coordinate then behaves like a harmonic oscillator.


3.2 A time-dependent stiffness
Energy can also enter a system when one of its parameters changes. Suppose that a device varies the spring stiffness according to
\[
k(t)=k_0[1+h\cos(\Omega t)],
\]
where \(h\) is the relative modulation amplitude. With \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k_0/m}\), the equation becomes
\[
\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x
+\omega_0^2[1+h\cos(\Omega t)]x=0.
\tag{33}\]
This is a damped Mathieu equation. There is no added force on the right-hand side, but the device can still do work. For \(E=m\dot x^2/2+k(t)x^2/2\),
\[
\dot E=-b\dot x^2+\frac12\dot k(t)x^2.
\]
Increasing the stiffness when \(|x|\) is large adds energy. Decreasing it when \(x\) is near zero removes less energy. Since \(x^2\) has two maxima during one oscillation, the main parametric resonance occurs near
\[
\Omega\simeq2\omega_0.
\tag{34}\]
We can estimate the growth rate when \(0<h\ll1\), \(\gamma\ll\omega_0\) and \(\Omega=2\omega_0\). Write
\[
x(t)=a(t)\cos(\omega_0t)+c(t)\sin(\omega_0t),
\]
where \(a\) and \(c\) vary slowly. Neglect their second derivatives and products such as \(\gamma\dot a\). The terms containing \(\cos(2\omega_0t)\) produce frequencies \(\omega_0\) and \(3\omega_0\). Keeping the terms at \(\omega_0\), which drive the slow change, gives
\[
\dot a=-\gamma a-\frac{h\omega_0}{4}c,
\qquad
\dot c=-\gamma c-\frac{h\omega_0}{4}a.
\]
The combination \(a-c\) therefore satisfies
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(a-c)
=\left(\frac{h\omega_0}{4}-\gamma\right)(a-c).
\]
The growing component has an envelope1
\[
R(t)\propto
\exp\left[\left(\frac{h\omega_0}{4}-\gamma\right)t\right].
\tag{35}\]
To this order, growth begins when \(h\omega_0/4>\gamma\). The exact state \(x=\dot x=0\) stays at rest, but a small disturbance with a growing component is amplified. The next example starts with a small nonzero displacement.


Python code
omega0 = 1.0
gamma = 0.02
Omega = 2.0 * omega0
temps = np.linspace(0, 220, 6000)

def acceleration_parametrique(t, x, v, omega0, gamma, h, Omega):
    return -2 * gamma * v - omega0**2 * (1 + h * np.cos(Omega * t)) * x

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
for h, couleur in [(0.05, "tab:blue"), (0.16, "tab:red")]:
    x, v = resoudre_oscillateur(
        acceleration_parametrique,
        (1e-2, 0.0),
        temps,
        args=(omega0, gamma, h, Omega),
    )
    amplitude_instantanee = np.sqrt(x**2 + (v / omega0)**2)
    ax.semilogy(temps, amplitude_instantanee, color=couleur, label=rf"$h={h}$")

ax.set(xlabel=r"$t$", ylabel=r"$\sqrt{x^2+(\dot x/\omega_0)^2}$")
ax.legend(title="modulation")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5: Parametric stability and instability near \(\Omega=2\omega_0\).

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
4 Nonlinear oscillators

4.1 The pendulum
Consider a point mass \(m\) at the end of a rigid, massless rod of length \(\ell\). The pivot is fixed and \(\theta\) is measured from the downward vertical. Gravity gives the torque \(-mg\ell\sin\theta\), while the moment of inertia is \(m\ell^2\). Thus,
\[
m\ell^2\ddot\theta=-mg\ell\sin\theta,
\]
or
\[
\ddot\theta+\frac g\ell\sin\theta=0.
\tag{36}\]
For \(|\theta|\ll1\) in radians,
\[
\sin\theta=\theta-\frac{\theta^3}{6}+\mathcal O(\theta^5).
\]
Keeping the first term gives
\[
\ddot\theta+\omega_0^2\theta=0,
\qquad
\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac g\ell}.
\tag{37}\]
The neglected term is smaller than the linear term by about \(\theta^2/6\). The small-angle approximation is therefore controlled by the angle, not by the mass or the rod length.
Multiplying the exact equation by \(m\ell^2\dot\theta\) gives the conserved energy
\[
E=\frac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+mg\ell(1-\cos\theta).
\tag{38}\]
The top position \(\theta=\pi\) has energy \(E_s=2mg\ell\). For \(0<E<E_s\), the pendulum swings between two turning points; this motion is called libration. For \(E>E_s\), it can pass over the top and keep rotating. At \(E=E_s\), a moving pendulum approaches the top only as \(t\to\infty\). This limiting trajectory is the separatrix.


4.2 Why the period increases with amplitude
Release the pendulum from rest at an angle \(0<\theta_{\max}<\pi\). Energy conservation gives
\[
\frac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2
=mg\ell(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_{\max}),
\]
so
\[
|\dot\theta|
=\sqrt{\frac{2g}{\ell}(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_{\max})}.
\]
A quarter of a period is the time taken to travel from \(0\) to \(\theta_{\max}\). Therefore,
\[
\frac T4=\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{2g}}
\int_0^{\theta_{\max}}
\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_{\max}}}.
\]
Use \(\sin(\theta/2)=\sin(\theta_{\max}/2)\sin\phi\). The limits become \(0\) and \(\pi/2\), giving
\[
T(\theta_{\max})
=4\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}\,
K\left(\sin^2\frac{\theta_{\max}}2\right),
\tag{39}\]
where
\[
K(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\mathrm d\phi}{\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\phi}}.
\]
This integral is called the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Expanding its integrand in powers of \(p\) gives
\[
K(p)=\frac\pi2
\left(1+\frac p4+\frac{9p^2}{64}+\cdots\right).
\]
Using \(p=\sin^2(\theta_{\max}/2)\) then gives, with the angle in radians,
\[
T(\theta_{\max})
=T_0\left[
1+\frac{\theta_{\max}^2}{16}
+\frac{11\theta_{\max}^4}{3072}
+\mathcal O(\theta_{\max}^6)
\right],
\qquad
T_0=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}.
\tag{40}\]
The period increases with amplitude. As \(\theta_{\max}\to\pi\), the pendulum spends longer near the unstable top position and the period diverges.


Python code
g, ell = 9.81, 1.0
omega0 = np.sqrt(g / ell)
T0 = 2 * np.pi / omega0
temps = np.linspace(0, 6 * T0, 3000)
angles_deg = [10, 60, 120]
couleurs = ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:red"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))

for angle_deg, couleur in zip(angles_deg, couleurs):
    theta0 = np.radians(angle_deg)

    def acceleration_pendule(t, theta, omega, g, ell):
        return -(g / ell) * np.sin(theta)

    theta, omega = resoudre_oscillateur(
        acceleration_pendule, (theta0, 0.0), temps, args=(g, ell)
    )
    theta_lineaire = theta0 * np.cos(omega0 * temps)

    axes[0].plot(temps / T0, np.degrees(theta), color=couleur,
                 label=rf"exact, $\theta_0={angle_deg}^\circ$")
    axes[0].plot(temps / T0, np.degrees(theta_lineaire), "--",
                 color=couleur, alpha=0.55)
    axes[1].plot(theta, omega, color=couleur, label=rf"${angle_deg}^\circ$")

axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$t/T_0$", ylabel=r"$\theta$ (degrees)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, ncol=1)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$\theta$ (rad)", ylabel=r"$\dot\theta$ (rad s$^{-1}$)")
axes[1].legend(title="amplitude")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: Difference between the exact pendulum and the harmonic approximation as the amplitude increases.





The dashed curves use the small-angle approximation. At large amplitude, the exact pendulum has a longer period, so the two solutions gradually move out of phase.


4.3 The Duffing oscillator
A spring may become harder or softer to stretch as its displacement increases. If the force is symmetric about equilibrium, \(F(-x)=-F(x)\), its expansion contains odd powers of \(x\). Keeping the first nonlinear term gives \(F=-kx-\alpha x^3\). With damping and driving,
\[
m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx+\alpha x^3
=F_0\cos(\Omega t).
\tag{41}\]
This is the Duffing equation. Without damping or driving, its potential energy is
\[
V(x)=\frac12kx^2+\frac14\alpha x^4.
\tag{42}\]
For \(k>0\) and \(\alpha>0\), the restoring force grows faster than in the harmonic model, so the oscillation frequency increases with amplitude. For \(\alpha<0\), it decreases for small enough amplitudes. The latter model is only local: the negative quartic term cannot describe a stable system at arbitrarily large \(|x|\).
Another case is \(k<0\) and \(\alpha>0\). Solving \(V'(x)=x(k+\alpha x^2)=0\) gives
\[
x=0,
\qquad
x=\pm\sqrt{-\frac{k}{\alpha}}.
\]
Since \(V''(0)=k<0\) and \(V''(\pm\sqrt{-k/\alpha})=-2k>0\), the origin is unstable and the other two positions are stable. This double-well model can describe a bent strip that can move between two stable shapes.
The following example uses the dimensionless equation \(x''+\delta x'-x+x^3=f\cos(\Omega t)\). With driving, the motion can cross between the wells and become irregular. We plot both \(x(t)\) and a Poincaré section: one point \((x,\dot x)\) is taken at each driving period \(T=2\pi/\Omega\), after the initial transient.


Python code
# Dimensionless equation: x'' + delta*x' - x + x^3 = f*cos(Omega*t)
delta, f, Omega = 0.20, 0.30, 1.20
periode = 2 * np.pi / Omega
n_periodes = 550
points_par_periode = 90
temps = np.linspace(0, n_periodes * periode,
                    n_periodes * points_par_periode + 1)

def acceleration_duffing(t, x, v, delta, f, Omega):
    return -delta * v + x - x**3 + f * np.cos(Omega * t)

x, v = resoudre_oscillateur(
    acceleration_duffing, (0.1, 0.0), temps, args=(delta, f, Omega)
)

# Remove the transient and take one point per period.
indices_poincare = np.arange(150, n_periodes + 1) * points_par_periode
masque_fin = temps > (n_periodes - 25) * periode

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
axes[0].plot(temps[masque_fin] / periode, x[masque_fin], lw=0.9)
axes[0].set(xlabel="number of periods", ylabel=r"$x(t)$")

axes[1].scatter(x[indices_poincare], v[indices_poincare], s=9, alpha=0.65)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$x(nT)$", ylabel=r"$\dot x(nT)$")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7: Double-well Duffing oscillator: late-time motion and Poincaré section.





A response that repeats after one driving period gives one point in this section. A response that repeats after several periods gives several points. A more complex set can occur in chaotic motion, where nearby initial states separate rapidly. The section alone is not a proof of chaos; that requires a separate stability study.


4.4 Energy balance
For a fixed potential \(V(x)\), the models above can be written as
\[
m\ddot x+b\dot x+\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dx}
=F_{\mathrm{ext}}(x,t).
\tag{43}\]
Multiplication by \(\dot x\) gives
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}
\left(\frac12m\dot x^2+V(x)\right)
=-b\dot x^2+F_{\mathrm{ext}}(x,t)\dot x.
\tag{44}\]
Friction removes energy, while the external force can add or remove it depending on its direction relative to the velocity. For a time-dependent potential, an additional term \(\partial V/\partial t\) appears, as in the parametric oscillator.

title: Newtonian oscillators
text:
5 Numerical methods

5.1 State variables and scales
The general equation becomes
\[
\dot x=v,
\qquad
\dot v=\frac1m\left[F_{\mathrm{ext}}(x,t)-bv-V'(x)\right].
\tag{45}\]
This is the system used by the Python function at the beginning of the chapter.
For the driven linear oscillator with \(F_0>0\), choose \(\tau=\omega_0t\) and \(x_s=F_0/k\), then set \(X=x/x_s\). Since \(\dot x=x_s\omega_0X'\) and \(\ddot x=x_s\omega_0^2X''\), division by \(kx_s=F_0\) gives
\[
X''+2\zeta X'+X=\cos(r\tau),
\qquad
r=\frac{\Omega}{\omega_0}.
\tag{46}\]
Primes now mean derivatives with respect to \(\tau\). In these units, the response depends only on \(\zeta\) and \(r\), together with the initial conditions. If \(F_0=0\), a nonzero initial amplitude can provide the length scale instead.


5.2 Velocity Verlet
The Python figures use an adaptive Runge–Kutta method. For a conservative force depending only on position, velocity Verlet is another useful choice. With \(a_n=F(x_n)/m\) and a fixed time step \(\Delta t\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1}&=x_n+v_n\Delta t+\frac12a_n\Delta t^2,\\
a_{n+1}&=\frac{F(x_{n+1})}{m},\\
v_{n+1}&=v_n+\frac12(a_n+a_{n+1})\Delta t.
\end{aligned}
\]
The position step uses the current acceleration; the velocity step uses the average of the old and new accelerations. This method does not conserve the energy exactly, but with a suitably small step it often keeps the energy error bounded over long integrations.


Python — velocity Verlet
def verlet_vitesse(force, x0, v0, temps, m=1.0):
    """Symplectic integration of m*x'' = force(x), on a uniform grid."""
    temps = np.asarray(temps)
    dt = temps[1] - temps[0]
    if not np.allclose(np.diff(temps), dt):
        raise ValueError("The time grid must be uniform.")

    x = np.empty_like(temps, dtype=float)
    v = np.empty_like(temps, dtype=float)
    x[0], v[0] = x0, v0
    a = force(x[0]) / m

    for n in range(len(temps) - 1):
        x[n + 1] = x[n] + v[n] * dt + 0.5 * a * dt**2
        a_suivante = force(x[n + 1]) / m
        v[n + 1] = v[n] + 0.5 * (a + a_suivante) * dt
        a = a_suivante

    return x, v


For a harmonic oscillator, compare the numerical result with Equation 7. For a nonlinear conservative system, check the energy and repeat the calculation with a smaller time step. These comparisons tell us whether a visible change comes from the physics or from the numerical method.
