title: Riemannian geometry
text:
1 Manifolds and tangent spaces
A smooth manifold of dimension \(n\) is a space which locally looks like \(\mathbb R^n\). A coordinate chart is a map
\[
x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n):U\subset M\longrightarrow x(U)\subset\mathbb R^n
\]
whose transition maps are smooth. Coordinates are only local labels. A coordinate singularity does not necessarily mean that the geometry itself is singular.
At a point \(p\), the tangent space \(T_pM\) is an \(n\)-dimensional vector space. In a chart its natural basis is
\[
\partial_i=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}.
\]
The dual basis of the cotangent space \(T_p^*M\) is denoted by \(dx^i\) and satisfies
\[
dx^i(\partial_j)=\delta^i{}_j.
\]
A vector and a one-form are written
\[
X=X^i\partial_i,
\qquad
\alpha=\alpha_i\,dx^i.
\]
Their pairing, \(\alpha(X)=\alpha_iX^i\), is independent of the chosen coordinates.

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
2 The Riemannian metric
A Riemannian metric assigns a scalar product to every tangent space. In coordinates,
\[
g=g_{ij}\,dx^i\otimes dx^j,
\qquad
g_{ij}=g_{ji},
\]
and the matrix \((g_{ij})\) is positive definite. Its inverse satisfies
\[
g^{ik}g_{kj}=\delta^i{}_j.
\]
The line element is
\[
ds^2=g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j.
\]
For a curve \(\gamma(t)\), its length and energy are
\[
L(\gamma)=\int_a^b
\sqrt{g_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j}\,dt,
\]
\[
E(\gamma)=\frac12\int_a^b
g_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j\,dt.
\]
The Riemannian volume form on an oriented manifold is
\[
dV_g=\sqrt{|g|}\,dx^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^n,
\qquad
|g|=\det(g_{ij}).
\tag{1}\]
For example, the Euclidean plane in polar coordinates has
\[
ds^2=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2.
\]
The sphere of radius \(R\) has
\[
ds^2=R^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2),
\]
and the Poincaré half-plane has
\[
ds^2=\frac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2},
\qquad y>0.
\]

2.1 Gradient, divergence and Laplacian
The gradient of a function \(f\) is defined by
\[
g(\operatorname{grad}f,X)=df(X).
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{grad}f
=g^{ij}(\partial_jf)\partial_i.
\]
The divergence of a vector field and the Laplace–Beltrami operator are
\[
\operatorname{div}X
=\frac1{\sqrt{|g|}}
\partial_i\left(\sqrt{|g|}X^i\right),
\tag{2}\]
\[
\boxed{
\Delta_gf
=\frac1{\sqrt{|g|}}
\partial_i\left(\sqrt{|g|}g^{ij}\partial_jf\right).}
\tag{3}\]
With this sign convention, \(\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2\) in Euclidean space.

title: Riemannian geometry
Riemannian geometry
text:
4 Geodesics
A geodesic has a velocity vector which is parallel along the curve:
\[
\frac{D\dot\gamma}{dt}=0.
\]
In coordinates,
\[
\boxed{
\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j=0.}
\tag{6}\]
An affine parameter gives constant speed. Geodesics are stationary points of the energy functional and locally minimize length over sufficiently short intervals.
The exponential map is defined by
\[
\exp_p(v)=\gamma_v(1),
\]
where \(\gamma_v(0)=p\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\). A connected manifold is geodesically complete if every geodesic can be extended for all real parameter values. The Hopf–Rinow theorem relates this property to completeness of the metric distance.

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
5 Curvature
Our sign convention for the Riemann tensor is
\[
R(X,Y)Z
=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.
\]
Its coordinate components are
\[
R^\ell{}_{kij}
=\partial_i\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}
-\partial_j\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik}
+\Gamma^m{}_{jk}\Gamma^\ell{}_{im}
-\Gamma^m{}_{ik}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jm}.
\tag{7}\]
For two independent vectors \(X,Y\), the sectional curvature is
\[
K(X,Y)
=\frac{g(R(X,Y)Y,X)}
{g(X,X)g(Y,Y)-g(X,Y)^2}.
\]
The Ricci tensor and scalar curvature are contractions of the Riemann tensor:
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=R^k{}_{ikj},
\qquad
S=g^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}.
\]
In dimension two, the Riemann tensor is completely determined by the Gaussian curvature \(K\), and
\[
S=2K.
\]
Euclidean space has \(K=0\), a sphere of radius \(R\) has \(K=1/R^2\), and hyperbolic space of radius \(R\) has \(K=-1/R^2\).






NoteRiemann’s idea of intrinsic geometry





In 1854, Bernhard Riemann proposed that geometry could be defined from measurements made inside a space, without referring to an external Euclidean space. The metric and its curvature make this idea precise: inhabitants of a surface can detect its curvature using distances, angles and geodesics alone.

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
6 Coordinate exercises
The stars indicate the difficulty. Each solution is folded so that the question can be attempted first.

6.1 Exercise 1 — Polar coordinates
Let
\[
F(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta),
\qquad r>0.
\]
Find the Jacobian, the natural basis and the Euclidean metric. Explain why polar coordinates fail at \(r=0\) and why the angular interval must be restricted.






NoteSolution





The Jacobian matrix and its determinant are
\[
DF=\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta&r\cos\theta
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det DF=r.
\]
The basis vectors are
\[
e_r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),
\qquad
e_\theta=(-r\sin\theta,r\cos\theta).
\]
They are orthogonal, with norms \(1\) and \(r\), so
\[
ds^2=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2.
\]
At \(r=0\), the Jacobian vanishes and every angle represents the same point. For \(r>0\), \(\theta\) and \(\theta+2\pi\) also represent the same point, so one chooses an open angular interval and removes a ray if needed.





6.2 Exercise 2 — Cylindrical coordinates
In \(\mathbb R^3\), let
\[
F(\rho,\varphi,z)=(\rho\cos\varphi,\rho\sin\varphi,z).
\]
Describe the coordinate surfaces and calculate the natural basis, metric and volume element.






NoteSolution





\(\rho=\rho_0\) gives a cylinder, \(\varphi=\varphi_0\) a half-plane and \(z=z_0\) a horizontal plane. The basis is
\[
e_\rho=(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi,0),
\quad
e_\varphi=(-\rho\sin\varphi,\rho\cos\varphi,0),
\quad
e_z=(0,0,1).
\]
Thus
\[
ds^2=d\rho^2+\rho^2d\varphi^2+dz^2,
\qquad
dV=\rho\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,dz.
\]





6.3 Exercise 3 — Parabolic coordinates
Consider
\[
x=\frac12(u^2-v^2),
\qquad
y=uv.
\]
Show that the coordinate curves are parabolas. Find the Jacobian and metric, then express \(u^2\) and \(v^2\) in terms of \(x,y\).






NoteSolution





For fixed \(u=u_0\),
\[
x=\frac{u_0^2}{2}-\frac{y^2}{2u_0^2},
\]
and a similar calculation for fixed \(v\) gives the second family of parabolas. The basis vectors are
\[
e_u=(u,v),
\qquad
e_v=(-v,u).
\]
Their determinant is \(u^2+v^2\), and they are orthogonal. Therefore
\[
ds^2=(u^2+v^2)(du^2+dv^2).
\]
If \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), then
\[
u^2=r+x,
\qquad
v^2=r-x.
\]
The signs must still be chosen so that \(uv=y\); the inverse is only local.





6.4 Exercise 4 — A helix
The curve
\[
\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,t),
\qquad 0\leq t\leq2\pi,
\]
is given in Cartesian coordinates. Express it in cylindrical and spherical coordinates, then calculate its length.






NoteSolution





In cylindrical coordinates,
\[
\rho=1,
\qquad
\varphi=t,
\qquad
z=t.
\]
In spherical coordinates with colatitude \(\theta\),
\[
r=\sqrt{1+t^2},
\qquad
\varphi=t,
\qquad
\theta=\arccos\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}.
\]
Since \(\dot\gamma=(-\sin t,\cos t,1)\), its speed is \(\sqrt2\) and
\[
L=2\pi\sqrt2.
\]





6.5 Exercise 5 — Stereographic projection
Project the unit sphere without its north pole onto the plane \(z=0\). Derive the direct and inverse maps, then find the spherical metric in the projected coordinates \((X,Y)\).






NoteSolution





The line through the north pole and \((x,y,z)\) gives
\[
X=\frac{x}{1-z},
\qquad
Y=\frac{y}{1-z}.
\]
With \(R^2=X^2+Y^2\), the inverse is
\[
x=\frac{2X}{1+R^2},
\quad
y=\frac{2Y}{1+R^2},
\quad
z=\frac{R^2-1}{1+R^2}.
\]
Differentiation gives
\[
g=\frac{4}{(1+X^2+Y^2)^2}(dX^2+dY^2).
\]
The projection is conformal: it preserves angles but not lengths. Two such charts, from opposite poles, cover the sphere.

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
7 Metric and measure exercises

7.1 Exercise 6 — A metric with a cross term
For
\[
ds^2=2(du^2+du\,dv+dv^2),
\]
find \((g_{ij})\) and its inverse. Use \(x=(u+v)/\sqrt2\), \(y=(u-v)/\sqrt2\) to diagonalize the metric.






NoteSolution





Because the cross term is \(2g_{uv}du\,dv\),
\[
(g_{ij})=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(g^{ij})=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The coordinates are not orthogonal. Substitution gives
\[
ds^2=3dx^2+dy^2.
\]
With \(X=\sqrt3x\) and \(Y=y\), this becomes \(ds^2=dX^2+dY^2\).





7.2 Exercise 7 — Metric and area of a sphere
For
\[
F(\theta,\varphi)
=R(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta),
\]
calculate the induced metric, area element and total area.






NoteSolution





The tangent vectors are orthogonal and have norms \(R\) and \(R\sin\theta\). Hence
\[
ds^2=R^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2),
\]
\[
dA=R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi.
\]
Integrating over \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi\) and \(0\leq\varphi<2\pi\) gives
\[
\operatorname{Area}(S_R^2)=4\pi R^2.
\]





7.3 Exercise 8 — Geometry of a torus
For \(R>a>0\), consider
\[
F(\theta,\varphi)
=((R+a\cos\theta)\cos\varphi,
(R+a\cos\theta)\sin\varphi,a\sin\theta).
\]
Find the induced metric, surface area and enclosed volume.






NoteSolution





The tangent vectors are orthogonal, with norms \(a\) and \(R+a\cos\theta\). Thus
\[
ds^2=a^2d\theta^2+(R+a\cos\theta)^2d\varphi^2,
\]
\[
dA=a(R+a\cos\theta)\,d\theta\,d\varphi,
\qquad
A=4\pi^2Ra.
\]
Replacing \(a\) by \(0\leq\rho\leq a\) gives
\[
dV=\rho(R+\rho\cos\theta)\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\varphi,
\]
and therefore
\[
V=2\pi^2Ra^2.
\]





7.4 Exercise 9 — Conformal change of metric
Let
\[
g=e^{2\sigma(x,y)}(dx^2+dy^2).
\]
Find the inverse metric and area element. Show that angles are unchanged and determine the local scale factors for lengths and areas.






NoteSolution





We have
\[
g_{ij}=e^{2\sigma}\delta_{ij},
\qquad
g^{ij}=e^{-2\sigma}\delta^{ij},
\qquad
dA_g=e^{2\sigma}dx\,dy.
\]
The factor \(e^{2\sigma}\) cancels in the cosine formula for an angle. Infinitesimal lengths are multiplied by \(e^\sigma\) and areas by \(e^{2\sigma}\).





7.5 Exercise 10 — Radial metrics
For
\[
g=dr^2+f(r)^2d\theta^2,
\]
find the circumference of \(r=r_0\) and the area of \(0\leq r\leq r_0\). Apply the result to \(f(r)=r\), \(R\sin(r/R)\) and \(R\sinh(r/R)\).






NoteSolution





Directly from the metric,
\[
L(r_0)=2\pi f(r_0),
\qquad
A(r_0)=2\pi\int_0^{r_0}f(r)\,dr.
\]
For the plane,
\[
L=2\pi r_0,
\qquad A=\pi r_0^2.
\]
For the sphere,
\[
L=2\pi R\sin(r_0/R),
\quad
A=2\pi R^2[1-\cos(r_0/R)].
\]
For the hyperbolic plane,
\[
L=2\pi R\sinh(r_0/R),
\quad
A=2\pi R^2[\cosh(r_0/R)-1].
\]





7.6 Exercise 11 — Mercator projection
On a sphere, use latitude \(\lambda\) and longitude \(\varphi\):
\[
g=R^2(d\lambda^2+\cos^2\lambda\,d\varphi^2).
\]
Set \(x=\varphi\) and find \(y(\lambda)\) such that the metric is conformal to \(dx^2+dy^2\).






NoteSolution





Equal coefficients require
\[
\frac{dy}{d\lambda}=\frac1{\cos\lambda}.
\]
Hence one may choose
\[
y=\log\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\lambda2\right).
\]
Since \(\cos\lambda=\operatorname{sech}y\),
\[
g=R^2\operatorname{sech}^2y\,(dx^2+dy^2).
\]
The map preserves angles, but distances and areas are distorted, and the poles are sent to \(y=\pm\infty\).

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
8 Differential-operator exercises

8.1 Exercise 12 — Gradient in polar coordinates
For the Euclidean polar metric and
\[
f(r,\theta)=r^2\cos(2\theta),
\]
find \(\operatorname{grad}f\) and its squared norm. Check the answer in Cartesian coordinates.






NoteSolution





Using \(g^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(1,r^{-2})\),
\[
\operatorname{grad}f
=2r\cos(2\theta)\partial_r
-2\sin(2\theta)\partial_\theta.
\]
Since \(f=x^2-y^2\), the Cartesian result is \(2x\partial_x-2y\partial_y\). Finally,
\[
\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2=4r^2.
\]





8.2 Exercise 13 — Divergence and flux
On the punctured plane, let \(X=r\partial_r\). Find its divergence and verify the divergence theorem on the disk \(D_R\). Generalize to \(X_p=r^p\partial_r\).






NoteSolution





Since \(\sqrt{|g|}=r\),
\[
\operatorname{div}X=\frac1r\partial_r(r^2)=2.
\]
Thus
\[
\int_{D_R}\operatorname{div}X\,dA=2\pi R^2.
\]
On the boundary, \(n=\partial_r\) and \(ds=R\,d\theta\), so the flux is also \(2\pi R^2\). More generally,
\[
\operatorname{div}(r^p\partial_r)=(p+1)r^{p-1}.
\]





8.3 Exercise 14 — Laplacian on the sphere
Derive the Laplace–Beltrami operator on \(S_R^2\) and apply it to \(f=\cos\theta\).






NoteSolution





Using Equation 3,
\[
\Delta f
=\frac1{R^2\sin\theta}
\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f)
+\frac1{R^2\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2f.
\]
For \(f=\cos\theta\),
\[
\Delta f=-\frac2{R^2}f.
\]
Since \(f=z/R\), it is the restriction of a Cartesian coordinate and is a spherical harmonic of degree one.





8.4 Exercise 15 — Radial harmonic functions
For \(u(x)=U(r)\) in \(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\), show that
\[
\Delta u=U''+\frac{n-1}{r}U'.
\]
Solve \(\Delta u=0\) for \(n=2\) and \(n\geq3\).






NoteSolution





The radial part of the Euclidean volume contains \(r^{n-1}\), hence
\[
\Delta u=\frac1{r^{n-1}}\frac d{dr}
\left(r^{n-1}U'\right).
\]
Therefore \(r^{n-1}U'=C\). The solutions are
\[
U=A+B\log r
\quad(n=2),
\]
and
\[
U=A+Br^{2-n}
\quad(n\geq3).
\]
The non-constant solutions are singular at the origin and are not smooth harmonic functions on all of \(\mathbb R^n\).





8.5 Exercise 16 — Green’s identity
Let \((M,g)\) be compact, connected and without boundary. Prove
\[
\int_Mf\Delta f\,dV_g
=-\int_M\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2dV_g,
\]
and deduce that every harmonic function on \(M\) is constant.






NoteSolution





The product rule gives
\[
\operatorname{div}(f\operatorname{grad}f)
=\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2+f\Delta f.
\]
Its integral is zero because \(M\) has no boundary. This proves the identity. If \(\Delta f=0\), then the integral of \(\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2\) vanishes, so \(\operatorname{grad}f=0\). Connectedness makes \(f\) constant.
With a boundary, one adds
\[
\int_{\partial M}f\,\partial_nf\,dA_g.
\]

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
9 Connection exercises

9.1 Exercise 17 — Christoffel symbols in polar coordinates
Find all non-zero Christoffel symbols for
\[
g=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2.
\]
Write the covariant derivatives of the coordinate basis and explain why the plane can still be flat.






NoteSolution





The only non-zero metric derivative is \(\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=2r\). Thus
\[
\Gamma^r{}_{\theta\theta}=-r,
\qquad
\Gamma^\theta{}_{r\theta}
=\Gamma^\theta{}_{\theta r}=\frac1r.
\]
Therefore
\[
\nabla_{\partial_r}\partial_\theta
=\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_r
=\frac1r\partial_\theta,
\qquad
\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta=-r\partial_r.
\]
These coefficients describe the variation of the polar basis. Curvature is tensorial and remains zero.





9.2 Exercise 18 — Christoffel symbols on the sphere
For the spherical metric, find the non-zero Christoffel symbols. Determine which regular curves with constant \(\theta\) are geodesics.






NoteSolution





The non-zero symbols are
\[
\Gamma^\theta{}_{\varphi\varphi}
=-\sin\theta\cos\theta,
\]
\[
\Gamma^\varphi{}_{\theta\varphi}
=\Gamma^\varphi{}_{\varphi\theta}=\cot\theta.
\]
For constant \(\theta=\theta_0\), the first geodesic equation requires
\[
\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0=0.
\]
The polar cases are degenerate, so the only regular parallel which is a geodesic is the equator, \(\theta_0=\pi/2\).





9.3 Exercise 19 — A conformal metric
For \(g_{ij}=e^{2\sigma}\delta_{ij}\), show that
\[
\Gamma^k{}_{ij}
=\delta^k{}_j\partial_i\sigma
+\delta^k{}_i\partial_j\sigma
-\delta_{ij}\delta^{k\ell}\partial_\ell\sigma.
\]
Apply this formula to the Poincaré half-plane.






NoteSolution





Insert \(g^{ij}=e^{-2\sigma}\delta^{ij}\) and
\[
\partial_i g_{j\ell}
=2e^{2\sigma}(\partial_i\sigma)\delta_{j\ell}
\]
into Equation 4. For \(\sigma=-\log y\), the non-zero symbols are
\[
\Gamma^x{}_{xy}=\Gamma^x{}_{yx}=-\frac1y,
\]
\[
\Gamma^y{}_{xx}=\frac1y,
\qquad
\Gamma^y{}_{yy}=-\frac1y.
\]





9.4 Exercise 20 — Uniqueness of the Levi–Civita connection
Let \(\nabla\) and \(\widetilde\nabla\) be torsion-free and compatible with the same metric. Set
\[
A(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\widetilde\nabla_XY,
\qquad
B(X,Y,Z)=g(A(X,Y),Z).
\]
Prove that the two connections are equal.






NoteSolution





The difference of two connections is tensorial. The torsion-free condition gives
\[
B(X,Y,Z)=B(Y,X,Z),
\]
while metric compatibility gives
\[
B(X,Y,Z)=-B(X,Z,Y).
\]
Applying these two symmetries repeatedly yields
\[
B(X,Y,Z)=-B(X,Y,Z),
\]
so \(B=0\). Since the metric is non-degenerate, \(A=0\) and
\[
\nabla=\widetilde\nabla.
\]





9.5 Exercise 21 — Christoffel symbols are not a tensor
Compare the Euclidean connection in Cartesian and polar coordinates. Use the transformation law to identify the non-tensorial term.






NoteSolution





The Cartesian Christoffel symbols vanish, while in polar coordinates
\[
\Gamma^r{}_{\theta\theta}=-r,
\qquad
\Gamma^\theta{}_{r\theta}=\frac1r.
\]
A tensor which vanishes in one chart vanishes in every chart. The connection law contains the additional term
\[
\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^k}
\frac{\partial^2x^k}{\partial y^b\partial y^c},
\]
which prevents tensoriality. This term cancels in the difference between two connections.





9.6 Exercise 22 — Contracted Christoffel symbol
Show that
\[
\Gamma^i{}_{ik}=\partial_k\log\sqrt{|g|},
\]
and deduce the coordinate formula for the divergence.






NoteSolution





Contracting Equation 4 and exchanging dummy indices gives
\[
\Gamma^i{}_{ik}=\frac12g^{i\ell}\partial_k g_{i\ell}.
\]
Jacobi’s determinant formula gives
\[
\partial_k\log|g|=g^{i\ell}\partial_k g_{i\ell}.
\]
Hence
\[
\Gamma^i{}_{ik}=\partial_k\log\sqrt{|g|}.
\]
Using \(\nabla_iX^i=\partial_iX^i+\Gamma^i{}_{ik}X^k\) gives Equation 2.

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
10 Geodesic exercises

10.1 Exercise 23 — Plane geodesics in polar coordinates
Derive the polar geodesic equations, show that \(r^2\dot\theta\) is constant, and decide whether radial lines and circles are geodesics.






NoteSolution





Using Exercise 17 in Equation 6 gives
\[
\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2=0,
\qquad
\ddot\theta+\frac2r\dot r\dot\theta=0.
\]
The second equation is equivalent to
\[
\frac d{dt}(r^2\dot\theta)=0.
\]
If \(\theta\) is constant, \(\ddot r=0\), so radial lines at constant speed are geodesics. If \(r=r_0>0\), the first equation forces \(\dot\theta=0\); non-trivial circles are not geodesics.





10.2 Exercise 24 — Geodesics of the sphere
Let \(\gamma(t)\in S_R^2\) be a constant-speed geodesic. Show that
\[
\ddot\gamma=-\frac{v^2}{R^2}\gamma
\]
and deduce that non-constant geodesics are great circles.






NoteSolution





The tangential part of \(\ddot\gamma\) vanishes, so \(\ddot\gamma\) is parallel to the normal vector \(\gamma\). Differentiating \(\gamma\cdot\gamma=R^2\) twice gives
\[
v^2+\gamma\cdot\ddot\gamma=0.
\]
Thus the stated equation follows. If \(p=\gamma(0)\) and \(w=\dot\gamma(0)\),
\[
\gamma(t)=
\cos\left(\frac{vt}{R}\right)p
+\frac Rv\sin\left(\frac{vt}{R}\right)w.
\]
The curve stays in the plane spanned by \(p\) and \(w\), whose intersection with the sphere is a great circle.





10.3 Exercise 25 — Hyperbolic geodesics
For
\[
g=\frac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2},
\]
find the unit-speed geodesics and show that the boundary \(y=0\) is infinitely far away.






NoteSolution





The geodesic Lagrangian is
\[
L=\frac{\dot x^2+\dot y^2}{2y^2}.
\]
Since \(x\) is cyclic,
\[
\frac{\dot x}{y^2}=c.
\]
Unit speed gives \(\dot x^2+\dot y^2=y^2\). If \(c=0\), the geodesics are vertical lines. Otherwise integration gives
\[
(x-a)^2+y^2=\frac1{c^2}.
\]
They are semicircles orthogonal to the boundary. Along a vertical line,
\[
\int_\varepsilon^{y_0}\frac{dy}{y}
=\log\frac{y_0}{\varepsilon}\to\infty,
\]
so the boundary lies at infinite distance.





10.4 Exercise 26 — Energy and length
For a regular curve \(\gamma:[a,b]\to M\), prove
\[
L(\gamma)^2\leq2(b-a)E(\gamma),
\]
and determine the equality case.






NoteSolution





Let \(v(t)=\|\dot\gamma(t)\|\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\[
\left(\int_a^bv\,dt\right)^2
\leq(b-a)\int_a^bv^2dt
=2(b-a)E.
\]
Equality holds exactly when the speed is constant. Length is unchanged by an increasing reparametrization, while energy usually changes because it contains the square of the speed.





10.5 Exercise 27 — Clairaut’s relation
A surface of revolution has metric
\[
g=du^2+f(u)^2dv^2.
\]
For a unit-speed geodesic, show that
\[
f(u)\sin\alpha=\text{constant},
\]
where \(\alpha\) is the angle with a meridian.






NoteSolution





The coordinate \(v\) is cyclic in
\[
L=\frac12(\dot u^2+f(u)^2\dot v^2),
\]
so \(f(u)^2\dot v=C\). In the orthonormal basis
\[
e_u=\partial_u,
\qquad
e_v=\frac1{f(u)}\partial_v,
\]
the azimuthal component of the unit velocity is \(f(u)\dot v=\sin\alpha\). Hence \(f(u)\sin\alpha=C\).

title: Riemannian geometry
text:
11 Curvature exercises

11.1 Exercise 28 — The polar plane is flat
Use the polar Christoffel symbols to calculate \(R^r{}_{\theta r\theta}\) and deduce the Gaussian curvature.






NoteSolution





From Equation 7,
\[
R^r{}_{\theta r\theta}
=\partial_r(-r)
-\Gamma^\theta{}_{r\theta}\Gamma^r{}_{\theta\theta}
=-1-\frac1r(-r)=0.
\]
In dimension two, the Riemann tensor is determined by \(K\), so
\[
K=0.
\]
The non-zero Christoffel symbols came only from the polar coordinates.





11.2 Exercise 29 — Curvature of conformal metrics
For
\[
g=e^{2\sigma}(dx^2+dy^2),
\]
use
\[
K=-e^{-2\sigma}(\partial_x^2\sigma+\partial_y^2\sigma)
\]
to find the curvature of the stereographic unit-sphere metric and the Poincaré half-plane.






NoteSolution





For the sphere,
\[
\sigma=\log2-\log(1+r^2),
\qquad
\Delta\sigma=-\frac4{(1+r^2)^2}.
\]
Since \(e^{-2\sigma}=(1+r^2)^2/4\), we obtain \(K=1\).
For the half-plane,
\[
\sigma=-\log y,
\qquad
\Delta\sigma=\frac1{y^2},
\qquad
e^{-2\sigma}=y^2,
\]
so \(K=-1\).





11.3 Exercise 30 — Constant-curvature spaces
Suppose an \(n\)-dimensional manifold satisfies
\[
R(X,Y)Z
=K[g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y].
\]
Find the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature, then apply the result to \(S_R^n\).






NoteSolution





In an orthonormal basis \((e_a)\),
\[
\operatorname{Ric}(Y,Z)
=\sum_a g(R(e_a,Y)Z,e_a).
\]
Substitution gives \(nKg(Y,Z)-Kg(Y,Z)\), hence
\[
\operatorname{Ric}=(n-1)Kg,
\qquad
S=n(n-1)K.
\]
For \(S_R^n\), \(K=1/R^2\), so
\[
\operatorname{Ric}=\frac{n-1}{R^2}g,
\qquad
S=\frac{n(n-1)}{R^2}.
\]





11.4 Exercise 31 — Gauss–Bonnet theorem
For a compact oriented surface without boundary,
\[
\int_MK\,dA=2\pi\chi(M).
\]
Check the theorem on a sphere, find the integral for a torus and discuss the possible sign of curvature for a surface of genus \(q\).






NoteSolution





On \(S_R^2\),
\[
\int K\,dA=\frac1{R^2}(4\pi R^2)=4\pi
=2\pi\chi(S^2).
\]
For the torus, \(\chi=0\), so \(\int K\,dA=0\). For an orientable surface of genus \(q\),
\[
\int_MK\,dA=4\pi(1-q).
\]
Everywhere positive curvature is possible only when \(q=0\). Everywhere negative curvature requires \(q\geq2\). A torus cannot have curvature of one strict sign everywhere.





11.5 Exercise 32 — Jacobi fields
Along a unit-speed geodesic in a constant-curvature space, let \(E\) be parallel, unit and normal to \(\dot\gamma\). Set \(J=fE\) and solve
\[
\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0
\]
with \(f(0)=0\), \(f'(0)=1\) for \(K=1/R^2\), \(0\) and \(-1/R^2\).






NoteSolution





Since \(E\) is parallel and normal to \(\dot\gamma\),
\[
f''+Kf=0.
\]
The three solutions are
\[
f(t)=R\sin(t/R)
\quad(K=1/R^2),
\]
\[
f(t)=t
\quad(K=0),
\]
and
\[
f(t)=R\sinh(t/R)
\quad(K=-1/R^2).
\]
Positive curvature can refocus geodesics, flat geometry gives linear separation, and negative curvature makes nearby geodesics diverge rapidly.

text:
12 Further reading
Natural continuations are differential forms and the Hodge operator, submanifolds and the second fundamental form, comparison theorems, conjugate points and the cut locus. Introductory references include M. do Carmo, Riemannian Geometry, and J. Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds.

title: The hydrogen atom
text:
A hydrogen atom contains one electron and one proton. Their Coulomb attraction produces bound states. We will derive their energies, describe their spatial wave functions and connect the energy differences to spectral lines.
We consider a point nucleus of charge \(+Ze\) and mass \(m_N\), with one electron of charge \(-e\) and mass \(m_e\). The model is non-relativistic and has no external field. We first leave out spin and nuclear structure. Hydrogen has \(Z=1\); the same calculation applies to one-electron ions such as \(\mathrm{He}^+\) and \(\mathrm{Li}^{2+}\).


Let \(\mathbf r_e\) and \(\mathbf r_N\) be the positions of the electron and the nucleus. The two-body Hamiltonian is
\[
\widehat H
=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla_e^2
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_N}\nabla_N^2
-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|\mathbf r_e-\mathbf r_N|}.
\tag{1}\]
Both particles move. To separate the motion of the whole atom from its internal motion, introduce the center-of-mass position
\[
\mathbf R
=\frac{m_e\mathbf r_e+m_N\mathbf r_N}{m_e+m_N},
\]
and the relative coordinate
\[
\mathbf r=\mathbf r_e-\mathbf r_N.
\]
With the total mass \(M=m_e+m_N\) and the reduced mass
\[
\mu=\frac{m_em_N}{m_e+m_N},
\tag{2}\]
the chain rule gives
\[
\nabla_e=\frac{m_e}{M}\nabla_R+\nabla_r,
\qquad
\nabla_N=\frac{m_N}{M}\nabla_R-\nabla_r.
\]
On squaring and adding the two kinetic terms, the mixed derivatives cancel:
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla_e^2
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_N}\nabla_N^2
=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}\nabla_R^2
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\nabla_r^2.
\]
The Hamiltonian therefore becomes
\[
\widehat H
=\underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}\nabla_R^2}_{\widehat H_{\mathrm{CM}}}
+\underbrace{\left(
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\nabla_r^2
-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
\right)}_{\widehat H_{\mathrm{rel}}}.
\tag{3}\]
The center of mass behaves like a free particle. The internal motion is equivalent to that of a particle of mass \(\mu\) in the potential
\[
V(r)=-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}.
\tag{4}\]
Since \(m_N\gg m_e\), the fixed-nucleus approximation \(\mu\simeq m_e\) is often sufficient. Keeping \(\mu\) accounts for the leading effect of nuclear motion on the spectrum.



Confining the electron to a region of size \(a\) gives a momentum of order \(\hbar/a\). A simple estimate of its energy is
\[
E(a)\sim\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu a^2}
-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}.
\]
The positive term grows faster as \(a\to0\) than the attraction. Minimizing this estimate gives \(a\sim a_\mu/Z\), where
\[
a_\mu=\frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{\mu e^2}.
\tag{5}\]
The length \(a_\mu\) is the Bohr radius corrected for nuclear motion. With \(\mu=m_e\), it becomes
\[
a_0=5.29\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm m.
\]
The associated energy scale is the reduced Hartree
\[
E_{\mathrm h}^{(\mu)}
=\frac{\mu e^4}{(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^2\hbar^2}.
\]
In atomic units, we set \(\hbar=e=4\pi\varepsilon_0=m_e=1\). For an infinitely heavy nucleus, the Hamiltonian becomes
\[
\widehat H=-\frac12\nabla^2-\frac{Z}{r}.
\tag{6}\]
The radial plots use \(a_0\) for lengths and Hartree for energies, with a fixed nucleus. Energy diagrams also show electronvolts. The spectral-line plot includes the hydrogen reduced mass.






NoteFrom spectral lines to wave functions





Balmer found a formula for hydrogen’s visible lines in 1885. Bohr reproduced the spectrum with quantized orbits in 1913. Schrödinger’s equation later gave the same leading energies from wave functions and their boundary conditions.






The potential tends to \(-\infty\) as \(r\to0\) and to zero as \(r\to\infty\). Bound states have \(E<0\); the threshold \(E=0\) separates the discrete spectrum from the ionization continuum.

from pathlib import Path
import re
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

folders = [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
stylesheet = next((p / "styles.css" for p in folders
                   if (p / "styles.css").is_file()), None)
palette = dict(re.findall(r"--([\w-]+)\s*:\s*([^;{}]+)",
                         stylesheet.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if stylesheet else ""))
defaults = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"]
plot_colors = [palette.get(f"plot-{i}", defaults[i-1]).strip() for i in range(1, 6)]
BLEU, ORANGE, VERT, ROUGE, VIOLET = plot_colors
GRIS = palette.get("muted", "0.45").strip()
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = plt.cycler(color=plot_colors)

def laguerre_associe(p, alpha, x):
    """Associated Laguerre polynomial L_p^alpha(x), with p a non-negative integer."""
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    if p == 0:
        return np.ones_like(x)
    if p == 1:
        return 1 + alpha - x
    L_avant = np.ones_like(x)
    L_courant = 1 + alpha - x
    for k in range(2, p + 1):
        L_suivant = ((2*k - 1 + alpha - x) * L_courant
                     - (k - 1 + alpha) * L_avant) / k
        L_avant, L_courant = L_courant, L_suivant
    return L_courant

def R_nl(n, l, r, Z=1.0):
    """Hydrogen-like radial function in atomic units (fixed nucleus)."""
    if not (n >= 1 and 0 <= l < n):
        raise ValueError("We must have n >= 1 and 0 <= l < n.")
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    rho = 2 * Z * r / n
    prefacteur = (2*Z/n)**1.5 * np.sqrt(
        math.factorial(n-l-1) / (2*n*math.factorial(n+l))
    )
    return (prefacteur * np.exp(-rho/2) * rho**l
            * laguerre_associe(n-l-1, 2*l+1, rho))

def probabilite_radiale(n, l, r, Z=1.0):
    return r**2 * np.abs(R_nl(n, l, r, Z))**2

def harmonique_reelle(type_orbitale, theta, phi):
    """Normalized real spherical harmonics for s, p and d."""
    if type_orbitale == "s":
        return np.ones_like(theta) / np.sqrt(4*np.pi)
    if type_orbitale == "pz":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.cos(theta)
    if type_orbitale == "px":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta) * np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "py":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta) * np.sin(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dz2":
        return np.sqrt(5/(16*np.pi)) * (3*np.cos(theta)**2 - 1)
    if type_orbitale == "dxz":
        return np.sqrt(15/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)*np.cos(theta)*np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dxy":
        return np.sqrt(15/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)**2*np.sin(phi)*np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dx2y2":
        return np.sqrt(15/(16*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)**2*np.cos(2*phi)
    raise ValueError("Unknown orbital type.")

GRIS = palette.get("muted", "0.45").strip()
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = plt.cycler(color=plot_colors)

def laguerre_associe(p, alpha, x):
    """Associated Laguerre polynomial L_p^alpha(x), with p a non-negative integer."""
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    if p == 0:
        return np.ones_like(x)
    if p == 1:
        return 1 + alpha - x
    L_avant = np.ones_like(x)
    L_courant = 1 + alpha - x
    for k in range(2, p + 1):
        L_suivant = ((2*k - 1 + alpha - x) * L_courant
                     - (k - 1 + alpha) * L_avant) / k
        L_avant, L_courant = L_courant, L_suivant
    return L_courant

def R_nl(n, l, r, Z=1.0):
    """Hydrogen-like radial function in atomic units (fixed nucleus)."""
    if not (n >= 1 and 0 <= l < n):
        raise ValueError("We must have n >= 1 and 0 <= l < n.")
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    rho = 2 * Z * r / n
    prefacteur = (2*Z/n)**1.5 * np.sqrt(
        math.factorial(n-l-1) / (2*n*math.factorial(n+l))
    )
    return (prefacteur * np.exp(-rho/2) * rho**l
            * laguerre_associe(n-l-1, 2*l+1, rho))

def probabilite_radiale(n, l, r, Z=1.0):
    return r**2 * np.abs(R_nl(n, l, r, Z))**2

def harmonique_reelle(type_orbitale, theta, phi):
    """Normalized real spherical harmonics for s, p and d."""
    if type_orbitale == "s":
        return np.ones_like(theta) / np.sqrt(4*np.pi)
    if type_orbitale == "pz":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.cos(theta)
    if type_orbitale == "px":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta) * np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "py":
        return np.sqrt(3/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta) * np.sin(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dz2":
        return np.sqrt(5/(16*np.pi)) * (3*np.cos(theta)**2 - 1)
    if type_orbitale == "dxz":
        return np.sqrt(15/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)*np.cos(theta)*np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dxy":
        return np.sqrt(15/(4*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)**2*np.sin(phi)*np.cos(phi)
    if type_orbitale == "dx2y2":
        return np.sqrt(15/(16*np.pi)) * np.sin(theta)**2*np.cos(2*phi)
    raise ValueError("Unknown orbital type.")

title: The hydrogen atom
text:
2 Separating variables in spherical coordinates
The potential Equation 4 depends only on the distance \(r\). We use spherical coordinates \((r,\theta,\varphi)\) to separate the radial and angular dependence. The time-independent equation for the relative motion is
\[
\left[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\nabla^2
-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
\right]\psi(\mathbf r)=E\psi(\mathbf r).
\tag{7}\]

2.1 Laplacian and angular momentum
In spherical coordinates,
\[
\nabla^2
=\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}
\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\varphi^2}.
\tag{8}\]
The angular part is related to the square of the orbital angular momentum:
\[
\widehat L^2
=-\hbar^2\left[
\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right)
+\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\varphi^2}
\right].
\tag{9}\]
The Laplacian can therefore be written as
\[
\nabla^2
=\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}
\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right)
-\frac{\widehat L^2}{\hbar^2r^2}.
\]
Since \([\widehat H,\widehat L^2]=[\widehat H,\widehat L_z]=0\), we can look for common eigenstates of the form
\[
\psi_{n\ell m}(r,\theta,\varphi)
=R_{n\ell}(r)Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi).
\tag{10}\]


2.2 Angular equation and the numbers \(\ell\) and \(m\)
The spherical harmonics satisfy
\[
\widehat L^2Y_\ell^m
=\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)Y_\ell^m,
\tag{11}\]
\[
\widehat L_zY_\ell^m
=\hbar mY_\ell^m.
\tag{12}\]
Periodicity in the azimuthal angle requires
\[
Y(\theta,\varphi+2\pi)=Y(\theta,\varphi),
\]
which gives a factor \(e^{im\varphi}\) with integer \(m\). Regularity at the poles \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\pi\) then requires
\[
\ell=0,1,2,\ldots,
\qquad
m=-\ell,-\ell+1,\ldots,\ell.
\tag{13}\]
To fix the phase convention, define
\[
P_\ell^m(x)=(-1)^m(1-x^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^mP_\ell(x)}{dx^m},
\]
where \(P_\ell\) is the Legendre polynomial. For \(m\ge0\), the normalized spherical harmonics are
\[
Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi)
=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}
\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}}
P_\ell^m(\cos\theta)e^{im\varphi}.
\tag{14}\]
The phase convention is specified explicitly because it varies between references; see NIST DLMF, spherical harmonics. For negative \(m\),
\[
Y_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\left(Y_\ell^m\right)^*.
\]
The first ones are
\[
Y_0^0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}},
\]
\[
Y_1^0=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\cos\theta,
\qquad
Y_1^{\pm1}=\mp\sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\varphi},
\]
\[
Y_2^0=\sqrt{\frac{5}{16\pi}}(3\cos^2\theta-1).
\]
The index \(\ell\) sets the magnitude of the angular momentum,
\[
|\mathbf L|=\hbar\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)},
\]
while \(m\) sets its measurable projection along the chosen axis,
\[
L_z=m\hbar.
\]
Since the components of \(\mathbf L\) do not commute, they cannot in general all have definite values. The basis \(|\ell,m\rangle\) fixes \(L^2\) and \(L_z\).
For \(m\ne0\), \(Y_\ell^m\) is generally complex. The familiar real orbitals \(p_x\), \(p_y\), \(d_{xy}\) and \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) combine the states \(m\) and \(-m\). They remain energy eigenstates in the Coulomb potential, but they do not have a definite \(L_z\).


2.3 Radial equation
By inserting Equation 10 into Equation 7 and then using Equation 11, we obtain
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}
\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dr}
\left(r^2\frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dr}\right)
+\frac{\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)}{2\mu r^2}R
-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}R
=ER.
\tag{15}\]
To remove the first derivative, set
\[
u(r)=rR(r).
\tag{16}\]
Indeed,
\[
R=\frac{u}{r},
\qquad
r^2\frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dr}=ru'-u,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dr}(ru'-u)=ru''.
\]
After multiplying by \(r\), the equation becomes a one-dimensional Schrödinger equation on \(r>0\):
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\frac{\mathrm d^2u}{\mathrm dr^2}
+V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)u(r)=Eu(r),
\tag{17}\]
with the effective potential
\[
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)
=-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
+\frac{\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)}{2\mu r^2}.
\tag{18}\]
The second term is the centrifugal barrier. It is absent for \(s\) states (\(\ell=0\)) and pushes states with large \(\ell\) away from the nucleus. The physical conditions are
\[
u(0)=0,
\qquad
u(r)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }r\to\infty
\]
for a normalizable bound state.

title: The hydrogen atom
text:
3 Radial solutions and energy levels
We now look for bound states, so \(E<0\). Let us introduce
\[
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{-2\mu E}}{\hbar}>0,
\qquad
\rho=2\kappa r,
\tag{19}\]
as well as the dimensionless parameter
\[
\gamma
=\frac{\mu Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2\kappa}
=\frac{Z}{a_\mu\kappa}.
\tag{20}\]
Equation Equation 17 becomes
\[
\frac{\mathrm d^2u}{\mathrm d\rho^2}
+\left[
-\frac14+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}
-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{\rho^2}
\right]u=0.
\tag{21}\]

3.1 Behavior at small and large distances
As \(\rho\to\infty\), the terms in \(1/\rho\) disappear and
\[
u''-\frac14u\simeq0.
\]
The leading exponential factors are \(e^{\pm\rho/2}\). A bound state must have the decaying factor \(e^{-\rho/2}\), possibly multiplied by powers of \(\rho\).
Near the origin, inserting \(u\sim\rho^s\) and keeping the lowest powers gives
\[
s(s-1)-\ell(\ell+1)=0,
\]
which gives \(s=\ell+1\) or \(s=-\ell\). The second branch diverges for \(\ell>0\) and tends to a nonzero constant for \(\ell=0\). In both cases it fails \(u(0)=0\), so
\[
u(\rho)\sim\rho^{\ell+1}.
\]
These two behaviors suggest the factorization
\[
u(\rho)=\rho^{\ell+1}e^{-\rho/2}v(\rho).
\tag{22}\]


3.2 Power series and termination condition
By substituting Equation 22 into Equation 21 and simplifying, we find
\[
\rho v''+(2\ell+2-\rho)v'
+(\gamma-\ell-1)v=0.
\tag{23}\]
Let us expand
\[
v(\rho)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_j\rho^j.
\]
After shifting the indices, the coefficient of \(\rho^j\) gives
\[
(j+1)(j+2\ell+2)a_{j+1}
+(\gamma-\ell-1-j)a_j=0.
\]
The recurrence relation is therefore
\[
a_{j+1}
=\frac{j+\ell+1-\gamma}
{(j+1)(j+2\ell+2)}a_j.
\tag{24}\]
At large \(j\), the recurrence has \(a_{j+1}/a_j\sim1/j\). A non-terminating regular solution contains an \(e^\rho\) growth, up to powers of \(\rho\). Multiplication by \(e^{-\rho/2}\) then leaves a growing \(u\), which is not normalizable. The series must stop: its numerator must vanish at an integer \(j=n_r\ge0\). Thus
\[
n_r+\ell+1-\gamma=0.
\]
We define the principal quantum number
\[
n=n_r+\ell+1=1,2,3,\ldots
\tag{25}\]
and the quantization condition becomes
\[
\gamma=n.
\]
Since \(\gamma=Z/(a_\mu\kappa)\),
\[
\kappa=\frac{Z}{na_\mu}.
\]
Finally, the definition of \(\kappa\) in Equation 19 gives
\[
\boxed{
E_n
=-\frac{\mu Z^2e^4}
{2(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}
=-\frac{\mu c^2(Z\alpha)^2}{2n^2}.
}
\tag{26}\]
Here \(\alpha=e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c)\) is the fine-structure constant. For an infinitely heavy nucleus and \(Z=1\),
\[
E_n=-\frac{13.6057\ \mathrm{eV}}{n^2}.
\]
Including the proton mass gives a ground-state ionization energy of about \(13.598\ \mathrm{eV}\) in this model.
The allowed energies are the values for which the radial solution is regular at the origin and normalizable at infinity. This series method is also developed in the MIT notes on the hydrogen atom.


3.3 Normalized radial functions
The terminated series is an associated Laguerre polynomial. Now setting
\[
\rho=\frac{2Zr}{na_\mu},
\]
the normalized solution is
\[
R_{n\ell}(r)
=\left(\frac{2Z}{na_\mu}\right)^{3/2}
\sqrt{\frac{(n-\ell-1)!}{2n(n+\ell)!}}
e^{-\rho/2}\rho^\ell
L_{n-\ell-1}^{2\ell+1}(\rho).
\tag{27}\]
It satisfies
\[
\int_0^\infty |R_{n\ell}(r)|^2r^2\,\mathrm dr=1.
\]
For \(Z=1\), the first examples are
\[
R_{10}(r)=2a_\mu^{-3/2}e^{-r/a_\mu},
\]
\[
R_{20}(r)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,a_\mu^{-3/2}
\left(2-\frac{r}{a_\mu}\right)e^{-r/(2a_\mu)},
\]
\[
R_{21}(r)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\,a_\mu^{-3/2}
\frac{r}{a_\mu}e^{-r/(2a_\mu)}.
\]
For a hydrogen-like ion, we only need to replace \(a_\mu\) with \(a_\mu/Z\) in these expressions.


3.4 Radial distribution and nodes
The quantity \(|R_{n\ell}(r)|^2\) is not directly the probability density for the distance from the nucleus. The volume of a spherical shell of radius \(r\) and thickness \(\mathrm dr\) contains the factor \(r^2\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\Omega\). Since the spherical harmonics are normalized,
\[
\int |Y_\ell^m|^2\,\mathrm d\Omega=1,
\]
the probability of finding the electron between \(r\) and \(r+\mathrm dr\) is
\[
\mathrm dP=P_{n\ell}(r)\,\mathrm dr,
\qquad
P_{n\ell}(r)=r^2|R_{n\ell}(r)|^2.
\tag{28}\]
In particular, \(R_{10}(r)\) is largest at the nucleus, but \(P_{10}(0)=0\) because a shell of zero radius has zero volume. For the \(1s\) state,
\[
P_{10}(r)=\frac{4r^2}{a_\mu^3}e^{-2r/a_\mu}.
\]
Its derivative vanishes when
\[
\frac{\mathrm dP_{10}}{\mathrm dr}
\propto 2r\left(1-\frac{r}{a_\mu}\right)e^{-2r/a_\mu}=0.
\]
The maximum of the radial distribution is therefore at
\[
r_{\mathrm{mp}}=a_\mu.
\tag{29}\]
The polynomial \(L_{n-\ell-1}^{2\ell+1}\) has \(n-\ell-1\) positive zeros. Therefore,
\[
N_{\mathrm{radial}}=n-\ell-1.
\]
For the usual real orbitals built from a single \(|m|\), there are also \(\ell\) angular nodes (planes or cones). Counting these with the radial nodes gives
\[
N_{\mathrm{total}}=(n-\ell-1)+\ell=n-1.
\tag{30}\]
This surface count refers to that real basis. A complex harmonic such as \(Y_1^1\propto\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\) has no nodal plane: its angular zeros lie on the \(z\) axis.

3.5 Shells, subshells and orbitals
A shell is specified by \(n\). Within it, a subshell has fixed \((n,\ell)\), with \(0\le\ell<n\). In the \(L_z\) basis, an orbital has a further label \(m\), from \(-\ell\) to \(\ell\).
The letters \(s,p,d,f\) stand for \(\ell=0,1,2,3\). For example, the \(3d\) subshell has \(n=3\) and \(\ell=2\); its five values of \(m\) give five spatial orbitals. Adding the subshells of a shell gives
\[
g_n=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(2\ell+1)=n^2.
\tag{31}\]
With two spin states per orbital, a shell contains \(2n^2\) one-electron states. Hydrogen occupies only one of them.
In the Coulomb model, all these spatial states have the same energy \(E_n\). Rotational symmetry explains the degeneracy in \(m\). The additional degeneracy in \(\ell\) is a special property of the \(1/r\) potential.

title: The hydrogen atom
section: 4 The shape and size of orbitals
text:
4 The shape and size of orbitals
A hydrogen-like orbital is the function
\[
\psi_{n\ell m}(r,\theta,\varphi)
=R_{n\ell}(r)Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi).
\]
Its probability density is
\[
\rho_{n\ell m}(\mathbf r)
=|R_{n\ell}(r)|^2|Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi)|^2.
\tag{32}\]
An orbital drawing describes this spatial distribution. A surface may mark a chosen density value; a cloud of sampled points shows where position measurements are more likely. Neither gives the electron a definite path.

4.1 Nodes and the sign of the wave function
A radial node is a sphere on which \(R_{n\ell}(r)=0\). An angular node is a plane, cone or other surface on which \(Y_\ell^m=0\).
For a real orbital, two colors indicate opposite signs of \(\psi\). Both regions have positive probability density \(|\psi|^2\). The relative sign matters when amplitudes interfere.
The \(1s\) state is spherical and has no node. The \(2s\) state has a nodal sphere at \(r=2a_\mu\) for \(Z=1\). A real \(2p_z\) orbital instead has the nodal plane \(z=0\), since its angular factor is \(\cos\theta\). The real \(3p_z\) orbital has both a radial node and this plane.
The usual real orbitals can be written, for example, as
\[
p_z\propto\cos\theta,
\qquad
p_x\propto\sin\theta\cos\varphi,
\qquad
p_y\propto\sin\theta\sin\varphi,
\]
\[
d_{z^2}\propto3\cos^2\theta-1,
\qquad
d_{xy}\propto\sin^2\theta\sin(2\varphi),
\]
\[
d_{x^2-y^2}\propto\sin^2\theta\cos(2\varphi).
\]


Show Python code
def coupe_orbitale(n, l, type_orbitale, etendue, points=420):
    x = np.linspace(-etendue, etendue, points)
    z = np.linspace(-etendue, etendue, points)
    X, Zm = np.meshgrid(x, z)
    Ycoord = np.zeros_like(X)
    rayon = np.sqrt(X**2 + Ycoord**2 + Zm**2)
    theta = np.arccos(np.divide(
        Zm, rayon, out=np.ones_like(rayon), where=rayon > 1e-14
    ))
    phi = np.arctan2(Ycoord, X)
    psi = R_nl(n, l, rayon) * harmonique_reelle(type_orbitale, theta, phi)
    psi /= np.max(np.abs(psi))
    return x, z, psi

4.2 Mean values and the size of the atom
A mean distance averages over the radial distribution:
\[
\langle r^p\rangle=\int_0^\infty r^p P_{n\ell}(r)\,dr.
\]
For the \(1s\) state of hydrogen, for example,
\[
\langle r\rangle_{100}
=\frac4{a_\mu^3}\int_0^\infty r^3e^{-2r/a_\mu}\,dr
=\frac4{a_\mu^3}\frac{3!}{(2/a_\mu)^4}
=\frac32a_\mu.
\]
Integrating the general radial functions gives
\[
\left\langle\frac1r\right\rangle_{n\ell}
=\frac{Z}{a_\mu n^2},
\tag{33}\]
\[
\langle r\rangle_{n\ell}
=\frac{a_\mu}{2Z}
\left[3n^2-\ell(\ell+1)\right],
\tag{34}\]
\[
\langle r^2\rangle_{n\ell}
=\frac{a_\mu^2n^2}{2Z^2}
\left[5n^2+1-3\ell(\ell+1)\right].
\tag{35}\]
For the \(Z=1\) ground state,
\[
r_{\mathrm{mp}}=a_\mu,
\qquad
\langle r\rangle_{100}=\frac32a_\mu,
\qquad
\sqrt{\langle r^2\rangle_{100}}=\sqrt{3}\,a_\mu.
\]
The most probable distance, the mean and the root-mean-square distance differ because the electron has a distribution of distances.
The virial theorem for a stationary bound state is \(2\langle T\rangle=\langle rV'(r)\rangle\). Since \(V\propto-1/r\), it gives
\[
2\langle T\rangle=-\langle V\rangle.
\]
Since \(E=\langle T\rangle+\langle V\rangle\), it follows that
\[
\langle T\rangle=-E_n,
\qquad
\langle V\rangle=2E_n.
\tag{36}\]
The total energy is negative even though the mean kinetic energy is positive. The energy \(|E_n|\) must be supplied to ionize the atom from level \(n\).


Show Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
marqueurs = ["o", "s", "^", "D", "P", "X"]
couleurs = [BLEU, ORANGE, VERT, ROUGE, VIOLET, GRIS]

for n in range(1, 7):
    ls = np.arange(n)
    rayon_moyen = 0.5 * (3*n*n - ls*(ls+1))
    ax.plot(ls, rayon_moyen, marker=marqueurs[n-1], color=couleurs[n-1],
            lw=1.8, ms=7, label=fr"$n={n}$")

ax.set(xlabel=r"quantum number $\ell$", ylabel=r"$\langle r\rangle/a_0$",
       title="A shell does not have a single radius",
       xticks=range(6))
ax.legend(ncol=3)
plt.show()








Figure 5: Mean distance from the nucleus for every subshell in the first six shells.

title: The hydrogen atom
text:
5 Hydrogen spectrum and quantum transitions
For an energy eigenstate, \(\Psi(\mathbf r,t)=\psi(\mathbf r)e^{-iEt/\hbar}\), so \(|\Psi|^2\) is time independent. The Coulomb Hamiltonian alone does not describe emission. Coupling the atom to the electromagnetic field allows transitions; spontaneous emission requires a quantum description of that field.
A spectral line appears when an interaction, usually with the electromagnetic field, takes the atom from an initial level \(n_i\) to a final level \(n_f\). For emission,
\[
n_i>n_f,
\qquad
h\nu=E_{n_i}-E_{n_f}>0.
\tag{37}\]
Using Equation 26,
\[
h\nu
=\frac{\mu Z^2e^4}{2(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^2\hbar^2}
\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2}-\frac{1}{n_i^2}\right).
\]
Since \(\nu=c/\lambda\), we obtain the Rydberg formula:
\[
\frac{1}{\lambda}
=R_\mu Z^2
\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2}-\frac{1}{n_i^2}\right),
\tag{38}\]
where
\[
R_\mu=\frac{\mu e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^3c}.
\]
For hydrogen, \(R_\mathrm H\simeq1.0968\times10^7\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\). The dependence on reduced mass explains why hydrogen and deuterium have slightly shifted lines.

5.1 Spectral series
Transitions ending at \(n_f=1\) form the Lyman series in the ultraviolet. Those ending at \(n_f=2\) form the Balmer series; the first line, \(3\to2\), has a wavelength of about \(656\ \mathrm{nm}\). The Paschen and Brackett series end at \(n_f=3\) and \(4\) and lie in the infrared.
As \(n_i\to\infty\), the lines approach the series limit. From Equation 38,
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{limit}}=\frac{n_f^2}{R_\mu Z^2}.
\]
The corresponding photon energy is the energy required to ionize level \(n_f\). Wavelengths below are measured in vacuum.


Show Python code
R_H = 1.0967758e7  # m^-1

def longueur_onde_nm(ni, nf, Z=1):
    inverse_lambda = R_H * Z**2 * (1/nf**2 - 1/ni**2)
    return 1e9 / inverse_lambda

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.7))

# Diagram of the levels and a few transitions

transitions = [

axes[1].legend(fontsize=9, ncol=2)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: Hydrogen levels and lines of the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series.







5.2 Dipole selection rules
Energy conservation tells us where a line is located, but not whether it is strong or even allowed. When the wavelength is much larger than the atom, the leading interaction is the electric dipole term \(H_I=-\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf E\). In the fixed-nucleus approximation, \(\mathbf d=-e\mathbf r\), so the transition amplitude contains
\[
\mathbf d_{fi}
=-e\langle n_f\ell_fm_f|\widehat{\mathbf r}|
n_i\ell_im_i\rangle.
\tag{39}\]
Each Cartesian component of \(\mathbf r\) has angular momentum one. Adding angular momenta therefore permits \(\ell_f=\ell_i-1,\ell_i,\ell_i+1\). The matrix element must also have even overall parity. Since the states have parity \((-1)^\ell\) and \(\mathbf r\) is odd, \(\ell_i+\ell_f\) must be odd, excluding \(\ell_f=\ell_i\). The angular integral thus requires
\[
\Delta\ell=\pm1,
\qquad
\Delta m=0,\pm1.
\tag{40}\]
The photon’s polarization determines which value of \(\Delta m\) occurs. In the absence of an interaction acting on spin,
\[
\Delta s=0.
\]
A transition that does not follow these rules is forbidden at the electric dipole level, but it can still occur much more slowly through a higher-order mechanism. Thus, the \(2s\) state cannot decay to \(1s\) by emitting a single dipole photon; it decays mainly through two-photon emission.
A transition changes the quantum state. The energy difference fixes the photon frequency; it does not describe a trajectory between two orbital surfaces.


5.3 Numerical check of the radial equation
We can recover the levels without using their analytical expression. In atomic units, let us discretize Equation 17 on a grid \(r_j=j\Delta r\). The centered second derivative is
\[
u''(r_j)\simeq
\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{\Delta r^2}.
\]
On \(0<r<r_{\max}\) we set \(u(0)=u(r_{\max})=0\). The matrix entries are
\[
H_{jj}=\frac1{\Delta r^2}+\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2r_j^2}-\frac1{r_j},
\qquad
H_{j,j\pm1}=-\frac1{2\Delta r^2}.
\]
Its negative eigenvalues approximate bound-state energies. A smaller \(\Delta r\) improves the derivative approximation; a larger \(r_{\max}\) reduces the effect of the outer boundary, especially for excited states.


Show Python code
r_max = 100.0
N_grille = 800
dr = r_max / (N_grille + 1)
r = dr * np.arange(1, N_grille + 1)

def spectre_radial_numerique(l):
    diagonale = 1/dr**2 - 1/r + l*(l+1)/(2*r**2)
    hors_diagonale = -np.ones(N_grille - 1) / (2*dr**2)
    H = (np.diag(diagonale)
         + np.diag(hors_diagonale, 1)
         + np.diag(hors_diagonale, -1))
    energies, vecteurs = np.linalg.eigh(H)
    masque = energies < 0
    return energies[masque], vecteurs[:, masque]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 4.3))
resultats_radiaux = {}

    resultats_radiaux[l] = (energies, vecteurs)
    nombres_n = np.arange(l + 1, l + 1 + min(4, len(energies)))
    axes[0].plot(nombres_n, energies[:len(nombres_n)], "o",
                 color=couleur, ms=7, label=fr"numerical, $\ell={l}$")

n = np.arange(1, 7)
axes[0].plot(n, -1/(2*n**2), color="black", ls="--", lw=1.6,
             label=r"$-1/(2n^2)$")
axes[0].set(xlabel="$n$", ylabel="energy (Hartree)",
            title="Numerical and exact energies", xticks=range(1, 7))
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

energies_s, vecteurs_s = resultats_radiaux[0]
for indice, couleur in zip(range(3), [BLEU, ORANGE, VERT]):
    u = vecteurs_s[:, indice]
    u /= np.sqrt(np.sum(np.abs(u)**2) * dr)
    if u[np.argmax(np.abs(u))] < 0:
        u = -u
    axes[1].plot(r, u + 0.55*indice, color=couleur, lw=2,
                 label=fr"${indice+1}s$")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$r/a_0$", ylabel=r"$u_{n0}(r)$ (shifted)",
            title="Reduced radial functions", xlim=(0, 28))
axes[1].legend()

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7: Numerical radial solution: reduced functions and comparison with exact energies.







5.4 Corrections to the Coulomb spectrum
Relativistic motion and spin modify the energies. For a fixed point nucleus, the leading fine-structure correction is
\[
\Delta E_{nj}^{\mathrm{fine}}
=-\frac{m_ec^2(Z\alpha)^4}{2n^4}
\left(\frac{n}{j+1/2}-\frac34\right),
\tag{41}\]
where \(j=\ell\pm\tfrac12\) is the total electronic angular momentum (only \(j=\tfrac12\) for \(\ell=0\)). The energy now depends on \(j\) as well as \(n\). Nuclear recoil gives further corrections when the nucleus can move.
States with the same \(n\) and \(j\), such as \(2S_{1/2}\) and \(2P_{1/2}\), still coincide in this approximation. Their Lamb shift comes from radiative corrections. Coupling the nuclear and electronic spins gives hyperfine structure, including hydrogen’s \(21\ \mathrm{cm}\) line. External magnetic and electric fields give the Zeeman and Stark effects.
