title: L’équation de Schrödinger et les potentiels par morceaux
text:
2 États liés : confinement et quantification
Un état lié correspond à une particule localisée dans une région finie. Sa fonction d’onde est normalisable et son énergie appartient généralement à un spectre discret. Les puits carré infini et fini permettent de comprendre comment les conditions aux limites transforment une équation différentielle continue en une suite d’énergies quantifiées.

2.1 Le puits carré infini
Considérons le potentiel
\[
V(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & 0<x<L,\\
+\infty, & x\leq0\ \text{ou}\ x\geq L.
\end{cases}
\tag{15}\]
La particule ne peut être détectée à l’extérieur. La fonction d’onde doit donc satisfaire
\[
\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0.
\tag{16}\]
À l’intérieur, \(V=0\) et Equation 7 devient
\[
\psi''+k^2\psi=0,
\qquad
k=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar}.
\]
La solution générale est
\[
\psi(x)=A\sin(kx)+B\cos(kx).
\]
La condition \(psi(0)=0\) impose \(B=0\). La seconde condition donne
\[
A\sin(kL)=0.
\]
Pour une fonction d’onde non nulle, il faut donc
\[
kL=n\pi,
\qquad
n=1,2,3,\ldots
\]
et les énergies permises sont
\[
\boxed{E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}}.
\tag{17}\]
La valeur \(n=0\) donnerait \(\psi=0\) partout, qui ne représente aucun état physique. Après normalisation,
\[
\boxed{
\psi_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}
\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)}.
\tag{18}\]
Le niveau fondamental possède une énergie non nulle,
\[
E_1=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}.
\]
Cette énergie de point zéro est une conséquence du confinement. Une particule d’énergie nulle aurait une fonction d’onde constante dans le puits, incompatible avec les conditions aux murs ; la localiser exige donc une dispersion d’impulsion non nulle.


Afficher le code Python
L = 1.0
x = np.linspace(0, L, 1200)
niveaux = np.arange(1, 5)
energies = (niveaux * np.pi / L)**2  # unités hbar²/(2m)=1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))

# Schéma du potentiel
ax = axes[0]
ax.axvspan(-0.35, 0, color="0.88")
ax.axvspan(L, 1.35, color="0.88")
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 1], color="black", lw=4)
ax.plot([L, L], [0, 1], color="black", lw=4)
ax.plot([0, L], [0, 0], color=BLEU, lw=3)
ax.annotate("région accessible", (L / 2, 0.08), ha="center", color=BLEU)
ax.text(-0.18, 0.72, r"$V=+\infty$", rotation=90, ha="center")
ax.text(1.18, 0.72, r"$V=+\infty$", rotation=90, ha="center")
ax.set(xlim=(-0.35, 1.35), ylim=(-0.08, 1.05), xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$V(x)$")
ax.set_yticks([0], ["0"])

# États propres au-dessus des niveaux d'énergie
ax = axes[1]
for n, En in zip(niveaux, energies):
    psi = np.sqrt(2 / L) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L)
    amplitude = 0.28 * energies[0] * psi / np.max(np.abs(psi))
    ax.hlines(En, 0, L, color="0.72", lw=0.9)
    ax.plot(x, En + amplitude, lw=2, label=rf"$n={n}$")
ax.vlines([0, L], 0, 1.10 * energies[-1], color="black", lw=2.2)
ax.set(xlim=(-0.03, 1.03), ylim=(0, 1.10 * energies[-1]),
       xlabel=r"$x/L$", ylabel=r"énergie et $\psi_n$ décalée")
ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Puits carré infini et quatre premiers états propres, décalés verticalement de leur énergie.





Deux propriétés se lisent immédiatement sur le schéma : l’état \(n\) possède \(n-1\) nœuds internes et sa longueur d’onde diminue lorsque l’énergie augmente. En une dimension, les états liés d’un même potentiel ne sont pas dégénérés.






ImportantCe qui évolue dans une superposition



Un état propre isolé possède une densité stationnaire. En revanche, pour
\[
\Psi=c_n\psi_ne^{-iE_nt/\hbar}+c_m\psi_me^{-iE_mt/\hbar},
\]
la densité contient un terme d’interférence proportionnel à
\[
\cos\!\left(\frac{E_m-E_n}{\hbar}t+\phi\right).
\]
La fonction d’onde peut donc « respirer » ou déplacer sa densité dans un potentiel pourtant indépendant du temps. La première simulation interactif permettra de l’observer.




2.2 Le puits carré fini
Le puits infini est une idéalisation. Dans un confinement réel, les parois possèdent une hauteur finie et la fonction d’onde pénètre dans les régions classiquement interdites. Plaçons l’origine au centre du puits et choisissons
\[
V(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & |x|<L/2,\\
V_0, & |x|\geq L/2,
\end{cases}
\qquad V_0>0.
\tag{19}\]
Un état lié vérifie \(0<E<V_0\). À l’intérieur, la solution oscille avec
\[
k=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},
\]
tandis qu’à l’extérieur elle décroît avec
\[
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}.
\]
Le potentiel est pair, \(V(-x)=V(x)\). L’hamiltonien commute donc avec l’opérateur de parité et les états propres peuvent être choisis pairs ou impairs. Cette symétrie évite de manipuler quatre coefficients indépendants.
Pour un état pair, prenons sur \(x\geq0\)
\[
\psi_{\mathrm p}(x)=
\begin{cases}
A\cos(kx), & 0\leq x<L/2,\\
Ce^{-\kappa(x-L/2)}, & x\geq L/2.
\end{cases}
\]
Au bord \(x=L/2\), la continuité de \(\psi\) et de \(\psi'\) donne
\[
A\cos\!\left(\frac{kL}{2}\right)=C,
\]
\[
-Ak\sin\!\left(\frac{kL}{2}\right)=-\kappa C.
\]
En divisant la seconde relation par la première, les constantes disparaissent :
\[
\boxed{k\tan\!\left(\frac{kL}{2}\right)=\kappa}
\qquad\text{(états pairs).}
\tag{20}\]
Pour un état impair, la solution intérieure est proportionnelle à \(\sin(kx)\). Le même raccordement conduit à
\[
\boxed{-k\cot\!\left(\frac{kL}{2}\right)=\kappa}
\qquad\text{(états impairs).}
\tag{21}\]
Ces équations sont transcendantes : \(E\) apparaît à la fois dans \(k\), dans \(\kappa\) et dans les fonctions trigonométriques. Elles ne possèdent pas de solution algébrique générale.
Introduisons les variables sans dimension
\[
z=\frac{kL}{2},
\qquad
z_0=\frac{L}{2}\frac{\sqrt{2mV_0}}{\hbar}.
\]
Puisque
\[
\left(\frac{\kappa L}{2}\right)^2=z_0^2-z^2,
\]
les conditions de quantification deviennent
\[
z\tan z=\sqrt{z_0^2-z^2}
\qquad\text{(pair)},
\tag{22}\]
\[
-z\cot z=\sqrt{z_0^2-z^2}
\qquad\text{(impair)}.
\tag{23}\]
Le paramètre unique \(z_0\) mesure la profondeur effective du puits. Plus il est grand, plus le puits contient d’états liés. Contrairement au puits infini, leur nombre est fini.


Afficher le code Python
# Unités hbar²/(2m)=1
L = 2.0
V0 = 25.0
z0 = 0.5 * L * np.sqrt(V0)
eps = 1e-8
racines = []

# Une racine paire dans chaque intervalle (n*pi, n*pi + pi/2)
# et une racine impaire dans ((n+1/2)*pi, (n+1)*pi).
for n in range(10):
    a_pair = n * np.pi + eps
    b_pair = min(n * np.pi + np.pi / 2 - eps, z0 - eps)
    if a_pair < b_pair:
        f_pair = lambda z: z * np.tan(z) - np.sqrt(z0**2 - z**2)
        try:
            racines.append((bisection(f_pair, a_pair, b_pair), "pair"))
        except ValueError:
            pass

    a_impair = n * np.pi + np.pi / 2 + eps
    b_impair = min((n + 1) * np.pi - eps, z0 - eps)
    if a_impair < b_impair:
        f_impair = lambda z: -z / np.tan(z) - np.sqrt(z0**2 - z**2)
        try:
            racines.append((bisection(f_impair, a_impair, b_impair), "impair"))
        except ValueError:
            pass

racines.sort(key=lambda element: element[0])
x = np.linspace(-2.2 * L, 2.2 * L, 3000)
V = np.where(np.abs(x) < L / 2, 0.0, V0)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.8))

# Schéma simple de la situation
axes[0].plot(x / L, V, color="black", lw=2.4)
axes[0].fill_between(x / L, V, V0 + 4, where=np.abs(x) >= L / 2,
                     color="0.90", alpha=0.8)
axes[0].annotate("onde évanescente", xy=(0.75, 8), xytext=(1.20, 15),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=VIOLET), color=VIOLET)
axes[0].annotate("région oscillante", xy=(0, 3), xytext=(-0.45, 9),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=BLEU), color=BLEU)
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$x/L$", ylabel=r"$V(x)$",
            xlim=(-1.7, 1.7), ylim=(-1, V0 + 4))

# États analytiques raccordés et normalisés
axes[1].plot(x / L, V, color="black", lw=1.8, label=r"$V(x)$")
for indice, (z, parite) in enumerate(racines, start=1):
    k = 2 * z / L
    E = k**2
    kappa = np.sqrt(V0 - E)
    interieur = np.abs(x) < L / 2

    if parite == "pair":
        bord = np.cos(k * L / 2)
        psi = np.where(interieur, np.cos(k * x),
                       bord * np.exp(-kappa * (np.abs(x) - L / 2)))
    else:
        bord = np.sin(k * L / 2)
        psi = np.where(interieur, np.sin(k * x),
                       np.sign(x) * bord * np.exp(-kappa * (np.abs(x) - L / 2)))

    psi /= np.sqrt(integrale_trapezes(psi**2, x))
    decalage = 1.15 * psi / np.max(np.abs(psi))
    axes[1].hlines(E, x[0] / L, x[-1] / L, color="0.75", lw=0.7)
    axes[1].plot(x / L, E + decalage, lw=1.8,
                 label=rf"$E_{indice}={E:.2f}$ ({parite})")

axes[1].axhline(V0, color=ROUGE, ls="--", lw=1.2)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$x/L$", ylabel="énergie et états décalés",
            xlim=(-1.7, 1.7), ylim=(-1, V0 + 4))
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: Puits carré fini : potentiel, niveaux liés et pénétration exponentielle des fonctions d’onde.





La fonction d’onde ne s’annule pas brutalement aux parois : elle possède des queues exponentielles de longueur caractéristique \(1/\kappa\). L’énergie d’un niveau est donc plus faible que celle du niveau correspondant dans un puits infini de même largeur, car la région effectivement explorée par la particule est plus grande.






ImportantLecture physique des limites




Lorsque \(V_0\to+\infty\), \(\kappa\to+\infty\), les queues disparaissent et les niveaux tendent vers ceux du puits infini.
Lorsque \(E\to V_0^-\), \(\kappa\to0\) : l’état s’étale très loin hors du puits et est faiblement lié.
En une dimension, tout puits attractif localisé suffisamment régulier possède au moins un état lié, même s’il est très peu profond.





2.3 Le potentiel delta attractif
Le potentiel delta constitue la limite idéale d’un puits extrêmement étroit et profond dont l’aire reste finie :
\[
V(x)=-g\,\delta(x),
\qquad g>0.
\tag{24}\]
Partout sauf en \(x=0\), le potentiel est nul. Pour un état lié \(E<0\), posons
\[
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{-2mE}}{\hbar}.
\]
La normalisabilité impose une décroissance de part et d’autre de l’origine :
\[
\psi(x)=A e^{-\kappa|x|}.
\tag{25}\]
La fonction est continue mais sa dérivée change brutalement. Intégrons l’équation de Schrödinger autour de l’origine :
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}
\left[\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)\right]
-g\psi(0)=0.
\]
Le saut vaut donc
\[
\boxed{
\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)
=-\frac{2mg}{\hbar^2}\psi(0)}.
\tag{26}\]
Pour \(Ae^{-\kappa|x|}\), on a \(\psi'(0^+)=-\kappa A\) et \(\psi'(0^-)=+\kappa A\). La condition précédente donne
\[
-2\kappa A=-\frac{2mg}{\hbar^2}A,
\qquad
\kappa=\frac{mg}{\hbar^2}.
\]
Il existe donc un unique état lié, d’énergie
\[
\boxed{E=-\frac{mg^2}{2\hbar^2}},
\tag{27}\]
et sa normalisation fournit
\[
\boxed{
\psi(x)=\sqrt{\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|}}.
\tag{28}\]


Afficher le code Python
kappa = 1.0
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 1800)
psi = np.sqrt(kappa) * np.exp(-kappa * np.abs(x))
E = -kappa**2  # unités hbar²/(2m)=1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))

axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=1.2)
axes[0].annotate("", xy=(0, -1.7), xytext=(0, 0),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", lw=4, color=ROUGE))
axes[0].text(0.15, -1.2, r"$-g\,\delta(x)$", color=ROUGE)
axes[0].set(xlim=(-3, 3), ylim=(-2, 0.4), xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$V(x)$")

axes[1].plot(x, psi, color=BLEU, lw=2.3, label=r"$\psi(x)$")
axes[1].plot(x, psi**2, color=ORANGE, lw=2.0, label=r"$|\psi(x)|^2$")
axes[1].axvline(0, color=ROUGE, ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel="amplitude", xlim=(-5, 5))
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: Potentiel delta attractif et unique état lié exponentiellement localisé.





Le coin visible de \(\psi\) à l’origine est précisément la manifestation du saut de dérivée. Le potentiel delta est singulier, mais il résume avec une grande économie mathématique le comportement de nombreux défauts ou interactions de très courte portée.

title: L’équation de Schrödinger et les potentiels par morceaux
section: 3 Diffusion quantique : marche, barrière et effet tunnel
text:
3 Diffusion quantique : marche, barrière et effet tunnel
Dans un problème de diffusion, la particule n’est pas localisée. On prépare une onde incidente, puis on calcule les ondes réfléchie et transmise par le potentiel. Ces états ne sont pas normalisables au sens usuel sur toute la droite ; leur interprétation repose sur des rapports de courants.
Si \(j_{\mathrm i}\), \(j_{\mathrm r}\) et \(j_{\mathrm t}\) désignent respectivement les courants incident, réfléchi et transmis, nous définissons
\[
R=\frac{|j_{\mathrm r}|}{j_{\mathrm i}},
\qquad
T=\frac{j_{\mathrm t}}{j_{\mathrm i}}.
\tag{29}\]
Pour un potentiel réel et stationnaire qui n’absorbe pas la particule, la conservation du courant impose
\[
\boxed{R+T=1}.
\tag{30}\]

3.1 La marche de potentiel avec \(E>V_0\)
Considérons
\[
V(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x<0,\\
V_0, & x\geq0.
\end{cases}
\tag{31}\]
Une particule arrive depuis la gauche avec une énergie \(E>V_0\). Les nombres d’onde sont
\[
k_1=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},
\qquad
k_2=\frac{\sqrt{2m(E-V_0)}}{\hbar}.
\]
Il existe une onde incidente et une onde réfléchie dans la région I. Dans la région II, aucune onde ne revient de \(+infty\). En fixant l’amplitude incidente à un, écrivons
\[
\psi_{\mathrm I}(x)=e^{ik_1x}+r e^{-ik_1x},
\qquad
\psi_{\mathrm{II}}(x)=t e^{ik_2x}.
\tag{32}\]
Au point \(x=0\), la continuité de \(\psi\) donne
\[
1+r=t,
\]
et celle de \(\psi'\) donne
\[
k_1(1-r)=k_2t.
\]
En remplaçant \(t\) par \(1+r\) dans la seconde relation,
\[
k_1-k_1r=k_2+k_2r,
\]
d’où
\[
r=\frac{k_1-k_2}{k_1+k_2},
\qquad
t=1+r=\frac{2k_1}{k_1+k_2}.
\tag{33}\]
Attention : \(|t|^2\) n’est pas directement la probabilité de transmission, car les vitesses diffèrent dans les deux régions. Les courants conduisent à
\[
R=|r|^2
=\left(\frac{k_1-k_2}{k_1+k_2}\right)^2,
\]
\[
T=\frac{k_2}{k_1}|t|^2
=\frac{4k_1k_2}{(k_1+k_2)^2}.
\tag{34}\]
On vérifie immédiatement que \(R+T=1\).






ImportantUne réflexion sans point de rebroussement classique



Classiquement, une particule avec \(E>V_0\) franchit toujours la marche. Quantiquement, \(R\) est généralement non nul : le changement brusque de longueur d’onde crée une réflexion partielle. La réflexion disparaît seulement lorsque \(V_0=0\), donc lorsque \(k_1=k_2\).




3.2 La marche de potentiel avec \(E<V_0\)
Si \(0<E<V_0\), la région II est classiquement interdite. Posons
\[
k=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},
\qquad
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}.
\]
La solution qui ne diverge pas lorsque \(x\to+\infty\) est
\[
\psi_{\mathrm I}(x)=e^{ikx}+r e^{-ikx},
\qquad
\psi_{\mathrm{II}}(x)=C e^{-\kappa x}.
\tag{35}\]
Les raccordements en \(x=0\) sont
\[
1+r=C,
\qquad
ik(1-r)=-\kappa C.
\]
En éliminant \(C\), on trouve
\[
r=\frac{k-i\kappa}{k+i\kappa},
\qquad
C=\frac{2k}{k+i\kappa}.
\tag{36}\]
Le numérateur et le dénominateur de \(r\) sont complexes conjugués. Par conséquent,
\[
|r|=1,
\qquad
R=1,
\qquad
T=0.
\tag{37}\]
Il existe pourtant une densité non nulle dans la région interdite :
\[
|\psi_{\mathrm{II}}(x)|^2
=|C|^2e^{-2\kappa x}.
\]
Elle décroît sur une longueur de pénétration de l’ordre de
\[
\ell_{\mathrm p}=\frac{1}{\kappa}.
\tag{38}\]
Cette onde évanescente ne transporte aucun courant vers \(+infty\), car \(C e^{-\kappa x}\) peut être choisie réelle à une phase globale près. Il n’y a donc aucune contradiction entre \(|\psi|^2\neq0\) près de la marche et \(T=0\).


Afficher le code Python
V0 = 1.0
xg = np.linspace(-9, 0, 1500, endpoint=False)
xd = np.linspace(0, 9, 1500)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7.0),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.85, 1.4]})

cas = [(2.0, "propagation : $E>V_0$"), (0.55, "évanescence : $E<V_0$")]
for ligne, (E, titre) in enumerate(cas):
    axV, axPsi = axes[ligne]

    # Dessin du potentiel et de l'énergie
    axV.plot([-5, 0, 0, 5], [0, 0, V0, V0], color="black", lw=2.5)
    axV.axhline(E, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=2, label=r"énergie $E$")
    axV.annotate("onde incidente", xy=(-0.7, 0.12), xytext=(-4.4, 0.12),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=BLEU), color=BLEU)
    axV.annotate("réfléchie", xy=(-4.3, 0.28), xytext=(-1.2, 0.28),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ROUGE), color=ROUGE)
    if E > V0:
        axV.annotate("transmise", xy=(4.2, V0 + 0.12), xytext=(0.6, V0 + 0.12),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=VERT), color=VERT)
    else:
        axV.text(0.35, V0 + 0.12, "queue évanescente", color=VIOLET)
    axV.set(xlim=(-5, 5), ylim=(-0.1, 2.3), ylabel=r"$V(x)$", title=titre)
    axV.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")

    k1 = np.sqrt(E)
    if E > V0:
        k2 = np.sqrt(E - V0)
        r = (k1 - k2) / (k1 + k2)
        t = 2 * k1 / (k1 + k2)
        psi_g = np.exp(1j * k1 * xg) + r * np.exp(-1j * k1 * xg)
        psi_d = t * np.exp(1j * k2 * xd)
        axPsi.plot(xg, np.real(psi_g), color=BLEU, lw=1.8)
        axPsi.plot(xd, np.real(psi_d), color=VERT, lw=1.8)
        axPsi.set_ylabel(r"$\operatorname{Re}\psi$")
        T = 4 * k1 * k2 / (k1 + k2)**2
        axPsi.text(0.97, 0.88, rf"$T={T:.3f}$", transform=axPsi.transAxes,
                   ha="right", color=VERT)
    else:
        kappa = np.sqrt(V0 - E)
        r = (k1 - 1j * kappa) / (k1 + 1j * kappa)
        C = 2 * k1 / (k1 + 1j * kappa)
        psi_g = np.exp(1j * k1 * xg) + r * np.exp(-1j * k1 * xg)
        psi_d = C * np.exp(-kappa * xd)
        axPsi.plot(xg, np.abs(psi_g)**2, color=BLEU, lw=1.8)
        axPsi.plot(xd, np.abs(psi_d)**2, color=VIOLET, lw=2.2)
        axPsi.set_ylabel(r"$|\psi|^2$")
        axPsi.text(0.97, 0.88, r"$R=1$, $T=0$", transform=axPsi.transAxes,
                   ha="right", color=VIOLET)

    axPsi.axvline(0, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
    axPsi.set(xlim=(-9, 9), xlabel=r"$x$")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4: Marche de potentiel : propagation partielle pour une énergie supérieure à la marche et onde évanescente pour une énergie inférieure.







3.3 La barrière rectangulaire
Plaçons maintenant une région interdite de largeur finie entre deux régions libres :
\[
V(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x<0,\\
V_0, & 0\leq x\leq a,\\
0, & x>a.
\end{cases}
\tag{39}\]
La différence avec la marche est importante. L’onde évanescente peut atteindre la seconde interface et y engendrer une onde propagative. Une particule peut donc traverser la barrière même lorsque \(E<V_0\).

3.3.1 Cas \(E>V_0\) : propagation et résonances
Définissons
\[
k=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},
\qquad
q=\frac{\sqrt{2m(E-V_0)}}{\hbar}.
\]
Les trois solutions sont choisies sous la forme
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi_{\mathrm I}(x)&=e^{ikx}+r e^{-ikx},\\
\psi_{\mathrm{II}}(x)&=Ae^{iqx}+Be^{-iqx},\\
\psi_{\mathrm{III}}(x)&=t e^{ik(x-a)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{40}\]
La phase de la dernière onde a été choisie pour que \(\psi_{\mathrm{III}}(a)=t\). Les raccordements en \(0\) donnent
\[
1+r=A+B,
\qquad
k(1-r)=q(A-B),
\]
et ceux en \(a\) donnent
\[
Ae^{iqa}+Be^{-iqa}=t,
\]
\[
q\left(Ae^{iqa}-Be^{-iqa}\right)=kt.
\]
La résolution de ces quatre équations linéaires conduit à
\[
t=\left[
\cos(qa)-i\frac{k^2+q^2}{2kq}\sin(qa)
\right]^{-1}.
\tag{41}\]
Les nombres d’onde étant les mêmes à gauche et à droite, \(T=|t|^2\). En utilisant \(k^2-q^2=2mV_0/\hbar^2\), on obtient
\[
\boxed{
T(E>V_0)=
\left[
1+\frac{V_0^2}{4E(E-V_0)}\sin^2(qa)
\right]^{-1}}.
\tag{42}\]
Lorsque \(qa=n\pi\), l’onde effectue un nombre entier de demi-longueurs d’onde dans la barrière et
\[
T=1.
\]
La barrière devient parfaitement transparente par interférence constructive, bien que chaque interface prise séparément soit réfléchissante.


3.3.2 Cas \(E<V_0\) : effet tunnel
Posons maintenant
\[
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}.
\]
Dans la barrière, il faut conserver les deux exponentielles,
\[
\psi_{\mathrm{II}}(x)=Ae^{\kappa x}+Be^{-\kappa x},
\]
car la région interdite possède une largeur finie. Le terme croissant ne diverge pas sur l’intervalle \([0,a]\) et participe au raccordement sur la seconde interface.
Le résultat précédent se prolonge en remplaçant \(q\) par \(i\kappa\), avec
\[
\cos(i\kappa a)=\cosh(\kappa a),
\qquad
\sin(i\kappa a)=i\sinh(\kappa a).
\]
On trouve
\[
\boxed{
T(E<V_0)=
\left[
1+\frac{V_0^2}{4E(V_0-E)}\sinh^2(\kappa a)
\right]^{-1}}.
\tag{43}\]
Pour une barrière opaque, \(\kappa a\gg1\), on utilise \(\sinh(\kappa a)\simeq e^{\kappa a}/2\) :
\[
T\simeq
16\frac{E(V_0-E)}{V_0^2}
e^{-2\kappa a}.
\tag{44}\]
Le facteur exponentiel est le résultat important. Une légère augmentation de la largeur \(a\), de la masse \(m\) ou de l’écart \(V_0-E\) peut réduire la transmission de plusieurs ordres de grandeur.


Afficher le code Python
epsilon = np.linspace(0.015, 4.0, 2600)  # E/V0
largeurs = [0.8, 2.0, 4.0]               # a*sqrt(2mV0)/hbar

def transmission_barriere(epsilon, alpha):
    epsilon = np.asarray(epsilon, dtype=float)
    T = np.empty_like(epsilon)
    dessous = epsilon < 1 - 1e-7
    dessus = epsilon > 1 + 1e-7
    seuil = ~(dessous | dessus)

    e = epsilon[dessous]
    T[dessous] = 1 / (1 + np.sinh(alpha * np.sqrt(1 - e))**2 /
                      (4 * e * (1 - e)))

    e = epsilon[dessus]
    T[dessus] = 1 / (1 + np.sin(alpha * np.sqrt(e - 1))**2 /
                     (4 * e * (e - 1)))

    T[seuil] = 1 / (1 + alpha**2 / 4)
    return T

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.85, 1.45]})

# Dessin de la barrière
axes[0].plot([-1.5, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2.5], [0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0],
             color="black", lw=2.5)
axes[0].fill_between([0, 1], [0, 0], [1, 1], color="0.88")
axes[0].axhline(0.58, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=2)
axes[0].annotate("incidente", xy=(-0.1, 0.18), xytext=(-1.3, 0.18),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=BLEU), color=BLEU)
axes[0].annotate("réfléchie", xy=(-1.25, 0.34), xytext=(-0.15, 0.34),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ROUGE), color=ROUGE)
axes[0].annotate("transmise", xy=(2.3, 0.18), xytext=(1.15, 0.18),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=VERT), color=VERT)
axes[0].text(0.5, 1.06, r"$V_0$", ha="center")
axes[0].text(0.5, -0.12, r"largeur $a$", ha="center")
axes[0].set(xlim=(-1.5, 2.5), ylim=(-0.2, 1.25), xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$V(x)$")
axes[0].set_xticks([0, 1], ["0", "$a$"])

# Courbes de transmission
for alpha, couleur in zip(largeurs, [VERT, BLEU, VIOLET]):
    axes[1].plot(epsilon, transmission_barriere(epsilon, alpha),
                 color=couleur, lw=2, label=rf"$a\sqrt{{2mV_0}}/\hbar={alpha}$")
axes[1].axvline(1, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].text(0.55, 0.08, "effet tunnel", ha="center", color=VIOLET)
axes[1].text(2.5, 0.08, "résonances", ha="center", color=VERT)
axes[1].set(xlim=(0, 4), ylim=(-0.02, 1.04), xlabel=r"$E/V_0$", ylabel=r"$T$")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5: Barrière rectangulaire et coefficient de transmission en fonction de l’énergie pour plusieurs largeurs réduites.











NoteRepère historique : l’effet tunnel





En 1928, George Gamow ainsi que Ronald Gurney et Edward Condon expliquent la désintégration alpha par effet tunnel. Une particule alpha, dont l’énergie est inférieure à la barrière coulombienne du noyau, possède néanmoins une probabilité de s’échapper. La dépendance exponentielle de \(T\) explique pourquoi de petites variations d’énergie conduisent à des durées de vie nucléaires allant de fractions de seconde à des milliards d’années.






3.4 Diffusion par un potentiel delta
Reprenons le potentiel delta sous sa forme générale
\[
V(x)=\lambda\delta(x),
\]
où \(\lambda\) peut être positif ou négatif. Pour une particule incidente depuis la gauche,
\[
\psi(x)=
\begin{cases}
e^{ikx}+r e^{-ikx}, & x<0,\\
t e^{ikx}, & x>0.
\end{cases}
\]
La continuité donne \(1+r=t\). Le saut de dérivée est cette fois
\[
\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)
=\frac{2m\lambda}{\hbar^2}\psi(0).
\tag{45}\]
En substituant les ondes planes,
\[
ikt-ik(1-r)=\frac{2m\lambda}{\hbar^2}t.
\]
Avec \(t=1+r\) et
\[
\eta=\frac{m\lambda}{\hbar^2k},
\]
nous obtenons
\[
t=\frac{1}{1+i\eta},
\qquad
r=\frac{-i\eta}{1+i\eta}.
\tag{46}\]
Par conséquent,
\[
\boxed{
T=\frac{1}{1+\eta^2},
\qquad
R=\frac{\eta^2}{1+\eta^2}}.
\tag{47}\]
La transmission ne dépend que de \(\lambda^2\), mais seul le cas attractif \(\lambda<0\) possède l’état lié trouvé précédemment.


Afficher le code Python
k = np.linspace(0.05, 5, 1200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
for alpha, couleur in zip([0.5, 1.0, 2.0], [VERT, BLEU, VIOLET]):
    # alpha = m|lambda|/hbar² ; eta = alpha/k
    T = 1 / (1 + (alpha / k)**2)
    ax.plot(k, T, color=couleur, lw=2, label=rf"$m|\lambda|/\hbar^2={alpha}$")
ax.set(xlabel=r"nombre d'onde $k$", ylabel=r"transmission $T$",
       xlim=(0, 5), ylim=(0, 1.03))
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: Transmission à travers un potentiel delta pour plusieurs intensités sans dimension.





À basse énergie, la particule est presque totalement réfléchie. À grande énergie, sa longueur d’onde devient courte devant l’échelle introduite par \(\lambda\) et le défaut devient presque transparent.


3.5 Plusieurs interfaces et matrices de propagation
Répéter les raccordements à la main devient fastidieux pour une succession de puits et de barrières. Une formulation matricielle rassemble le calcul. Dans une région de largeur \(d\) où \(V\) est constant et \(E>V\), la connaissance de \(\psi\) et \(\psi'\) au bord gauche détermine leur valeur au bord droit :
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi(x+d)\\[2mm]
\psi'(x+d)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos(kd) & \dfrac{\sin(kd)}{k}\\[3mm]
-k\sin(kd) & \cos(kd)
\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf P(k,d)}
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi(x)\\[2mm]
\psi'(x)
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{48}\]
Cette relation se vérifie en écrivant la solution comme combinaison de \(\cos(kx)\) et \(\sin(kx)\). Pour \(E<V\), il suffit de prendre \(k=i\kappa\) ; les fonctions trigonométriques deviennent automatiquement hyperboliques.
Pour \(N\) couches successives, la matrice totale est le produit ordonné
\[
\mathbf P_{\mathrm{tot}}
=\mathbf P_N\mathbf P_{N-1}\cdots\mathbf P_1.
\tag{49}\]
La continuité de \(\psi\) et de \(\psi'\) aux interfaces est déjà incorporée, puisque le même vecteur d’état est transmis d’une couche à la suivante.
Un système à deux barrières illustre l’intérêt de la méthode. Entre les deux barrières, les réflexions multiples peuvent construire une onde quasi liée. À certaines énergies, cette interférence rend l’ensemble presque parfaitement transparent : c’est le tunnel résonant.


Afficher le code Python
def matrice_propagation(E, V, largeur):
    q = np.sqrt(complex(E - V))
    if abs(q) < 1e-11:
        return np.array([[1, largeur], [0, 1]], dtype=complex)
    c = np.cos(q * largeur)
    s = np.sin(q * largeur)
    return np.array([[c, s / q], [-q * s, c]], dtype=complex)

def transmission_couches(E, couches):
    """couches est une liste de couples (V, largeur), en unités hbar²/(2m)=1."""
    k = np.sqrt(E)
    matrice = np.eye(2, dtype=complex)
    for V, largeur in couches:
        matrice = matrice_propagation(E, V, largeur) @ matrice

    incident = np.array([1, 1j * k], dtype=complex)
    reflechi = np.array([1, -1j * k], dtype=complex)
    sortant = np.array([1, 1j * k], dtype=complex)

    # M(incident + r*réfléchi) = t*sortant
    systeme = np.column_stack((matrice @ reflechi, -sortant))
    r, t = np.linalg.solve(systeme, -(matrice @ incident))
    return float(np.clip(abs(t)**2, 0, 1 + 1e-10))

V0, a, d = 1.0, 1.25, 3.2
energies = np.linspace(0.02, 0.995, 1800)
simple = [(V0, a)]
double = [(V0, a), (0.0, d), (V0, a)]
T_simple = np.array([transmission_couches(E, simple) for E in energies])
T_double = np.array([transmission_couches(E, double) for E in energies])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.9, 1.45]})

x_schema = [-2, 0, 0, a, a, a + d, a + d, 2 * a + d,
            2 * a + d, 2 * a + d + 2]
V_schema = [0, 0, V0, V0, 0, 0, V0, V0, 0, 0]
axes[0].plot(x_schema, V_schema, color="black", lw=2.4)
axes[0].fill_between([0, a], 0, V0, color="0.88")
axes[0].fill_between([a + d, 2 * a + d], 0, V0, color="0.88")
axes[0].annotate("état quasi lié", xy=(a + d / 2, 0.25),
                 xytext=(a + d / 2, 0.62), ha="center",
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=VIOLET), color=VIOLET)
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$V(x)$", ylim=(-0.08, 1.18))
axes[0].set_xticks([])

axes[1].plot(energies / V0, T_simple, color=GRIS, lw=1.7,
             label="une barrière")
axes[1].plot(energies / V0, T_double, color=VIOLET, lw=2.0,
             label="double barrière")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$E/V_0$", ylabel=r"$T$", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.03))
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7: Double barrière et tunnel résonant : des pics étroits de transmission apparaissent sous la hauteur des barrières.











NoteLimite de la matrice de transfert





Pour des barrières très épaisses, les termes \(e^{\kappa d}\) peuvent devenir gigantesques et rendre le produit matriciel numériquement mal conditionné. Les calculs professionnels utilisent alors souvent une matrice de diffusion, des méthodes récursives ou des renormalisations intermédiaires. Le formalisme reste physiquement correct ; c’est sa mise en œuvre naïve en précision finie qui devient fragile.

title: L’équation de Schrödinger et les potentiels par morceaux
section: 4 Résoudre numériquement un potentiel quelconque par morceaux
text:
4 Résoudre numériquement un potentiel quelconque par morceaux
Les problèmes précédents exploitent des solutions analytiques dans chaque région. Pour une géométrie plus compliquée, on peut discrétiser directement l’hamiltonien.

4.1 Discrétisation de l’hamiltonien
Sur une grille uniforme \(x_i=x_{\min}+i\Delta x\), la dérivée seconde est approchée par
\[
\psi''(x_i)
\simeq
\frac{\psi_{i+1}-2\psi_i+\psi_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2}.
\tag{50}\]
L’équation stationnaire devient un problème matriciel
\[
\mathbf H\boldsymbol\psi=E\boldsymbol\psi,
\tag{51}\]
avec
\[
H_{ii}=\frac{\hbar^2}{m\Delta x^2}+V(x_i),
\]
\[
H_{i,i+1}=H_{i+1,i}
=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m\Delta x^2}.
\tag{52}\]
La matrice est réelle symétrique, donc ses valeurs propres sont réelles et ses vecteurs propres peuvent être choisis orthogonaux. Les conditions de Dirichlet \(\psi=0\) aux extrémités jouent le rôle de murs éloignés.
Le code suivant étudie deux puits séparés par une barrière carrée centrale. Lorsque la barrière est haute, les deux premiers états forment un doublet presque dégénéré : l’un est symétrique, l’autre antisymétrique.


Afficher le code Python
# Unités hbar²/(2m)=1 ; murs numériques en x = +-4
N = 420
x_complet = np.linspace(-4, 4, N + 2)
x = x_complet[1:-1]
dx = x[1] - x[0]

V = np.zeros_like(x)
V[np.abs(x) < 0.48] = 13.0

diagonale = 2 / dx**2 + V
hors_diagonale = -np.ones(N - 1) / dx**2
H = np.diag(diagonale) + np.diag(hors_diagonale, 1) + np.diag(hors_diagonale, -1)

energies, vecteurs = np.linalg.eigh(H)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))
ax.plot(x, V, color="black", lw=2.1, label=r"$V(x)$")
for n in range(4):
    psi = vecteurs[:, n]
    psi /= np.sqrt(integrale_trapezes(abs(psi)**2, x))
    # Fixe un signe uniquement pour rendre les figures reproductibles.
    if psi[np.argmax(abs(psi))] < 0:
        psi = -psi
    amplitude = 1.15 * psi / np.max(abs(psi))
    ax.hlines(energies[n], x[0], x[-1], color="0.76", lw=0.7)
    ax.plot(x, energies[n] + amplitude, lw=1.9,
            label=rf"$E_{n+1}={energies[n]:.3f}$")

ax.set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel="énergie et états décalés", xlim=(-4, 4))
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 8: Diagonalisation numérique d’un double puits carré : les quatre premiers états propres sont décalés de leur énergie.





La faible différence \(E_2-E_1\) contrôle le temps de tunnel d’un paquet initialement localisé dans un seul puits. Une combinaison \((\psi_1+\psi_2)/\sqrt2\) peut être concentrée à gauche, puis évoluer vers la droite avec une période de battement
\[
T_{\mathrm{tun}}=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{E_2-E_1}.
\tag{53}\]






ImportantContrôles numériques



Une diagonalisation qui renvoie des nombres n’est pas encore un résultat physique. Il faut vérifier :

la convergence des premières énergies lorsque \(N\) augmente ;
la petitesse de la fonction d’onde aux bords de la boîte ;
la normalisation et l’orthogonalité des états ;
le nombre de nœuds, qui doit croître avec le niveau en une dimension ;
les symétries attendues lorsque le potentiel est pair.

ImportantErreurs classiques à éviter




Confondre une amplitude \(t\) avec une probabilité \(T\) lorsque les nombres d’onde asymptotiques diffèrent.
Poser \(\psi=0\) dès que \(E<V\) : la solution est en général évanescente, pas nulle.
Éliminer l’exponentielle croissante dans une barrière de largeur finie : elle ne diverge pas sur un intervalle borné.
Imposer la continuité de \(\psi'\) à travers un potentiel delta.
Croire qu’une fonction d’onde stationnaire est indépendante du temps : seule sa densité l’est.
Interpréter une sortie numérique sans vérifier convergence, normalisation et courant.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text: ← Back to the course list

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
1 Fields and particles
The Poincaré group classifies a massive particle by its mass \(m\) and spin \(s\). A massless particle is instead classified by its helicity. This tells us what a particle is, but it does not yet give a local theory for its motion or interactions. For that purpose we introduce fields.
A field transforms in a finite-dimensional representation of the Lorentz group. Its components are not all necessarily physical. For example, a four-vector has four components, while a massive spin-\(1\) particle has three polarization states and a photon has only two. Equations of motion, constraints and gauge symmetry remove the extra components.
We use natural units, \(\hbar=c=1\), and the metric
\[
\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
\]
Therefore
\[
p^2=(p^0)^2-\mathbf p^2,
\qquad
\Box=\partial_t^2-\nabla^2.
\]
The main question throughout the chapter is simple: starting from a covariant field, how do we identify its physical particle states?

1.1 Lorentz representations
Finite-dimensional irreducible representations of the proper Lorentz group are labelled by two half-integers,
\[
(j_L,j_R).
\]
A scalar transforms as \((0,0)\). Left- and right-handed Weyl spinors transform as \((1/2,0)\) and \((0,1/2)\). A four-vector transforms as \((1/2,1/2)\). Under ordinary rotations,
\[
(j_L,j_R) ig|_{SO(3)}
=\bigoplus_{j=|j_L-j_R|}^{j_L+j_R}j.
\tag{1}\]
Thus a four-vector contains \(j=0\) and \(j=1\) sectors before its dynamics is imposed. A field representation and a physical particle representation are related, but they are not the same object.
The two Casimir operators of the Poincaré group are \(P^2\) and \(W^2\), where
\[
W^\mu=\frac12\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}
P_\nu M_{\rho\sigma}
\]
is the Pauli–Lubanski vector. For a massive one-particle state,
\[
P^2=m^2,
\qquad
W^2=-m^2s(s+1).
\tag{2}\]
In the rest frame, \(P^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\) and \(\mathbf W=m\mathbf J\). This is why the second invariant measures spin. For a massless particle with discrete helicity,
\[
W^\mu=hP^\mu.
\]

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
2 The scalar field

2.1 Klein–Gordon equation
The simplest relativistic field is a real scalar \(\phi(x)\). Its free action is
\[
S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L,
\qquad
\mathcal L=\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi
-\frac12m^2\phi^2.
\tag{3}\]
The field Euler–Lagrange equation is
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi}
-\partial_\mu\frac{\partial\mathcal L}
{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}=0.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi}=-m^2\phi,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}
=\partial^\mu\phi,
\]
we obtain the Klein–Gordon equation
\[
\boxed{(\Box+m^2)\phi=0.}
\tag{4}\]
For a plane wave
\[
\phi(x)=Ae^{-ip\cdot x},
\]
the equation gives
\[
p^2=m^2,
\qquad
E_{\mathbf p}=\sqrt{\mathbf p^2+m^2}.
\tag{5}\]
Both signs \(p^0=\pm E_{\mathbf p}\) solve the classical equation. After quantization, they will be reinterpreted as particle creation and annihilation modes; they are not negative-energy particles propagating freely.
The canonical momentum is
\[
\pi(x)=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot\phi}=\dot\phi.
\]
The Hamiltonian density is
\[
\mathcal H=\pi\dot\phi-\mathcal L
=\frac12\pi^2+\frac12(\nabla\phi)^2+\frac12m^2\phi^2.
\tag{6}\]
It is non-negative for \(m^2\geq0\). This is an important test of the stability of the free theory.






NoteThe first relativistic wave equation





The Klein–Gordon equation appeared before the Dirac equation as the direct quantum version of \(E^2=\mathbf p^2+m^2\). Its conserved density is not positive definite, so it could not serve as a one-particle probability density. In quantum field theory this difficulty disappears: the field describes particles and antiparticles, and its conserved current is interpreted as a charge current.





2.2 Complex scalar field
A charged scalar field must be complex. Its Lagrangian density is
\[
\mathcal L
=\partial_\mu\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-m^2\phi^*\phi.
\tag{7}\]
It is invariant under the global phase transformation
\[
\phi\to e^{-iq\alpha}\phi,
\qquad
\phi^*\to e^{iq\alpha}\phi^*.
\]
The Noether current is
\[
j^\mu=iq\left(
\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-phi\partial^\mu\phi^*
\right),
\qquad
\partial_\mu j^\mu=0.
\tag{8}\]
The field and its complex conjugate carry opposite charges. After quantization, their two sets of modes create particles and antiparticles.


2.3 Degrees of freedom
The Klein–Gordon equation is second order in time. A real solution is fixed by two real functions, \(\phi(t_0,\mathbf x)\) and \(\dot\phi(t_0,\mathbf x)\). In momentum space, these data combine into one annihilation amplitude and its complex conjugate. The quantized real field therefore describes one neutral spin-\(0\) particle species.
A complex field is equivalent to two real fields,
\[
\phi=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\phi_1+i\phi_2),
\]
and describes a charged particle together with its antiparticle.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
3 The Dirac field

3.1 Linearizing the relativistic dispersion relation
The Klein–Gordon equation is second order in time. Dirac looked for an equation that was first order in both time and space,
\[
(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu-m)\psi=0.
\tag{9}\]
We use the slash notation
\[
\not\!p=\gamma^\mu p_\mu,
\qquad
\not\!\partial=\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu.
\]
To recover the relativistic mass-shell relation, multiply Equation 9 by \((i\not\!\partial+m)\):
\[
(i\not\!\partial+m)(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi
=\left[-\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\partial_\mu\partial_\nu-m^2\right]\psi.
\]
The derivatives are symmetric in \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), so only the symmetric part of the matrix product contributes. We must impose the Clifford algebra
\[
\boxed{\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf1_4.}
\tag{10}\]
Then every component of the spinor satisfies
\[
(\Box+m^2)\psi=0.
\]
No set of ordinary numbers can satisfy Equation 10. In four dimensions, the smallest matrices are \(4\times4\), so a Dirac spinor has four complex components.
In the Dirac representation,
\[
\gamma^0=
\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&-I\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\gamma^i=
\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma^i\\-\sigma^i&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The explicit matrices depend on the chosen basis, but physical results do not.


3.2 Action and Lorentz covariance
The Dirac adjoint is defined by
\[
\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\gamma^0.
\]
The free action is
\[
S=\int d^4x\,\bar\psi(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi.
\tag{11}\]
Varying \(\bar\psi\) gives the Dirac equation. Varying \(\psi\) and integrating by parts gives the adjoint equation
\[
i(\partial_\mu\bar\psi)\gamma^\mu+m\bar\psi=0.
\tag{12}\]
Under a Lorentz transformation,
\[
\psi'(x')=S(\Lambda)\psi(x).
\]
Covariance of the equation requires
\[
S^{-1}(\Lambda)\gamma^\mu S(\Lambda)
=\Lambda^\mu{}_{\nu}\gamma^\nu.
\]
For an infinitesimal transformation,
\[
S(\Lambda)=1-\frac{i}{4}\omega_{\mu\nu}\sigma^{\mu\nu},
\qquad
\sigma^{\mu\nu}=\frac{i}{2}[\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu].
\tag{13}\]
The matrices \(\sigma^{\mu\nu}/2\) are the Lorentz generators in the spinor representation.
The phase symmetry \(\psi\to e^{-iq\alpha}\psi\) gives the current
\[
j^\mu=q\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi.
\tag{14}\]
Using Equation 9 and Equation 12,
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu=0.
\]
Its time component is
\[
j^0=q\psi^\dagger\psi.
\]
For \(q>0\) it is non-negative. In field theory, however, \(j^0\) is interpreted as a charge density, and the quantized field contains states of both charges.


3.3 Plane-wave spinors
Positive-frequency solutions are written
\[
\psi(x)=u_s(p)e^{-ip\cdot x},
\]
and satisfy
\[
(\not\!p-m)u_s(p)=0.
\tag{15}\]
Negative-frequency solutions are written
\[
\psi(x)=v_s(p)e^{ip\cdot x},
\]
and satisfy
\[
(\not\!p+m)v_s(p)=0.
\tag{16}\]
At rest, \(p^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\). In the Dirac basis, two independent \(u\) solutions occupy the upper components and two independent \(v\) solutions occupy the lower components. They correspond to the two spin projections of the particle and antiparticle.
For general momentum, a useful normalization is
\[
\bar u_r(p)u_s(p)=2m\delta_{rs},
\qquad
\bar v_r(p)v_s(p)=-2m\delta_{rs}.
\]
The completeness relations are
\[
\sum_su_s(p)\bar u_s(p)=\not\!p+m,
\]
\[
\sum_sv_s(p)\bar v_s(p)=\not\!p-m.
\tag{17}\]
They remove explicit spinors when squared amplitudes are calculated.
One possible explicit form is
\[
u_s(p)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{E_{\mathbf p}+m}\,\xi_s\\
\dfrac{\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p}
{\sqrt{E_{\mathbf p}+m}}\,\xi_s
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(\xi_s\) is a two-component spinor. The lower components become small when \(|\mathbf p|\ll m\), which leads to the nonrelativistic Pauli theory.






NoteDirac and the positron





Dirac’s equation combined special relativity with a first-order time evolution and naturally described spin \(1/2\). Its second family of solutions could not be removed consistently. In quantum field theory these modes create antiparticles. The positron, discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932, was the first experimental example.





3.4 Chirality and helicity
Define
\[
\gamma^5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3.
\]
It satisfies
\[
(\gamma^5)^2=1,
\qquad
\{\gamma^5,\gamma^\mu\}=0.
\]
The chiral projectors are
\[
P_L=\frac{1-\gamma^5}{2},
\qquad
P_R=\frac{1+\gamma^5}{2},
\]
so
\[
\psi_L=P_L\psi,
\qquad
\psi_R=P_R\psi,
\qquad
\psi=\psi_L+\psi_R.
\tag{18}\]
In terms of these fields, the mass term is
\[
m\bar\psi\psi
=m(\bar\psi_L\psi_R+\bar\psi_R\psi_L).
\tag{19}\]
Mass therefore couples the two chiralities. When \(m=0\), the left- and right-handed equations separate.
Helicity is the projection of spin along momentum,
\[
h=\frac{\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf p}{|\mathbf p|}.
\]
For a massive particle, a faster observer can reverse the direction of its momentum without reversing its spin, so helicity is frame-dependent. Chirality is defined by the Lorentz representation and is not changed by a proper Lorentz transformation. For massless positive-energy particles, chirality and helicity agree. For antiparticles, the relation must be handled with the corresponding \(v\) solutions.
The axial current is
\[
j_5^\mu=\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\psi.
\]
Classically,
\[
\partial_\mu j_5^\mu=2im\bar\psi\gamma^5\psi.
\tag{20}\]
It is conserved for a massless free Dirac field, although quantum interactions may introduce an anomaly.


3.5 Discrete symmetries
Parity reverses spatial coordinates,
\[
P:(t,\mathbf x)\to(t,-\mathbf x),
\]
and acts on a Dirac field, up to an intrinsic phase, as
\[
\psi_P(t,\mathbf x)=\gamma^0\psi(t,-\mathbf x).
\]
It exchanges left and right chirality. Charge conjugation transforms a particle field into its antiparticle field,
\[
\psi^C=C\bar\psi^{\,T},
\]
where
\[
C^{-1}\gamma^\mu C=-(\gamma^\mu)^T.
\]
A Majorana field satisfies \(\psi^C=\psi\) and is therefore neutral. Time reversal is antiunitary; the complex conjugation contained in an antiunitary transformation is essential. A local Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory with the usual assumptions is invariant under the combined CPT transformation.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
4 Vector fields

4.1 Massive vector: Proca theory
For a real vector field, define
\[
F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu.
\]
The Proca Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm P}
=-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}
+\frac12m^2A_\mu A^\mu.
\tag{21}\]
Varying \(A_\nu\) gives
\[
\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}+m^2A^\nu=0.
\tag{22}\]
Taking the divergence,
\[
\partial_\nu\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}
+m^2\partial_\nu A^\nu=0.
\]
The first term vanishes because \(F^{\mu\nu}\) is antisymmetric, while the derivatives are symmetric. If \(m\neq0\),
\[
\boxed{\partial_\mu A^\mu=0.}
\tag{23}\]
Using this constraint in Equation 22 gives
\[
(\Box+m^2)A^\nu=0.
\]
The four components are therefore reduced by one constraint, leaving three physical polarizations. In the rest frame they are the three spin projections of a massive spin-\(1\) particle.
For a plane wave \(A^\mu=\varepsilon^\mu(p)e^{-ip\cdot x}\),
\[
p_\mu\varepsilon^\mu(p)=0.
\]
With the normalization \(\varepsilon^{(\lambda)}\cdot\varepsilon^{(\lambda')}=-\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}\), the polarization sum is
\[
\sum_{\lambda=1}^{3}
\varepsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)}(p)
\varepsilon_\nu^{(\lambda)*}(p)
=-\eta_{\mu\nu}+\frac{p_\mu p_\nu}{m^2}.
\tag{24}\]


4.2 Massless vector: Maxwell theory
Setting \(m=0\) gives
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm M}=-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}.
\tag{25}\]
The action is invariant under
\[
A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha(x).
\tag{26}\]
This is a redundancy: potentials related by this transformation describe the same electric and magnetic fields. The Maxwell equation in vacuum is
\[
\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0.
\]
The Lorenz condition
\[
\partial_\mu A^\mu=0
\]
does not remove all gauge freedom. Transformations satisfying \(\Box\alpha=0\) preserve it. The constraint and the remaining gauge freedom leave two transverse photon polarizations.
For momentum along the \(z\) axis, they may be chosen as
\[
\varepsilon_{(1)}^\mu=(0,1,0,0),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{(2)}^\mu=(0,0,1,0).
\]
Their circular combinations have helicities \(+1\) and \(-1\). There is no physical helicity-zero photon.
When the field is coupled to a current,
\[
\mathcal L=-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-j_\mu A^\mu,
\]
gauge invariance requires
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu=0.
\]
Indeed, the interaction changes by a boundary term plus \(\alpha\partial_\mu j^\mu\). Charge conservation is therefore necessary for a consistent gauge coupling.
The limit \(m\to0\) of Proca theory is not obtained by simply setting \(m=0\) in every expression. The term \(p_\mu p_\nu/m^2\) in Equation 24 becomes singular. Gauge symmetry appears only in the massless theory and changes the way degrees of freedom are counted.






NoteFrom Proca to gauge fields





Alexandru Proca introduced the relativistic equation for a massive spin-\(1\) field in 1936. Maxwell theory has a similar kinetic term, but its vanishing mass gives it a gauge symmetry. This changes both its constraint structure and its physical number of polarizations.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
5 Canonical quantization

5.1 Real scalar field
The classical field is replaced by an operator and equal-time canonical commutators are imposed:
\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]
=i\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),
\]
\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\phi(t,\mathbf y)]=0,
\qquad
[\pi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]=0.
\tag{27}\]
The field is expanded in normal modes,
\[
\phi(x)=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[
a(\mathbf p)e^{-ip\cdot x}
+a^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{ip\cdot x}
\right].
\tag{28}\]
The normalization is chosen so that
\[
[a(\mathbf p),a^\dagger(\mathbf q)]
=(2\pi)^3\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\]
The vacuum satisfies \(a(\mathbf p)|0\rangle=0\). A one-particle state is
\[
|\mathbf p\rangle=\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}\,
a^\dagger(\mathbf p)|0\rangle,
\]
with relativistic normalization
\[
\langle\mathbf q|\mathbf p\rangle
=2E_{\mathbf p}(2\pi)^3
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\]
Substituting the expansion into the Hamiltonian gives
\[
H=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
E_{\mathbf p}
\left[a^\dagger(\mathbf p)a(\mathbf p)
+\frac12(2\pi)^3\delta^{(3)}(0)\right].
\]
The infinite second term is the vacuum energy. In a theory without gravity it is often removed by normal ordering,
\[
:H:=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
E_{\mathbf p}a^\dagger(\mathbf p)a(\mathbf p).
\]
For a complex scalar field, independent operators \(a\) and \(b\) are needed:
\[
\phi(x)=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[a(\mathbf p)e^{-ip\cdot x}
+b^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{ip\cdot x}\right].
\tag{29}\]
\(a^\dagger\) creates a particle and \(b^\dagger\) creates its antiparticle. The normal-ordered charge is proportional to
\[
Q=q\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\left[a^\dagger a-b^\dagger b\right].
\]


5.2 Dirac field and anticommutators
The Dirac field expansion is
\[
\psi(x)=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\sum_s\left[
b_s(\mathbf p)u_s(p)e^{-ip\cdot x}
+d_s^\dagger(\mathbf p)v_s(p)e^{ip\cdot x}
\right].
\tag{30}\]
\(b_s^\dagger\) creates a fermion and \(d_s^\dagger\) creates an antifermion. The non-zero anticommutators are
\[
\{b_r(\mathbf p),b_s^\dagger(\mathbf q)\}
=(2\pi)^3\delta_{rs}\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\]
\[
\{d_r(\mathbf p),d_s^\dagger(\mathbf q)\}
=(2\pi)^3\delta_{rs}\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\tag{31}\]
Because \((b_s^\dagger)^2=0\), two identical fermions cannot occupy the same one-particle state. Anticommutators also make the Hamiltonian bounded below and ensure microcausality for fermionic observables. The connection between half-integer spin and Fermi–Dirac statistics is a general theorem, not a special choice for the Dirac field.
After normal ordering,
\[
H=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\sum_sE_{\mathbf p}
\left[b_s^\dagger b_s+d_s^\dagger d_s\right],
\]
and
\[
Q=q\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\sum_s\left[b_s^\dagger b_s-d_s^\dagger d_s\right].
\]
Particles and antiparticles have positive energy and opposite charge.


5.3 Vector fields
A massive vector field has an expansion over its three physical polarizations,
\[
A_\mu(x)=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\sum_{\lambda=1}^{3}
\left[
a_\lambda(\mathbf p)\varepsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)}(p)e^{-ip\cdot x}
+a_\lambda^\dagger(\mathbf p)\varepsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)*}(p)e^{ip\cdot x}
\right].
\]
For the electromagnetic field, direct canonical quantization is more delicate because \(A^0\) has no independent canonical momentum and gauge-related configurations describe the same state. One may quantize only the transverse modes, or first add a gauge-fixing term and later select the physical states. Both approaches must produce two photon helicities.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
6 Propagators and causality

6.1 Scalar propagator
The scalar Feynman propagator is
\[
\Delta_F(x-y)
=\langle0|T\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle.
\]
In momentum space,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta_F(x-y)
=\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}
\frac{i\,e^{-ip\cdot(x-y)}}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}.}
\tag{32}\]
It satisfies
\[
(\Box_x+m^2)\Delta_F(x-y)
=-i\delta^{(4)}(x-y).
\]
The \(i\epsilon\) prescription specifies how the poles are passed and produces time ordering. Retarded and advanced Green functions obey the same differential equation but different boundary conditions; they answer different physical questions.
The field commutator is
\[
[\phi(x),\phi(y)]=i\Delta(x-y),
\]
where \(\Delta\) is the Pauli–Jordan function. It vanishes for spacelike separation,
\[
(x-y)^2<0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
[\phi(x),\phi(y)]=0.
\tag{33}\]
This is microcausality: measurements in spacelike-separated regions cannot influence one another.


6.2 Spinor and vector propagators
The Dirac propagator is
\[
S_F(x-y)=\langle0|T\psi(x)\bar\psi(y)|0\rangle.
\]
Using
\[
(\not\!p-m)(\not\!p+m)=p^2-m^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{
S_F(x-y)=\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}
\frac{i(\not\!p+m)e^{-ip\cdot(x-y)}}
{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}.}
\tag{34}\]
For the Proca field,
\[
\boxed{
D_{\mu\nu}(p)
=\frac{-i}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}
\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{p_\mu p_\nu}{m^2}\right).}
\tag{35}\]
The numerator reflects the massive spin-\(1\) polarization sum. For a massless gauge field, the kinetic operator cannot be inverted until a gauge is fixed. With
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{gf}}
=-\frac{1}{2\xi}(\partial_\mu A^\mu)^2,
\]
the photon propagator is
\[
D_{\mu\nu}(p)
=\frac{-i}{p^2+i\epsilon}
\left[
\eta_{\mu\nu}-(1-\xi)\frac{p_\mu p_\nu}{p^2}
\right].
\tag{36}\]
The parameter \(\xi\) changes the propagator but not physical amplitudes coupled to conserved currents, because terms proportional to \(p_\mu\) then vanish.
A propagator is not a classical trajectory. It is a two-point correlation function and the inverse of a quadratic differential operator with specified boundary conditions.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
7 Higher spins

7.1 Spin \(3/2\)
A Rarita–Schwinger field \(\psi_\mu\) carries both a vector and a spinor index. The vector-spinor contains more rotation sectors than spin \(3/2\), so constraints are required. For a free massive field one imposes
\[
(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi_\mu=0,
\]
with
\[
\gamma^\mu\psi_\mu=0,
\qquad
\partial^\mu\psi_\mu=0.
\tag{37}\]
The first removes the gamma trace and the second removes the longitudinal part. The remaining particle states have \(2s+1=4\) spin projections, together with four antiparticle states for a charged field.
For a massless spin-\(3/2\) field, a gauge-like redundancy
\[
\psi_\mu\to\psi_\mu+\partial_\mu\epsilon
\]
removes unphysical components and leaves helicities \(\pm3/2\).


7.2 Spin \(2\)
A massive spin-\(2\) field is described by a symmetric tensor \(h_{\mu\nu}\). A symmetric tensor in four dimensions has ten components, while a massive spin-\(2\) particle has five physical polarizations. The Fierz–Pauli equations imply
\[
(\Box+m^2)h_{\mu\nu}=0,
\]
\[
\partial^\mu h_{\mu\nu}=0,
\qquad
h^\mu{}_{\mu}=0.
\tag{38}\]
The four divergence constraints and the trace constraint reduce ten components to five. The relative form of the mass term is important: a generic quadratic mass term introduces an extra unstable scalar mode.
In the massless case, linearised diffeomorphism invariance,
\[
h_{\mu\nu}\to h_{\mu\nu}
+\partial_\mu\xi_\nu+\partial_\nu\xi_\mu,
\]
leaves two helicities, \(+2\) and \(-2\). They correspond to the two polarizations of a gravitational wave.
Higher-spin theories make the general lesson of this chapter especially clear. Covariance alone is not enough. The field equations and their constraints must remove all lower-spin components without producing negative-energy or negative-norm states. Interactions make these consistency conditions even stronger.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
8 Summary of the method
To analyse a free relativistic theory, begin with its Lorentz representation and action. Derive the equations instead of reading them directly from the final result. Then identify every constraint and every gauge redundancy before counting degrees of freedom. Solve the plane-wave equations and compare the remaining modes with the Poincaré labels \((m,s)\) or \((0,h)\). Finally, quantize the modes with the statistics required by their spin and read the propagator from the inverse quadratic operator.
For the main examples studied here, the result is straightforward. A real scalar field gives one neutral spin-\(0\) species. A Dirac field gives a spin-\(1/2\) particle and antiparticle, each with two spin states. A Proca field gives three massive spin-\(1\) polarizations. A Maxwell field gives two photon helicities. The same reasoning extends to spin \(3/2\) and spin \(2\), but the constraints become increasingly important.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
9 Further reading
Clear introductions can be found in D. Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles, and M. Thomson, Modern Particle Physics. For quantization and propagators, see M. Schwartz, Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model, or M. Srednicki, Quantum Field Theory.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
10 Exercises and problems
The stars indicate the difficulty, from a direct application (★) to a long problem connecting several parts of the chapter (★★★★). The solutions are folded so that each question can be attempted first.
As in the course, we use natural units, \(\hbar=c=1\), with
\[
\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1),
\qquad
\varepsilon^{0123}=+1,
\qquad
E_{\mathbf p}=\sqrt{\mathbf p^2+m^2}.
\]
We write
\[
\not\! p=\gamma^\mu p_\mu,
\qquad
\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf1_4,
\qquad
\gamma^5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3.
\]
Unless stated otherwise, the fields vanish fast enough at infinity for boundary terms to be ignored. Dirac distributions and mode operators use the normalization conventions of the chapter.

title: Free relativistic fields, spin and quantization
text:
11 Track 1 — Focused exercises

11.1 A. Scalar fields, covariance, and degrees of freedom

11.1.1 Exercise 1 — Canonical dimensions of free fields ★
In \(d=4\) spacetime dimensions, the action is dimensionless. Find the mass dimensions of \(x^\mu\), \(\partial_\mu\), a scalar field \(\phi\), a Dirac spinor \(\psi\), and a vector field \(A_\mu\). Check that the mass terms \(m^2\phi^2\), \(m\overline\psi\psi\), and \(m^2A_\mu A^\mu\) have the dimension of a Lagrangian density.






NoteSolution





In natural units, length has the inverse dimension of energy. Therefore,
\[
[x^\mu]=-1,
\qquad
[\partial_\mu]=1,
\qquad
[d^4x]=-4.
\]
Since \(S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L\) is dimensionless, \([\mathcal L]=4\).
The scalar kinetic term gives
\[
[\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi]
=2+2[\phi]=4,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{[\phi]=1.}
\]
For the Dirac field,
\[
[\overline\psi i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi]
=1+2[\psi]=4,
\]
because the gamma matrices are dimensionless. Thus,
\[
\boxed{[\psi]=[\overline\psi]=\frac32.}
\]
Finally, \(F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu\) and \(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\) require
\[
2(1+[A_\mu])=4,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{[A_\mu]=1.}
\]
The three mass terms then have the respective dimensions
\[
[m^2\phi^2]=2+2=4,
\quad
[m\overline\psi\psi]=1+\frac32+\frac32=4,
\quad
[m^2A^2]=2+2=4.
\]
This calculation will later help us quickly classify interactions by their dimension.





11.1.2 Exercise 2 — Klein–Gordon plane waves ★
Consider a real scalar field satisfying
\[
(\Box+m^2)\phi=0.
\]

Insert a plane wave \(\phi(x)=A e^{-ip\cdot x}\) and recover the dispersion relation.
Calculate the phase velocity and the group velocity.
Show that the group velocity remains less than or equal to \(1\).







NoteSolution





The derivative acts on the plane wave as
\[
\partial_\mu e^{-ip\cdot x}=-ip_\mu e^{-ip\cdot x},
\qquad
\Box e^{-ip\cdot x}=-p^2e^{-ip\cdot x}.
\]
The equation therefore gives
\[
(-p^2+m^2)A e^{-ip\cdot x}=0.
\]
For a nonzero solution,
\[
\boxed{p^2=m^2},
\qquad
(p^0)^2=\mathbf p^2+m^2.
\]
The positive-energy branch is \(E_{\mathbf p}=\sqrt{\mathbf p^2+m^2}\). For \(|\mathbf p|=p\),
\[
v_{\rm ph}=\frac{E_p}{p}
=\sqrt{1+\frac{m^2}{p^2}},
\]
which can be greater than \(1\). This is not the speed at which information travels. The velocity of a wave packet is
\[
v_{\rm g}=\frac{dE_p}{dp}
=\frac{p}{\sqrt{p^2+m^2}}
=\frac{p}{E_p}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{0\leq v_{\rm g}<1\quad(m>0),}
\]
and \(v_{\rm g}=1\) in the massless limit. We also find \(v_{\rm ph}v_{\rm g}=1\).





11.1.3 Exercise 3 — From the action to Klein–Gordon ★
For a real scalar field,
\[
S[\phi]=\int d^4x\left(
\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi
-\frac12m^2\phi^2\right).
\]
Carefully derive the Euler–Lagrange equation. Identify the boundary term and explain why it does not contribute.






NoteSolution





Make an arbitrary variation \(\phi\to\phi+\delta\phi\):
\[
\delta S
=\int d^4x\left(
\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\delta\phi
-m^2\phi\,\delta\phi\right).
\]
Integrating the first term by parts gives
\[
\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\delta\phi
=\partial_\mu(\partial^\mu\phi\,\delta\phi)
-(\Box\phi)\delta\phi.
\]
We obtain
\[
\delta S
=\int_{\partial\Omega}d\Sigma_\mu\,
\partial^\mu\phi\,\delta\phi
-\int_\Omega d^4x\,
(\Box\phi+m^2\phi)\delta\phi.
\]
We fix the field at the boundary, so \(\delta\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0\), or assume that the variation has compact support. The boundary term vanishes. Since \(\delta\phi\) is arbitrary inside,
\[
\boxed{(\Box+m^2)\phi=0.}
\]
Integration by parts is not a trick: it transfers the derivative from the variation to the field so that setting \(\delta S\) to zero gives a local equation.





11.1.4 Exercise 4 — Energy–momentum tensor of the scalar field ★★
Starting from the real Lagrangian in the previous exercise:

calculate the canonical tensor \(T^{\mu\nu}\) associated with translations;
show that \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) for solutions;
write \(T^{00}\) explicitly and check that the energy is positive.







NoteSolution





For a translation, the canonical tensor is
\[
T^{\mu\nu}
=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}
\partial^\nu\phi-\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal L.
\]
Since \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)=\partial^\mu\phi\),
\[
\boxed{
T^{\mu\nu}=\partial^\mu\phi\,\partial^\nu\phi
-\eta^{\mu\nu}
\left(\frac12\partial_\rho\phi\partial^\rho\phi
-\frac12m^2\phi^2\right).
}
\]
Its divergence is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}
={}&(\Box\phi)\partial^\nu\phi
+\partial^\mu\phi\,\partial_\mu\partial^\nu\phi
-\partial^\nu\mathcal L.
\end{aligned}
\]
But
\[
\partial^\nu\mathcal L
=\partial_\rho\phi\,\partial^\nu\partial^\rho\phi
-m^2\phi\partial^\nu\phi.
\]
The terms containing two derivatives cancel, so
\[
\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}
=(\Box\phi+m^2\phi)\partial^\nu\phi=0.
\]
Finally,
\[
\mathcal L
=\frac12\dot\phi^2- rac12(\boldsymbol\nabla\phi)^2
-\frac12m^2\phi^2,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
T^{00}=\frac12\dot\phi^2
+\frac12(\boldsymbol\nabla\phi)^2
+\frac12m^2\phi^2\geq0.
}
\]
Positivity is clear here for \(m^2\geq0\).





11.1.5 Exercise 5 — Current of the complex scalar field ★★
Consider
\[
\mathcal L=\partial_\mu\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-m^2\phi^*\phi
\]
and the global transformation \(\phi\to e^{-iq\alpha}\phi\).

Derive the Noether current.
Check its conservation directly using the equations of motion.
Explain why the same current is identically zero for a real field.







NoteSolution





To first order in \(\alpha\),
\[
\delta\phi=-iq\alpha\phi,
\qquad
\delta\phi^*=+iq\alpha\phi^*.
\]
After removing the constant factor \(\alpha\), the Noether current is
\[
\begin{aligned}
j^\mu
&=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}(-iq\phi)
+\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi^*)}(iq\phi^*)\\
&=-iq\,\partial^\mu\phi^*\phi
+iq\,\partial^\mu\phi\phi^*.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
j^\mu=iq\left(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi
-\phi\partial^\mu\phi^*\right).
}
\]
Its divergence is
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu
=iq\left(\phi^*\Box\phi-\phi\Box\phi^*\right),
\]
because the cross terms cancel. Using \(\Box\phi=-m^2\phi\) and its complex conjugate,
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu
=iq(-m^2\phi^*\phi+m^2\phi\phi^*)=0.
\]
If \(\phi=\phi^*\), the two terms in the current are equal and opposite: \(j^\mu=0\). A real field does not have the continuous phase symmetry that distinguishes particles from antiparticles.





11.1.6 Exercise 6 — Negative frequencies and antiparticles ★★
The general solution for a complex scalar field contains modes \(e^{-ip\cdot x}\) and \(e^{+ip\cdot x}\) with \(p^0=E_{\mathbf p}>0\).

Show that the second mode has frequency \(-E_{\mathbf p}\) when written as \(e^{-ik\cdot x}\).
Explain why the quantized theory nevertheless contains no negative-energy particles.
Give the interpretation of the two creation operators.







NoteSolution





We can write
\[
e^{+ip\cdot x}=e^{-i(-p)\cdot x}.
\]
The four-vector \(k=-p\) has \(k^0=-E_{\mathbf p}\): classically, this is therefore a negative-frequency solution.
After quantization, the expansion takes the form
\[
\phi(x)=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[a(\mathbf p)e^{-ipx}
+b^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{+ipx}\right].
\]
The coefficient of the negative-frequency mode becomes a creation operator. The normal-ordered Hamiltonian is
\[
:H:=\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}E_{\mathbf p}
\left(a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b\right),
\]
which is positive. Also,
\[
:Q:=q\int\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3}
\left(a^\dagger a-b^\dagger b\right).
\]
Thus, \(a^\dagger\) creates a particle with energy \(E_{\mathbf p}\) and charge \(q\), while \(b^\dagger\) creates an antiparticle with energy \(E_{\mathbf p}\) and charge \(-q\):
\[
\boxed{
\text{classical negative frequency}
\longrightarrow
\text{creation of a positive-energy antiparticle}.
}
\]





11.1.7 Exercise 7 — Counting Cauchy data ★★
Compare a real scalar field, a complex scalar field, and a free Dirac field. For each one, state:

the number of real components of the field;
the time order of the equation;
the independent data that must be specified on a hypersurface \(t=t_0\).

Why is the number of components alone not yet the number of polarizations of a particle?






NoteSolution





A real scalar has one real component, and the Klein–Gordon equation is second order. We must therefore specify
\[
\phi(t_0,\mathbf x),
\qquad
\dot\phi(t_0,\mathbf x),
\]
that is, two real functions.
A complex scalar is equivalent to two real scalars. We must specify \(\phi\) and \(\dot\phi\), which means four real functions. After quantization, this doubling allows independent particles and antiparticles.
A Dirac spinor has four complex components, or eight real components, but the Dirac equation is first order in time. It is enough to specify \(\psi(t_0,\mathbf x)\): eight real functions, with no independent data for \(\dot\psi\).
These data include the particle and antiparticle branches. The number of polarizations at fixed momentum is found after imposing the equation of motion, any constraints, and the energy condition. For example, a Dirac spinor has two spin states for the particle and two for the antiparticle, not four spin orientations for one particle.





11.1.8 Exercise 8 — Local representation and physical particle ★★★
Explain the following two statements, which do not contradict each other:

a scalar field transforms in the \((0,0)\) representation of the Lorentz group;
a particle created by this field carries a unitary representation of the Poincaré group characterized by \((m,s=0)\).

Also show why the finite matrix that transforms the components of a vector field is not required to be unitary.






NoteSolution





A Lorentz transformation acts on a field according to
\[
U(\Lambda)\Phi_A(x)U^{-1}(\Lambda)
=D(\Lambda^{-1})_A{}^B\Phi_B(\Lambda x).
\]
Two distinct objects are involved:

\(U(\Lambda)\) acts on the Hilbert space of states; it must be unitary to preserve probabilities;
\(D(\Lambda)\) acts on the local indices of the field and belongs to a finite-dimensional representation of the Lorentz group.

For a scalar, \(D=1\): the value of the field is not mixed with other components. However, the state
\[
|\mathbf p\rangle=a^\dagger(\mathbf p)|0\rangle
\]
is transformed by \(U(\Lambda)\) into a state with momentum \(\Lambda p\). The set of these states carries a representation of the Poincaré group, whose invariants are \(P^2=m^2\) and \(W^2=0\), so \(s=0\).
The Lorentz group is noncompact. Its nontrivial finite-dimensional representations, such as \((1/2,1/2)\) for a four-vector, are generally not unitary for a positive inner product. This is not a problem: \(A^\mu\) is not a state vector, and its four components are not four probabilities. Physical unitarity belongs to \(U(\Lambda)\) on Fock space.






11.2 B. The Dirac field, chirality, and discrete symmetries

11.2.1 Exercise 9 — First consequences of the Clifford algebra ★
Starting from \(\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf1_4\), show that
\[
(\gamma^0)^2=\mathbf1_4,
\qquad
(\gamma^i)^2=-\mathbf1_4,
\qquad
\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu=-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\quad(\mu\neq\nu).
\]
Deduce that \((\not\! p)^2=p^2\mathbf1_4\).






NoteSolution





Setting \(\mu=\nu\), the Clifford relation becomes
\[
2(\gamma^\mu)^2=2\eta^{\mu\mu}\mathbf1_4.
\]
With the \((+---)\) signature, we immediately obtain
\[
(\gamma^0)^2=\mathbf1_4,
\qquad
(\gamma^i)^2=-\mathbf1_4.
\]
If \(\mu\neq\nu\), then \(\eta^{\mu\nu}=0\), so the anticommutator vanishes.
Finally,
\[
(\not\! p)^2
=\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu p_\mu p_\nu.
\]
The product \(p_\mu p_\nu\) is symmetric, so only the symmetric part of the gamma matrices contributes:
\[
\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu p_\mu p_\nu
=\frac12\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}p_\mu p_\nu
=\eta^{\mu\nu}p_\mu p_\nu\mathbf1_4.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{(\not\! p)^2=p^2\mathbf1_4.}
\]





11.2.2 Exercise 10 — Dirac implies Klein–Gordon ★★
Show that a solution of
\[
(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi=0
\]
also satisfies the Klein–Gordon equation component by component. Why is the converse false?






NoteSolution





Multiply the equation on the left by the conjugate operator \(i\not\!\partial+m\):
\[
(i\not\!\partial+m)(i\not\!\partial-m)\psi=0.
\]
The cross terms cancel, and
\[
(i\not\!\partial)^2
=-\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\partial_\mu\partial_\nu.
\]
Since the derivatives commute, the antisymmetric part of \(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\) does not contribute. This leaves
\[
(i\not\!\partial)^2
=-\frac12\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}
\partial_\mu\partial_\nu
=-\Box.
\]
Therefore,
\[
-(\Box+m^2)\psi=0,
\]
that is,
\[
\boxed{(\Box+m^2)\psi=0.}
\]
The converse is false because Klein–Gordon only imposes the mass-shell condition on each of the four components. The Dirac equation adds linear relations between these components and selects the spin-\(1/2\) content. Every Dirac solution is a Klein–Gordon solution, but an arbitrary collection of four scalar solutions is not a physical Dirac spinor.





11.2.3 Exercise 11 — Dirac current and positivity ★★
Starting from the Dirac equation and its adjoint equation:

show that \(j^\mu=q\overline\psi\gamma^\mu\psi\) is conserved;
calculate \(j^0\);
compare its positivity with that of the complex scalar charge density.







NoteSolution





The equation and its adjoint are
\[
i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi=m\psi,
\qquad
i(\partial_\mu\overline\psi)\gamma^\mu=-m\overline\psi.
\]
The divergence is
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu
=q(\partial_\mu\overline\psi)\gamma^\mu\psi
+q\overline\psi\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi.
\]
The first equation gives \(\overline\psi\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi=-im\overline\psi\psi\), while the adjoint gives \((\partial_\mu\overline\psi)\gamma^\mu\psi=+im\overline\psi\psi\). The two terms cancel:
\[
\boxed{\partial_\mu j^\mu=0.}
\]
Its time component is
\[
j^0=q\overline\psi\gamma^0\psi
=q\psi^\dagger\gamma^0\gamma^0\psi
=q\psi^\dagger\psi.
\]
For \(q>0\), \(j^0/q\) is positive at the one-particle wave-function level. The Klein–Gordon current contains a time derivative and does not have a definite sign. In quantum field theory, however, \(j^0\) is a charge density, not a many-particle probability density; its integral can be negative when antiparticles dominate.





11.2.4 Exercise 12 — Spinors at rest ★★
In the Dirac representation,
\[
\gamma^0=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf1&0\\0&-\mathbf1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Solve the equations \((\not\! p-m)u_s(p)=0\) and \((\not\! p+m)v_s(p)=0\) at rest, \(p^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\). Choose the normalization \(u_s^\dagger u_r=v_s^\dagger v_r=2m\delta_{sr}\).






NoteSolution





At rest, \(\not\! p=m\gamma^0\). For \(u\),
\[
m(\gamma^0-\mathbf1)u=0.
\]
The two lower components must vanish, while the two upper components are free. With two orthonormal Pauli spinors \(\xi_s\),
\[
\boxed{u_s(\mathbf0)=\sqrt{2m}
\begin{pmatrix}\xi_s\\0\end{pmatrix}.}
\]
For \(v\),
\[
m(\gamma^0+\mathbf1)v=0,
\]
so the upper components vanish. With orthonormal spinors \(\eta_s\),
\[
\boxed{v_s(\mathbf0)=\sqrt{2m}
\begin{pmatrix}0\\\eta_s\end{pmatrix}.}
\]
We check that
\[
\overline u_su_r=2m\delta_{sr},
\qquad
\overline v_sv_r=-2m\delta_{sr}.
\]
The minus sign in the second product comes from the internal metric defined by \(\gamma^0\); the Hilbert-space norm \(v^\dagger v\) remains positive.





11.2.5 Exercise 13 — Spinors in motion ★★★
Write a positive-energy spinor as \(u=(\varphi,\chi)^T\) in the Dirac representation. Solve \((\not\! p-m)u=0\) to express \(\chi\) in terms of \(\varphi\), then construct \(u_s(p)\) with \(u_s^\dagger u_r=2E_{\mathbf p}\delta_{sr}\). Also give one possible form of \(v_s(p)\).






NoteSolution





In the Dirac representation,
\[
\not\! p-m=
\begin{pmatrix}
E-m&-\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p\\
\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p&-E-m
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The two rows give
\[
(E-m)\varphi=(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p)\chi,
\qquad
\chi=\frac{\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p}{E+m}\varphi.
\]
The first relation is then satisfied because \((\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p)^2=\mathbf p^2\) and \((E-m)(E+m)=\mathbf p^2\).
Choose \(\varphi=\sqrt{E+m}\,\xi_s\). We obtain
\[
\boxed{
u_s(p)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{E+m}\,\xi_s\\[2mm]
\dfrac{\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p}{\sqrt{E+m}}\,\xi_s
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]
Its norm is
\[
u_s^\dagger u_r
=\left[(E+m)+\frac{\mathbf p^2}{E+m}\right]\delta_{sr}
=2E\delta_{sr}.
\]
A consistent convention for the negative-energy solutions is
\[
\boxed{
v_s(p)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p}{\sqrt{E+m}}\,\eta_s\\[2mm]
\sqrt{E+m}\,\eta_s
\end{pmatrix},
}
\]
which satisfies \((\not\! p+m)v_s=0\) and \(v_s^\dagger v_r=2E\delta_{sr}\). Phases or a different convention for \(\eta_s\) do not change any observable.





11.2.6 Exercise 14 — Completeness relations ★★★
Without explicitly choosing a representation of the gamma matrices, recover
\[
\sum_su_s(p)\overline u_s(p)=\not\! p+m,
\qquad
\sum_sv_s(p)\overline v_s(p)=\not\! p-m,
\]
from covariance, the Dirac equations, and the normalizations \(\overline u_su_r=2m\delta_{sr}\), \(\overline v_sv_r=-2m\delta_{sr}\).






NoteSolution





Let
\[
M_u(p)=\sum_su_s(p)\overline u_s(p).
\]
With no other four-vector available and no parity-odd structure, covariance requires the form
\[
M_u=A\not\! p+Bm.
\]
The equation \((\not\! p-m)u_s=0\) implies
\[
(\not\! p-m)M_u=0.
\]
On the mass shell,
\[
(\not\! p-m)(A\not\! p+Bm)
=m(A-B)(m-\not\! p),
\]
so \(A=B\). It remains to determine \(A\). Taking the trace,
\[
\operatorname{tr}M_u
=\sum_s\overline u_su_s=4m,
\]
because there are two spin states and each gives \(2m\). On the other hand,
\[
\operatorname{tr}[A(\not\! p+m)]
=4Am,
\]
since \(\operatorname{tr}\gamma^\mu=0\). Therefore \(A=1\), and
\[
\boxed{M_u=\not\! p+m.}
\]
For \(M_v=\sum_sv_s\overline v_s\), the equation \((\not\! p+m)v_s=0\) requires a structure proportional to \(\not\! p-m\). Its trace is \(-4m\), exactly the trace of \(\not\! p-m\), so
\[
\boxed{M_v=\not\! p-m.}
\]
These matrices are the covariant sums over the two spin states; on the mass shell, they act as projectors up to a factor \(2m\).





11.2.7 Exercise 15 — Vector bilinears for one particle ★★
Use the completeness relations or a covariant argument to show, with the chapter’s normalizations, that
\[
\overline u_s(p)\gamma^\mu u_s(p)=2p^\mu.
\]
Check the time component explicitly.






NoteSolution





For a fixed spin state, the bilinear \(\overline u_s\gamma^\mu u_s\) is a four-vector. With no other independent four-vector after averaging, or for the diagonal vector part, it must be proportional to \(p^\mu\):
\[
\overline u_s\gamma^\mu u_s=Cp^\mu.
\]
At rest, \(p^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\) and
\[
\overline u_s\gamma^0u_s=u_s^\dagger u_s=2m.
\]
Thus \(C=2\). By covariance,
\[
\boxed{\overline u_s(p)\gamma^\mu u_s(p)=2p^\mu.}
\]
The time component directly gives
\[
\overline u_s\gamma^0u_s=u_s^\dagger u_s=2E_{\mathbf p}=2p^0.
\]
For the spatial component, a calculation with the spinor from Exercise 13 gives \(2\mathbf p\). The result is independent of the spin direction: the vector bilinear measures the flux associated with momentum, while spin information appears in particular in the axial and tensor bilinears.





11.2.8 Exercise 16 — Nonrelativistic limit of Dirac ★★★
Write \(\psi=e^{-imt}(\varphi,\chi)^T\) in the Dirac representation and assume \(|\partial_t\varphi|,|\mathbf p|\ll m\). Show that the small component is
\[
\chi\simeq\frac{-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla}{2m}\varphi
\]
and that \(\varphi\) satisfies the free Schrödinger equation.






NoteSolution





The Hamiltonian equation is
\[
i\partial_t\psi
=\left(-i\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla+\beta m\right)\psi.
\]
After removing the rapid oscillation \(e^{-imt}\), the two components satisfy
\[
i\partial_t\varphi=-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla\chi,
\]
\[
i\partial_t\chi=-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla\varphi-2m\chi.
\]
In the nonrelativistic regime, \(i\partial_t\chi\) is small compared with \(2m\chi\). The second equation therefore gives
\[
\boxed{
\chi\simeq\frac{-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla}{2m}\varphi.
}
\]
Substituting it into the first equation,
\[
i\partial_t\varphi
=-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla
\left(\frac{-i\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla}{2m}\varphi\right).
\]
Now \((\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)^2=\boldsymbol\nabla^2\), because the antisymmetric part \(i\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k\) is contracted with \(\partial_i\partial_j\), which is symmetric. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{i\partial_t\varphi=-\frac{\boldsymbol\nabla^2}{2m}\varphi.}
\]
The large component becomes the nonrelativistic Pauli spinor; the small component is suppressed by a typical factor \(|\mathbf p|/m\).





11.2.9 Exercise 17 — Chiral projectors ★★
Define
\[
P_L=\frac{1-\gamma^5}{2},
\qquad
P_R=\frac{1+\gamma^5}{2}.
\]

Show that \(P_L\) and \(P_R\) are complementary orthogonal projectors.
Establish \(P_L\gamma^\mu=\gamma^\mu P_R\).
Split the Dirac kinetic and mass terms into left- and right-handed components.







NoteSolution





The identities \((\gamma^5)^2=1\) and \(\{\gamma^5,\gamma^\mu\}=0\) give
\[
P_L^2=P_L,
\qquad
P_R^2=P_R,
\qquad
P_LP_R=0,
\qquad
P_L+P_R=1.
\]
Next,
\[
P_L\gamma^\mu
=\frac12(1-\gamma^5)\gamma^\mu
=\frac12\gamma^\mu(1+\gamma^5)
=\gamma^\mu P_R.
\]
Let \(\psi_{L,R}=P_{L,R}\psi\). Since taking the adjoint exchanges the projectors,
\[
\overline{\psi_L}=\overline\psi P_R,
\qquad
\overline{\psi_R}=\overline\psi P_L.
\]
The kinetic term separates:
\[
\overline\psi i\not\!\partial\psi
=\overline\psi_Li\not\!\partial\psi_L
+\overline\psi_Ri\not\!\partial\psi_R.
\]
In contrast,
\[
\overline\psi\psi
=\overline\psi_L\psi_R+\overline\psi_R\psi_L,
\]
because \(\overline\psi_L\psi_L=\overline\psi P_RP_L\psi=0\). Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L
=\overline\psi_Li\not\!\partial\psi_L
+\overline\psi_Ri\not\!\partial\psi_R
-m(\overline\psi_L\psi_R+\overline\psi_R\psi_L).
}
\]
The mass therefore couples the two chiralities, while they evolve independently for \(m=0\).





11.2.10 Exercise 18 — Helicity and chirality ★★★
Let a positive-energy spinor have helicity \(h=\pm1\) such that
\[
(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\widehat{\mathbf p})\xi_h=h\xi_h.
\]
Using the spinor from Exercise 13, show that the expectation value of \(\gamma^5\) is
\[
\frac{u_h^\dagger\gamma^5u_h}{u_h^\dagger u_h}
=h\frac{|\mathbf p|}{E_{\mathbf p}}.
\]
Interpret the limits \(|\mathbf p|\ll m\) and \(m/E\to0\).






NoteSolution





In the Dirac basis used in the chapter,
\[
\gamma^5=
\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf1\\\mathbf1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For
\[
u_h=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{E+m}\,\xi_h\\
\dfrac{\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p}{\sqrt{E+m}}\xi_h
\end{pmatrix},
\]
we have \(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf p\,\xi_h=h|\mathbf p|\xi_h\). Thus,
\[
u_h^\dagger\gamma^5u_h
=2h|\mathbf p|\,\xi_h^\dagger\xi_h,
\]
while \(u_h^\dagger u_h=2E\,\xi_h^\dagger\xi_h\). Therefore,
\[
