title: The Jaynes–Cummings model
text:
2 Doublets and dressed states

2.1 Conserved excitation number
The operator
\[
N=a^\dagger a+\sigma_+\sigma_-
=a^\dagger a+|e\rangle\langle e|
\]
counts photons plus the atomic excitation. Absorption decreases the photon number by one and raises the atomic contribution by one; emission does the reverse. This gives \([H_{\mathrm{JC}},N]=0\), proved explicitly in Exercise 2.
The states \(|e,n\rangle\) and \(|g,n+1\rangle\) both have \(N=n+1\). The Hamiltonian only mixes these two states, so we solve it in each subspace
\[
\mathcal H_n=\operatorname{span}\{|e,n\rangle,|g,n+1\rangle\},
\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
The state \(|g,0\rangle\) is uncoupled and has energy \(-\hbar\omega_a/2\).


2.2 A two-by-two Hamiltonian
Set \(G_n=g\sqrt{n+1}\). Applying the Hamiltonian gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_{\mathrm{JC}}|e,n\rangle
&=\hbar\left(n\omega_c+\frac{\omega_a}{2}\right)|e,n\rangle
+\hbar G_n|g,n+1\rangle,\\
H_{\mathrm{JC}}|g,n+1\rangle
&=\hbar G_n|e,n\rangle
+\hbar\left((n+1)\omega_c-\frac{\omega_a}{2}\right)|g,n+1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the ordered basis \((|e,n\rangle,|g,n+1\rangle)\), subtracting the mean of the diagonal entries gives
\[
H_n=\hbar\omega_c\left(n+\frac12\right)I
+\hbar K_n,
\qquad
K_n=\begin{pmatrix}\Delta/2&G_n\\G_n&-\Delta/2\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}\]
If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(K_n\), its characteristic equation is
\[
\det(K_n-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-\frac{\Delta^2}{4}-G_n^2=0.
\]
Define the generalized Rabi angular frequency
\[
\Omega_n=\sqrt{\Delta^2+4g^2(n+1)}.
\tag{3}\]
The energies are then
\[
E_{n,\pm}=\hbar\omega_c\left(n+\frac12\right)
\pm\frac{\hbar\Omega_n}{2}.
\tag{4}\]
The eigenstates are called dressed states because they combine atomic and field excitations. To specify the mixing angle for either sign of \(\Delta\), choose \(0<\theta_n<\pi/2\) with
\[
\cos(2\theta_n)=\frac{\Delta}{\Omega_n},
\qquad
\sin(2\theta_n)=\frac{2G_n}{\Omega_n}.
\]
The corresponding normalized states are
\[
\begin{aligned}
|n,+\rangle&=\cos\theta_n|e,n\rangle+\sin\theta_n|g,n+1\rangle,\\
|n,-\rangle&=-\sin\theta_n|e,n\rangle+\cos\theta_n|g,n+1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
At resonance, \(\Delta=0\) and \(\theta_n=\pi/4\). The two states are equal-weight combinations, and their energy separation is \(2\hbar g\sqrt{n+1}\). For \(n=0\), the splitting \(2\hbar g\) is the vacuum Rabi splitting.


Plot settings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.figsize": (8.5, 4.8),
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.23,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "font.size": 11,
})

from pathlib import Path
import re

folders = [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
stylesheet = next((p / "styles.css" for p in folders
                   if (p / "styles.css").is_file()), None)
palette = dict(re.findall(r"--([\w-]+)\s*:\s*([^;{}]+)",
                         stylesheet.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if stylesheet else ""))
defaults = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"]
plot_colors = [palette.get(f"plot-{i}", defaults[i-1]).strip() for i in range(1, 6)]
BLEU, ORANGE, VERT, ROUGE, VIOLET = plot_colors
GRIS = palette.get("muted", "0.45").strip()
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = plt.cycler(color=plot_colors)




Show Python code
delta = np.linspace(-6, 6, 800)  # Delta / g
n = 0
omega = np.sqrt(delta**2 + 4 * (n + 1))

e_plus = 0.5 * omega
e_minus = -0.5 * omega
e_bare_1 = 0.5 * delta
e_bare_2 = -0.5 * delta

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(delta, e_plus, lw=2.4, color=BLEU, label=r"$E_{+}$")
ax.plot(delta, e_minus, lw=2.4, color=ORANGE, label=r"$E_{-}$")
ax.plot(delta, e_bare_1, "--", lw=1.2, color=GRIS, label="uncoupled levels")
ax.plot(delta, e_bare_2, "--", lw=1.2, color=GRIS)
ax.set_xlabel(r"Detuning $\Delta/g$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Shifted energy in units of $\hbar g$")
ax.set_title("Dressed energies near resonance")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Avoided crossing in the first doublet. The common energy is subtracted.





The uncoupled levels would cross at resonance. The interaction opens a gap, giving the avoided crossing in the figure.

title: The Jaynes–Cummings model
text:
3 Rabi oscillations
Suppose the initial state is \(|e,n\rangle\). The evolution stays within \(\mathcal H_n\). Since
\[
K_n^2=\frac{\Omega_n^2}{4}I,
\]
the even and odd powers in the exponential give
\[
e^{-iK_nt}=I\cos\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}
-\frac{2iK_n}{\Omega_n}\sin\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}.
\]
Applying this matrix to \((1,0)^T\) and restoring the common phase gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{-i\omega_c(n+1/2)t}\Bigg[&
\left(\cos\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}
-i\frac{\Delta}{\Omega_n}\sin\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}\right)|e,n\rangle\\
&-i\frac{2G_n}{\Omega_n}\sin\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}|g,n+1\rangle\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
Taking the squared modulus of the first amplitude yields
\[
P_e^{(n)}(t)=1-\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Omega_n^2}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}\right).
\tag{6}\]
At resonance this becomes \(P_e^{(n)}(t)=\cos^2(g\sqrt{n+1}\,t)\). The excitation moves back and forth between \(|e,n\rangle\) and \(|g,n+1\rangle\). For \(n=0\), the initially excited atom exchanges its excitation with the empty mode. This is a vacuum Rabi oscillation; the energy comes from the excited atom, not from the vacuum.


Show Python code
tau = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 1400)  # tau = g t

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for n, color in zip([0, 1, 4], [BLEU, ORANGE, VIOLET]):
    probability = np.cos(np.sqrt(n + 1) * tau) ** 2
    ax.plot(tau, probability, lw=2, color=color, label=fr"$n={n}$")

ax.set_xlabel(r"Scaled time $gt$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Probability $P_e(t)$")
ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 1.03)
ax.set_title("Rabi oscillations for different photon numbers")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 2: Excited-state probability at resonance, starting from the excited atom and a Fock state.





Away from resonance, the maximum transfer probability is
\[
P_{e,n\to g,n+1}^{\max}
=\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Delta^2+4g^2(n+1)}<1.
\]
Detuning therefore reduces the transfer, even though the oscillation frequency \(\Omega_n\) increases.

title: The Jaynes–Cummings model
section: 4 A coherent field: collapse and revival
text:
4 A coherent field: collapse and revival
A Fock state has a fixed photon number. A coherent state is a superposition,
\[
|\alpha\rangle=e^{-|\alpha|^2/2}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}|n\rangle,
\]
with Poisson probabilities
\[
p_n=e^{-\bar n}\frac{\bar n^n}{n!},
\qquad \bar n=|\alpha|^2.
\]
Start from \(|e\rangle\otimes|\alpha\rangle\) at resonance. Each component \(|e,n\rangle\) evolves with its own Rabi frequency. To find the probability of an excited atom, we sum over all final photon numbers. Their orthogonality removes cross terms, leaving
\[
P_e(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_n\cos^2(g\sqrt{n+1}\,t).
\tag{7}\]
Initially the oscillations add together. As their phases separate, their sum approaches \(1/2\) and the visible oscillations collapse. At later times, neighboring components partly return to phase and the oscillations revive. The total evolution remains unitary: the collapse is not energy loss.
For \(\bar n\gg1\), the first revival occurs at approximately
\[
t_{\mathrm{rev}}\simeq\frac{2\pi\sqrt{\bar n}}{g}.
\]
Exercise 5 derives this estimate. The collapse time is of order \(1/g\), so collapse and revival occur on different timescales when \(\bar n\) is large.


Show Python code
nbar = 16.0
nmax = int(nbar + 10 * np.sqrt(nbar) + 40)
n_values = np.arange(nmax + 1)

# Poisson probabilities from their recurrence relation.
poisson = np.empty(nmax + 1)
poisson[0] = np.exp(-nbar)
for n in range(nmax):
    poisson[n + 1] = poisson[n] * nbar / (n + 1)
poisson /= poisson.sum()

t_rev = 2 * np.pi * np.sqrt(nbar)  # scaled time g t
tau = np.linspace(0, 2.15 * t_rev, 4500)
phases = np.sqrt(n_values[:, None] + 1) * tau[None, :]
p_excited = np.sum(poisson[:, None] * np.cos(phases) ** 2, axis=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.plot(tau, p_excited, color=BLEU, lw=1.5)
ax.axvline(t_rev, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=1.3,
           label=r"$t_{\mathrm{rev}}\simeq2\pi\sqrt{\bar n}/g$")
ax.axvline(2 * t_rev, color=ORANGE, ls=":", lw=1.1)
ax.set_xlabel(r"Scaled time $gt$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Probability $P_e(t)$")
ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 1.03)
ax.set_title(r"Coherent field : $\bar n=16$")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 3: Collapse and revivals for an initially excited atom and a coherent field with mean photon number 16.

title: The Jaynes–Cummings model
text:
5 Exercises

5.1 Exercise 1 — Interaction processes
Consider \(V=\hbar g(a+a^\dagger)(\sigma_++\sigma_-)\).

Expand \(V\) into four terms.
Give the nonzero action of each term on \(|g,n\rangle\) or \(|e,n\rangle\).
Identify which terms conserve \(N\).
Explain why the other two can be neglected in the rotating-wave approximation.







NoteSolution





Expanding the product gives
\[
V=\hbar g(a\sigma_++a^\dagger\sigma_-+a\sigma_-+a^\dagger\sigma_+).
\]
Apply the field and atomic operators separately:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a\sigma_+|g,n\rangle&=\sqrt n\,|e,n-1\rangle,\\
a^\dagger\sigma_-|e,n\rangle&=\sqrt{n+1}\,|g,n+1\rangle,\\
a\sigma_-|e,n\rangle&=\sqrt n\,|g,n-1\rangle,\\
a^\dagger\sigma_+|g,n\rangle&=\sqrt{n+1}\,|e,n+1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
The terms containing \(a\) give zero when \(n=0\). Each term also gives zero on the other atomic state because \(\sigma_+|e\rangle=\sigma_-|g\rangle=0\).
For \(a\sigma_+\), the field loses one excitation and the atom gains one. For \(a^\dagger\sigma_-\), the changes are reversed. Both conserve \(N\). The other two change \(N\) by \(-2\) and \(+2\).
In the interaction picture, the exchange terms have factors \(e^{\pm i\Delta t}\). The counter-rotating terms have factors \(e^{\pm i(\omega_a+\omega_c)t}\). Near resonance and at weak coupling, these fast terms average out on the slower exchange timescale, leaving the Jaynes–Cummings interaction.





5.2 Exercise 2 — Conservation of excitations
Let \(N=a^\dagger a+\sigma_+\sigma_-\).

Show explicitly that \([N,a\sigma_+]=0\).
Show that \([N,a^\dagger\sigma_-]=0\).
Deduce \([H_{\mathrm{JC}},N]=0\).
Find the product basis states with exactly two excitations.







NoteSolution





Since atomic and field operators commute,
\[
[N,a\sigma_+]=[a^\dagger a,a]\sigma_+
+a[\sigma_+\sigma_-,\sigma_+].
\]
The field commutator is \([a^\dagger a,a]=-a\). For the atom, \(\sigma_+\sigma_-=|e\rangle\langle e|\), so
\[
[|e\rangle\langle e|,\sigma_+]=\sigma_+.
\]
Thus \([N,a\sigma_+]=-a\sigma_++a\sigma_+=0\). Similarly,
\[
[a^\dagger a,a^\dagger]=a^\dagger,
\qquad
[|e\rangle\langle e|,\sigma_-]=-\sigma_-,
\]
which gives \([N,a^\dagger\sigma_-]=a^\dagger\sigma_--a^\dagger\sigma_-=0\).
The free terms also commute with \(N\), since \(|e\rangle\langle e|=(I+\sigma_z)/2\). Every term of the Hamiltonian therefore commutes with \(N\).
Two excitations mean either an excited atom with one photon, \(|e,1\rangle\), or a ground-state atom with two photons, \(|g,2\rangle\). They span \(\mathcal H_1\).





5.3 Exercise 3 — Vacuum oscillations and entanglement
The atom starts in \(|e\rangle\) and the cavity in \(|0\rangle\), at resonance.

Write \(|\psi(t)\rangle\) in the interaction picture.
Find the first time when the excitation has been transferred completely to the field.
Find the first time when the atom and field are maximally entangled.
Calculate the reduced atomic density matrix at that time.







NoteSolution





Here \(n=0\) and \(\Omega_0=2g\). Removing the free evolution from Equation 5 gives
\[
|\psi(t)\rangle=\cos(gt)|e,0\rangle-i\sin(gt)|g,1\rangle.
\]
Complete transfer requires \(\cos(gt)=0\). The first positive time is
\[
t_{\mathrm{transfer}}=\frac{\pi}{2g}.
\]
At that time the state is \(-i|g,1\rangle\), a product state. Entanglement is instead maximal when the two coefficients have equal magnitude:
\[
\cos^2(gt)=\sin^2(gt)=\frac12,
\qquad t_{\mathrm{ent}}=\frac{\pi}{4g}.
\]
Then
\[
|\psi(t_{\mathrm{ent}})\rangle
=\frac{|e,0\rangle-i|g,1\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]
To trace out the field, use
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_c\bigl(|a,n\rangle\langle b,m|\bigr)
=\langle m|n\rangle\,|a\rangle\langle b|.
\]
The cross terms vanish because \(\langle0|1\rangle=0\), so
\[
\rho_a=\frac12|e\rangle\langle e|+\frac12|g\rangle\langle g|
=\frac I2.
\]
The total state is pure, while the atom is maximally mixed. Since the displayed two terms are already orthogonal product states with equal weights, they give maximal entanglement between the atom and this two-dimensional field subspace.





5.4 Exercise 4 — Detuning
Start from \(|e,n\rangle\) with arbitrary \(\Delta\).

Find \(P_{g,n+1}(t)\).
Find its maximum value and the first time it is reached.
Evaluate these quantities for \(\Delta=2g\sqrt{n+1}\).
Interpret the limit \(|\Delta|\gg g\sqrt{n+1}\).







NoteSolution





Squaring the second amplitude in Equation 5 gives
\[
P_{g,n+1}(t)=\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Omega_n^2}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\Omega_nt}{2}\right).
\]
The first maximum has \(\Omega_nt/2=\pi/2\), hence
\[
P_{g,n+1}^{\max}=\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Delta^2+4g^2(n+1)},
\qquad t_{\max}=\frac{\pi}{\Omega_n}.
\]
For \(\Delta=2g\sqrt{n+1}\),
\[
\Omega_n=2\sqrt2\,g\sqrt{n+1},
\qquad P_{g,n+1}^{\max}=\frac12,
\qquad t_{\max}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2\,g\sqrt{n+1}}.
\]
For large detuning,
\[
P_{g,n+1}^{\max}\simeq\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Delta^2}\ll1.
\]
Very little excitation is exchanged. The interaction still shifts the energies, as Exercise 6 shows.





5.5 Exercise 5 — Revival time
For an initially excited atom and a coherent field at resonance, the atomic inversion is
\[
W(t)=2P_e(t)-1=\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n\cos(\omega_nt),
\qquad \omega_n=2g\sqrt{n+1}.
\]
Assume \(\bar n\gg1\).

Expand \(\omega_n\) to first order about \(n=\bar n\).
Require neighboring components to recover a phase difference of \(2\pi\) and estimate \(t_{\mathrm{rev}}\).
Evaluate the large-\(\bar n\) estimate for \(\bar n=25\) and \(g/(2\pi)=50\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Explain why a single Fock state does not show collapse and revival.







NoteSolution





Since \(d\omega_n/dn=g/\sqrt{n+1}\),
\[
\omega_n\simeq2g\sqrt{\bar n+1}
+\frac{g}{\sqrt{\bar n+1}}(n-\bar n).
\]
Neighboring frequencies differ by approximately \(g/\sqrt{\bar n+1}\). Setting their phase difference to \(2\pi\) gives
\[
t_{\mathrm{rev}}\simeq\frac{2\pi\sqrt{\bar n+1}}g
\simeq\frac{2\pi\sqrt{\bar n}}g.
\]
Higher terms in the expansion prevent all the components from returning exactly to phase, so the revival is partial.
For the given values, \(g=2\pi\times50\times10^3\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(\sqrt{\bar n}=5\). Thus
\[
t_{\mathrm{rev}}\simeq
\frac{2\pi\times5}{2\pi\times50\times10^3}
=10^{-4}\ \mathrm s=100\ \mu\mathrm s.
\]
A single Fock state has only one Rabi frequency. Its oscillations are periodic, with no set of frequencies to lose and recover their relative phase.





5.6 Exercise 6 — The dispersive regime
Work within the Jaynes–Cummings model, with \(\Delta>0\) and \(g\sqrt{n+1}\ll\Delta\). Let \(H_0=H_a+H_c\).

Expand \(\Omega_n\) through second order in \(g/\Delta\).
Find the energy shifts of the states close to \(|e,n\rangle\) and \(|g,n+1\rangle\).
Show that, to this order, the effective Hamiltonian in the approximately uncoupled basis is
\[
H_{\mathrm{eff}}=H_0+\hbar\chi
\left[(a^\dagger a+1)|e\rangle\langle e|
-a^\dagger a|g\rangle\langle g|\right],
\qquad\chi=\frac{g^2}{\Delta}.
\]
Find the atomic transition angular frequency when the field contains \(n\) photons.







NoteSolution





Expand the square root using \(\sqrt{1+x}=1+x/2+O(x^2)\):
\[
\Omega_n=\Delta\sqrt{1+\frac{4g^2(n+1)}{\Delta^2}}
=\Delta+\frac{2g^2(n+1)}{\Delta}
+O\!\left(\frac{g^4(n+1)^2}{\Delta^3}\right).
\]
For \(\Delta>0\), the upper dressed state is close to \(|e,n\rangle\) and the lower one to \(|g,n+1\rangle\). Substituting the expansion into Equation 4 gives
\[
\delta E_{e,n}\simeq\frac{\hbar g^2(n+1)}{\Delta},
\qquad
\delta E_{g,n+1}\simeq-\frac{\hbar g^2(n+1)}{\Delta}.
\]
For a ground-state atom with \(n\) photons, relabel the second result:
\[
\delta E_{g,n}\simeq-\hbar\chi n,
\qquad \delta E_{e,n}\simeq\hbar\chi(n+1).
\]
The shift of \(|g,0\rangle\) is zero, as it must be for the uncoupled state. These shifts are reproduced by
\[
H_{\mathrm{eff}}=H_0+\hbar\chi
\left[(a^\dagger a+1)|e\rangle\langle e|
-a^\dagger a|g\rangle\langle g|\right].
\]
Using \(|e\rangle\langle e|=(I+\sigma_z)/2\) and \(|g\rangle\langle g|=(I-\sigma_z)/2\), the correction becomes
\[
\hbar\chi\left[\left(a^\dagger a+\frac12\right)\sigma_z+\frac12I\right].
\]
The last term is a common energy shift. For a fixed photon number, subtracting the two atomic energies gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hbar\omega_a(n)
&\simeq\hbar\omega_a+\delta E_{e,n}-\delta E_{g,n}\\
&=\hbar\omega_a+\hbar\chi(2n+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(\omega_a(n)\simeq\omega_a+\chi(2n+1)\). The photon number shifts the atomic frequency while excitation exchange remains weak. This is the basis of dispersive measurements.





5.7 Exercise 7 — Numerical diagonalization
Keep field states \(|0\rangle,\ldots,|N_{\max}\rangle\).

Construct the matrices \(a\), \(a^\dagger\) and \(a^\dagger a\).
Build \(H_{\mathrm{JC}}\) using Kronecker products.
For \(\hbar=1\), \(\omega_a=\omega_c=1\) and \(g=0.08\), compare the lowest numerical eigenvalues with the analytical ones.
Explain why the truncation leaves an artificial uncoupled state at the upper boundary.







NoteSolution





In the photon basis, \(a_{n-1,n}=\sqrt n\) and all other entries vanish. The creation matrix is its conjugate transpose.
The code uses the order \(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{field}}\otimes\mathcal H_{\mathrm{atom}}\), with atomic basis \((|g\rangle,|e\rangle)\). This only changes the ordering of basis vectors; the state \(|e,n\rangle\) is represented by \(|n\rangle\otimes|e\rangle\) in the code.


Show Python code
import numpy as np

nmax = 6
omega_c = 1.0
omega_a = 1.0
g = 0.08

# Field operators.
a = np.zeros((nmax + 1, nmax + 1), dtype=complex)
for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
    a[n - 1, n] = np.sqrt(n)

adag = a.conj().T
number = adag @ a
identity_field = np.eye(nmax + 1)

# Atomic operators in the basis (|g>, |e>).
sigma_z = np.array([[-1, 0], [0, 1]], dtype=complex)
sigma_plus = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0]], dtype=complex)
sigma_minus = sigma_plus.conj().T
identity_atom = np.eye(2)

H = (
    omega_c * np.kron(number, identity_atom)
    + 0.5 * omega_a * np.kron(identity_field, sigma_z)
    + g * (
        np.kron(a, sigma_plus)
        + np.kron(adag, sigma_minus)
    )
)

energies = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)
print("Numerical:", np.round(energies[:7], 6))

# Analytical energies: |g,0>, then the doublets n = 0, 1, 2.
analytic = [-0.5]
for n in range(3):
    analytic.extend([
        (n + 0.5) - g * np.sqrt(n + 1),
        (n + 0.5) + g * np.sqrt(n + 1),
    ])

print("Analytical:", np.round(sorted(analytic), 6))


Numerical: [-0.5       0.42      0.58      1.386863  1.613137  2.361436  2.638564]
Analytical: [-0.5       0.42      0.58      1.386863  1.613137  2.361436  2.638564]


The isolated state has energy \(E_{g,0}=-1/2\). At resonance the doublets have
\[
E_{n,\pm}=n+\frac12\pm g\sqrt{n+1}.
\]
The first pair is \(0.5\pm0.08\), giving \(0.42\) and \(0.58\). The next is \(1.5\pm0.08\sqrt2\), giving approximately \(1.3869\) and \(1.6131\). The numerical results agree with these values.
In the full space, \(|e,N_{\max}\rangle\) couples to \(|g,N_{\max}+1\rangle\). The latter is absent from the truncated basis, so the former is artificially uncoupled. With the parameters above it lies at the top of the numerical spectrum. It must be excluded from the doublet comparison; complete doublets with \(n<N_{\max}\) are represented exactly.

title: The Jaynes–Cummings model
text:
6 Further reading
Keeping the counter-rotating terms gives the quantum Rabi model. Cavity loss and emission into other modes require an open-system description, usually a master equation.
For a longer treatment of dressed states, Rabi oscillations and revivals, see Matteo Bina, The coherent interaction between matter and radiation: a tutorial on the Jaynes–Cummings model.

title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
1 Minkowski space
Energy, momentum, time and position depend on the inertial frame. A particle can be at rest for one observer and highly energetic for another. However, whether a reaction is possible and the mass of a particle cannot depend on the observer. Special relativity separates frame-dependent components from invariant physical quantities.
We use natural units, \(c=\hbar=1\), unless a conversion to metres or seconds is needed. Mass, energy and momentum then have the same unit, usually MeV or GeV. We choose the metric
\[
g_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
\]
A contravariant four-vector is written
\[
a^\mu=(a^0,\mathbf a).
\]
Lowering its index changes the signs of the spatial components:
\[
a_\mu=g_{\mu\nu}a^\nu=(a^0,-\mathbf a).
\]
The Minkowski scalar product is
\[
a\cdot b=a_\mu b^\mu=a^0b^0-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b.
\tag{1}\]
It is invariant under Lorentz transformations. For the separation \(\Delta x^\mu\) between two events,
\[
\Delta x^2=\Delta t^2-|\Delta\mathbf x|^2.
\]
Its sign gives three cases. A timelike interval has \(\Delta x^2>0\) and admits a frame in which both events occur at the same position. A lightlike interval has \(\Delta x^2=0\). A spacelike interval has \(\Delta x^2<0\) and admits a frame in which the events are simultaneous. This classification is the same for every inertial observer.
For a timelike trajectory, the proper time is defined by
\[
d\tau^2=dt^2-d\mathbf x^2=dt^2(1-v^2),
\]
so
\[
d\tau=\frac{dt}{\gamma},
\qquad
\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}.
\tag{2}\]






NoteFrom Lorentz transformations to space-time





Lorentz first obtained the transformations while studying electrodynamics. Einstein interpreted them in 1905 as relations between inertial observers, without a preferred medium. Minkowski then joined space and time into a four-dimensional geometry. This geometric form is why relativistic calculations can be organised with four-vectors and invariant scalar products.

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#lorentz-transformations
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#lorentz-transformations
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
2 Lorentz transformations
Consider a frame \(\mathcal R'\) moving at velocity \(\beta\) along \(+z\) relative to \(\mathcal R\). The coordinates of the same event satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
t'&=\gamma(t-\beta z),\\
z'&=\gamma(z-\beta t),\\
x'&=x,\qquad y'=y.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]
In matrix form, \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_{\nu}x^\nu\), with
\[
\Lambda(\beta)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma&0&0&-\gamma\beta\\
0&1&0&0\\
0&0&1&0\\
-\gamma\beta&0&0&\gamma
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Substituting Equation 3 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
t'^2-z'^2
&=\gamma^2\big[(t-\beta z)^2-(z-\beta t)^2\big]\\
&=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)(t^2-z^2)\\
&=t^2-z^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(x'^2=x^2\). In matrix notation, this condition is
\[
\Lambda^{\mathrm T}g\Lambda=g.
\tag{4}\]
The inverse boost is obtained by changing the sign of the velocity:
\[
\Lambda^{-1}(\beta)=\Lambda(-\beta).
\]
It is often useful to introduce the rapidity \(\eta\) through
\[
\beta=\tanh\eta,
\qquad
\gamma=\cosh\eta,
\qquad
\gamma\beta=\sinh\eta.
\]
Successive boosts along the same axis add their rapidities. If the first boost has velocity \(\beta_1\) and the second \(\beta_2\), the combined velocity is
\[
\beta=\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}.
\tag{5}\]
This expression never exceeds the speed of light when \(|\beta_1|<1\) and \(|\beta_2|<1\).

2.1 Four-velocity and four-momentum
The four-velocity is
\[
u^\mu=\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}=\gamma(1,\mathbf v),
\]
and satisfies \(u^2=1\). Multiplying by the invariant mass gives the four-momentum
\[
p^\mu=mu^\mu=(E,\mathbf p),
\]
where
\[
E=\gamma m,
\qquad
\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v.
\]
The invariant norm is the mass-shell relation
\[
\boxed{p^2=E^2-\mathbf p^2=m^2.}
\tag{6}\]
For \(|\mathbf p|\ll m\),
\[
E=\sqrt{m^2+\mathbf p^2}
=m+\frac{\mathbf p^2}{2m}+O\!\left(\frac{p^4}{m^3}\right).
\]
The rest energy and the classical kinetic energy appear as the first two terms. For a massless particle, \(E=|\mathbf p|\).
Under a boost along \(z\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
E'&=\gamma(E-\beta p_z),\\
p_z'&=\gamma(p_z-\beta E),\\
p_x'&=p_x,\qquad p_y'=p_y.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
The transverse momentum \(p_T=\sqrt{p_x^2+p_y^2}\) is unchanged by a longitudinal boost.

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#invariant-mass-and-scattering-variables
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#invariant-mass-and-scattering-variables
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
3 Invariant mass and scattering variables
For a reaction
\[
a+b\longrightarrow 1+2+\cdots,
\]
energy and momentum conservation form one four-vector equation:
\[
p_a+p_b=\sum_f p_f.
\tag{8}\]
If a set of particles has total momentum \(P=\sum_i p_i\), its invariant mass is
\[
M_{\mathrm{inv}}^2=P^2
=\left(\sum_iE_i\right)^2
-\left|\sum_i\mathbf p_i\right|^2.
\tag{9}\]
In the centre-of-momentum frame, \(P=(M_{\mathrm{inv}},\mathbf0)\), so the invariant mass is the total energy in that frame. It is not generally the sum of the individual masses: kinetic energy and relative directions also contribute.
For two particles,
\[
M_{12}^2=m_1^2+m_2^2
+2(E_1E_2-\mathbf p_1\cdot\mathbf p_2).
\]
For two photons separated by an angle \(\theta\),
\[
M_{\gamma\gamma}^2=2E_1E_2(1-\cos\theta).
\tag{10}\]
This is how a massive parent can be reconstructed from two massless decay products.
If some particles are not detected, define
\[
p_{\mathrm{miss}}=P_{\mathrm{initial}}-\sum_{\mathrm{visible}}p_i,
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{miss}}^2=p_{\mathrm{miss}}^2.
\]
The method requires the initial four-momentum to be known well enough.

3.1 Mandelstam variables
For the process \(a(p_a)+b(p_b)\to1(p_1)+2(p_2)\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
s&=(p_a+p_b)^2,\\
t&=(p_a-p_1)^2,\\
u&=(p_a-p_2)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}\]
The variable \(s\) is the square of the total centre-of-momentum energy. The variable \(t\) measures the four-momentum transfer between \(a\) and particle 1; it is often negative with our metric. Conservation gives
\[
s+t+u=m_a^2+m_b^2+m_1^2+m_2^2.
\tag{12}\]
To see this, expand the three definitions and use \(p_b-p_1-p_2=-p_a\). Only two of the three invariants are independent once the external masses are fixed.

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#two-body-kinematics
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#two-body-kinematics
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
4 Two-body kinematics

4.1 Centre-of-momentum frame
In this frame, marked with a star,
\[
P^*=p_a^*+p_b^*=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0).
\]
The scalar product \(P\cdot p_a\) is invariant. From \(P=p_a+p_b\),
\[
P\cdot p_a=\frac{s+m_a^2-m_b^2}{2}.
\]
In the centre-of-momentum frame it is also \(\sqrt{s}\,E_a^*\). Therefore
\[
E_a^*=\frac{s+m_a^2-m_b^2}{2\sqrt{s}},
\qquad
E_b^*=\frac{s+m_b^2-m_a^2}{2\sqrt{s}}.
\tag{13}\]
For the final state,
\[
E_1^*=\frac{s+m_1^2-m_2^2}{2\sqrt{s}},
\qquad
E_2^*=\frac{s+m_2^2-m_1^2}{2\sqrt{s}}.
\]
Introduce the Källén function
\[
\lambda(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xy-2xz-2yz.
\]
Using \(|\mathbf p^*|^2=E^{*2}-m^2\) gives
\[
|\mathbf p_i^*|
=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda(s,m_a^2,m_b^2)}}{2\sqrt{s}},
\qquad
|\mathbf p_f^*|
=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda(s,m_1^2,m_2^2)}}{2\sqrt{s}}.
\tag{14}\]
The condition \(\lambda(s,m_1^2,m_2^2)\ge0\) gives the physical threshold \(\sqrt{s}\ge m_1+m_2\).
If \(\theta^*\) is the angle between \(\mathbf p_a^*\) and \(\mathbf p_1^*\),
\[
t=m_a^2+m_1^2-2E_a^*E_1^*
+2|\mathbf p_i^*||\mathbf p_f^*|\cos\theta^*.
\tag{15}\]
At fixed \(s\), the scattering angle therefore determines \(t\).


4.2 Fixed target and collider
Let particle \(b\) be at rest in the laboratory frame. Then
\[
s=(p_a+p_b)^2=m_a^2+m_b^2+2m_bE_a.
\tag{16}\]
At high energy, \(\sqrt{s}\simeq\sqrt{2m_bE_a}\). Much of the projectile energy becomes kinetic energy of the centre of momentum rather than energy available to create new particles.
If the final masses are \(m_1,\ldots,m_n\), the threshold value is
\[
s_{\mathrm{th}}=\left(\sum_jm_j\right)^2.
\]
Thus the minimum total projectile energy is
\[
E_a^{\mathrm{th}}
=\frac{(\sum_jm_j)^2-m_a^2-m_b^2}{2m_b},
\tag{17}\]
and its minimum kinetic energy is \(T_a^{\mathrm{th}}=E_a^{\mathrm{th}}-m_a\). At threshold, the final particles are at rest relative to one another in their centre-of-momentum frame, not in the laboratory frame.
For two opposite ultrarelativistic beams,
\[
\sqrt{s}\simeq2\sqrt{E_aE_b}.
\]
With equal beam energies \(E\), this becomes \(\sqrt{s}\simeq2E\). A collider therefore uses beam energy much more efficiently than a fixed-target experiment.


4.3 Rapidity
The longitudinal rapidity of a particle is
\[
y=\frac12\ln\left(\frac{E+p_z}{E-p_z}\right).
\]
With \(m_T=\sqrt{m^2+p_T^2}\),
\[
E=m_T\cosh y,
\qquad
p_z=m_T\sinh y.
\]
A longitudinal boost of rapidity \(\eta\) gives \(y'=y-\eta\). Rapidity differences and \(p_T\) are therefore invariant under a common longitudinal boost. For a highly relativistic particle, \(y\) is close to the pseudorapidity
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=-\ln\tan\left(\frac\theta2\right),
\]
which depends only on the polar angle measured by the detector.

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#particle-decays
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#particle-decays
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
5 Particle decays
Consider the decay \(A\to1+2\), with parent mass \(M\). In the parent rest frame,
\[
P^*=(M,\mathbf0),
\qquad
P^*=p_1^*+p_2^*.
\]
Momentum conservation gives \(\mathbf p_2^*=-\mathbf p_1^*\). Squaring \(p_2^*=P^*-p_1^*\) gives
\[
m_2^2=M^2+m_1^2-2ME_1^*,
\]
so
\[
E_1^*=\frac{M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2}{2M},
\qquad
E_2^*=\frac{M^2+m_2^2-m_1^2}{2M}.
\tag{18}\]
The common momentum magnitude is
\[
p^*=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)}}{2M}.
\tag{19}\]
The decay is possible only when \(M\ge m_1+m_2\). Kinematics fixes the energies and momentum magnitude, while the interaction and the spin state determine the angular distribution.
If the parent moves along \(+z\) with velocity \(\beta\), a daughter emitted at angle \(\theta^*\) has
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_1^{\mathrm{lab}}&=\gamma(E_1^*+\beta p^*\cos\theta^*),\\
p_{1z}^{\mathrm{lab}}&=\gamma(p^*\cos\theta^*+\beta E_1^*),\\
p_{1T}^{\mathrm{lab}}&=p^*\sin\theta^*.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}\]
For an isotropic decay, \(\cos\theta^*\) is uniform. Since \(E_1^{\mathrm{lab}}\) is linear in \(\cos\theta^*\), the laboratory energy distribution is flat between
\[
E_{1,\min}^{\mathrm{lab}}=\gamma(E_1^*-\beta p^*),
\qquad
E_{1,\max}^{\mathrm{lab}}=\gamma(E_1^*+\beta p^*).
\]

5.1 Phase space, width and lifetime
For a final state with \(n\) particles, the Lorentz-invariant phase-space measure is
\[
d\Phi_n(P;p_1,\ldots,p_n)
=(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}\!\left(P-\sum_{i=1}^np_i\right)
\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{d^3\mathbf p_i}{(2\pi)^3,2E_i}.
\tag{21}\]
The decay rate is
\[
d\Gamma=\frac{1}{2M}\overline{|\mathcal M|^2},d\Phi_n.
\tag{22}\]
For a two-body decay,
\[
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega}
=\frac{p^*}{32\pi^2M^2}\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.
\]
If the squared matrix element is angle-independent,
\[
\Gamma=\frac{p^*}{8\pi M^2}\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.
\tag{23}\]
The factor \(p^*\) shows the phase-space suppression near threshold. If the final state contains identical particles, the phase-space integral must be divided by the appropriate factorial to avoid counting the same state several times.
An unstable state evolves as \(e^{-iMt-\Gamma t/2}\) in its rest frame. Its survival probability is \(e^{-\Gamma t}\), hence
\[
\tau_0=\frac{1}{\Gamma}
\]
in natural units, or \(\tau_0=\hbar/\Gamma\) in SI units. In the laboratory, the mean decay length is
\[
L=\beta\gamma c\tau_0=\frac{pc}{M}\tau_0.
\tag{24}\]

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#cross-sections-and-observed-events
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#cross-sections-and-observed-events
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
6 Cross sections and observed events
For a reaction with two incoming particles,
\[
d\sigma=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(p_a\cdot p_b)^2-m_a^2m_b^2}}
\overline{|\mathcal M|^2},d\Phi_n.
\tag{25}\]
For \(2\to2\) scattering in the centre-of-momentum frame,
\[
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}
=\frac{1}{64\pi^2s}
\frac{|\mathbf p_f^*|}{|\mathbf p_i^*|}
\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.
\tag{26}\]
If there is no azimuthal dependence, Equation 15 gives
\[
\frac{dt}{d\cos\theta^*}
=2|\mathbf p_i^*||\mathbf p_f^*|.
\]
Using \(d\Omega=2\pi,d\cos\theta^*\),
\[
\frac{d\sigma}{dt}
=\frac{1}{64\pi s|\mathbf p_i^*|^2}
\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.
\]
For massless incoming particles, \(|\mathbf p_i^*|=\sqrt{s}/2\) and
\[
\frac{d\sigma}{dt}
=\frac{1}{16\pi s^2}\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}.
\]
The number of observed events in a selected decay channel is
\[
N_{\mathrm{obs}}
=\sigma\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}\,\mathcal B\,\varepsilon,
\tag{27}\]
where \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}\) is the integrated luminosity, \(\mathcal B\) the product of branching fractions and \(\varepsilon\) the total acceptance and efficiency.
Useful conversions are
\[
1\ \mathrm{GeV}^{-2}\simeq0.3894\ \mathrm{mb},
\qquad
1\ \mathrm{pb}=10^{-12}\ \mathrm b.
\]

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#deep-inelastic-scattering
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#deep-inelastic-scattering
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
7 Deep-inelastic scattering
Consider
\[
e^-(k)+p(P)\longrightarrow e^-(k')+X.
\]
The momentum transferred to the proton is \(q=k-k'\). Neglecting the electron mass,
\[
q^2=-4EE'\sin^2\left(\frac\theta2\right),
\]
so one defines the positive quantity
\[
Q^2=-q^2=4EE'\sin^2\left(\frac\theta2\right).
\tag{28}\]
A large \(Q^2\) corresponds to a short distance scale. The invariant mass of the hadronic final state is
\[
W^2=(P+q)^2=M_p^2+2P\cdot q-Q^2.
\tag{29}\]
The Bjorken variable and the inelasticity are
\[
x=\frac{Q^2}{2P\cdot q},
\qquad
y=\frac{P\cdot q}{P\cdot k}.
\tag{30}\]
In the proton rest frame, \(y=(E-E')/E\). Eliminating \(P\cdot q\) gives
\[
W^2=M_p^2+Q^2\left(\frac1x-1\right).
\tag{31}\]
If the electron mass is neglected,
\[
s=(k+P)^2=M_p^2+2P\cdot k,
\]
and therefore
\[
Q^2=xy(s-M_p^2)\simeq xys
\tag{32}\]
at high energy. Elastic scattering has \(W=M_p\) and \(x=1\). In deep-inelastic scattering, \(W>M_p\) and \(0<x<1\). In the parton model and at large \(Q^2\), \(x\) is interpreted as the longitudinal momentum fraction of the struck parton. That interpretation uses dynamics in addition to kinematics.

objectID: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#exercises
href: cours EN/Relativité restreinte et cinématique des interactions - EN.html#exercises
title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
8 Exercises
Unless stated otherwise, use \(c=\hbar=1\) and \(g=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\).

8.1 Exercise 1 — Interval and proper time
Two events have separation \(\Delta x^\mu=(5,3,0,0)\ \mathrm{m}\), with the time component written as \(c\Delta t\).

Classify the interval.
Find the proper time between the events.
Find the velocity of the frame in which the events occur at the same place.







NoteSolution





The invariant interval is
\[
\Delta x^2=5^2-3^2=16\ \mathrm{m}^2>0,
\]
so it is timelike. In the frame where the spatial separation vanishes, \(c\Delta\tau=\sqrt{\Delta x^2}=4\ \mathrm m\), hence
\[
\Delta\tau=\frac4c\simeq1.33\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm s.
\]
From \(\Delta x'=\gamma(\Delta x-\beta c\Delta t)=0\),
\[
\beta=\frac{\Delta x}{c\Delta t}=\frac35.
\]





8.2 Exercise 2 — A boosted four-momentum
A particle has \(p^\mu=(10,0,0,8)\ \mathrm{GeV}\).

Find its invariant mass.
Find the velocity of its rest frame relative to the given frame.
Verify that a boost to this frame gives \(p'^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\).







NoteSolution





The mass is
\[
m=\sqrt{E^2-p_z^2}=\sqrt{100-64}=6\ \mathrm{GeV}.
\]
To set \(p_z'=\gamma(p_z-\beta E)\) to zero, choose \(\beta=p_z/E=0.8\). Then \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.8^2}=5/3\), and
\[
E'=\frac53(10-0.8\times8)=6\ \mathrm{GeV},
\qquad p_z'=0.
\]





8.3 Exercise 3 — Muon decay length
A muon has energy \(E=20\ \mathrm{GeV}\), mass \(m_\mu=105.7\ \mathrm{MeV}\) and proper lifetime \(\tau_0=2.20\ \mu\mathrm s\).

Calculate \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\).
Find its mean decay length.







NoteSolution





Using GeV throughout,
\[
\gamma=\frac{E}{m_\mu}=\frac{20}{0.1057}\simeq189.2.
\]
Also \(\beta=\sqrt{1-1/\gamma^2}\simeq0.999986\). Therefore
\[
L=\beta\gamma c\tau_0
\simeq189.2(2.998\times10^8)(2.20\times10^{-6})\ \mathrm m
\simeq1.25\times10^5\ \mathrm m.
\]





8.4 Exercise 4 — Diphoton invariant mass
Two photons have energies \(E_1=40\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and \(E_2=60\ \mathrm{GeV}\), with an angle of \(120^\circ\) between them. Find their invariant mass. What would happen if they were collinear?






NoteSolution





From Equation 10,
\[
M_{\gamma\gamma}^2
=2(40)(60)(1-\cos120^\circ)
=7200\ \mathrm{GeV}^2.
\]
Thus \(M_{\gamma\gamma}\simeq84.9\ \mathrm{GeV}\). If the photons were collinear in the same direction, \(\theta=0\) and their invariant mass would vanish.





8.5 Exercise 5 — Mandelstam variables
For massless elastic scattering \(a+b\to a+b\) in the centre-of-momentum frame, show that
\[
t=-\frac s2(1-\cos\theta^*),
\qquad
u=-\frac s2(1+\cos\theta^*),
\]
and verify \(s+t+u=0\).






NoteSolution





Every particle has \(E^*=|\mathbf p^*|=\sqrt{s}/2\). Equation Equation 15 gives
\[
t=-2p^{*2}(1-\cos\theta^*)
=-\frac s2(1-\cos\theta^*).
\]
Particle 2 is emitted in the opposite direction, so replacing \(\cos\theta^*\) by \(-\cos\theta^*\) gives
\[
u=-\frac s2(1+\cos\theta^*).
\]
Adding the three expressions gives zero, in agreement with Equation 12 for four massless particles.





8.6 Exercise 6 — Pion production on a fixed target
For \(p+p\to p+p+\pi^0\), use \(m_p=938.27\ \mathrm{MeV}\) and \(m_{\pi^0}=134.98\ \mathrm{MeV}\).

Find the threshold kinetic energy of the projectile proton.
Explain why it is larger than \(m_{\pi^0}\).







NoteSolution





The minimum final invariant mass is \(2m_p+m_{\pi^0}\). Equation Equation 17 gives
\[
E_p^{\mathrm{th}}
=\frac{(2m_p+m_{\pi^0})^2-2m_p^2}{2m_p}.
\]
Subtracting the projectile rest mass,
\[
T_p^{\mathrm{th}}
=2m_{\pi^0}+\frac{m_{\pi^0}^2}{2m_p}
\simeq279.7\ \mathrm{MeV}.
\]
The final state must keep the incident momentum. At threshold its particles have no relative motion in their centre-of-momentum frame, but that frame still moves in the laboratory. Some energy is therefore required for collective kinetic motion.





8.7 Exercise 7 — A two-body decay
A particle of mass \(M=5.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\) decays to particles of masses \(m_1=1.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and \(m_2=2.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\).

Find \(E_1^*\) and \(E_2^*\).
Find the common momentum magnitude.
Check energy conservation.







NoteSolution





Using Equation 18,
\[
E_1^*=\frac{25+1-4}{10}=2.2\ \mathrm{GeV},
\qquad
E_2^*=\frac{25+4-1}{10}=2.8\ \mathrm{GeV}.
\]
Then
\[
p^*=\sqrt{E_1^{*2}-m_1^2}
=\sqrt{2.2^2-1^2}
\simeq1.96\ \mathrm{GeV}.
\]
The second daughter gives the same value, and \(E_1^*+E_2^*=5.0\ \mathrm{GeV}=M\).





8.8 Exercise 8 — Energy endpoints after a boost
The parent in Exercise 7 has laboratory energy \(E_A=10\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and moves along \(+z\). Assume an isotropic decay.

Find \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\).
Find the minimum and maximum laboratory energies of particle 1.
Describe the energy distribution between them.







NoteSolution





Here \(\gamma=E_A/M=2\) and \(\beta=\sqrt{1-1/\gamma^2}=\sqrt3/2\). With \(E_1^*=2.2\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and \(p^*\simeq1.96\ \mathrm{GeV}\),
\[
E_{1,\min}^{\mathrm{lab}}
=2(2.2-0.866\times1.96)\simeq1.00\ \mathrm{GeV},
\]
\[
E_{1,\max}^{\mathrm{lab}}
=2(2.2+0.866\times1.96)\simeq7.80\ \mathrm{GeV}.
\]
For an isotropic decay, \(\cos\theta^*\) is uniform. Since the energy is linear in \(\cos\theta^*\), the ideal energy distribution is uniform between these endpoints.





8.9 Exercise 9 — Width and lifetime
A particle has total width \(\Gamma=4.0\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{GeV}\).

Find its proper lifetime using \(\hbar=6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}\).
If \(\beta\gamma=3\), find its mean decay length.







NoteSolution





The proper lifetime is
\[
\tau_0=\frac{\hbar}{\Gamma}
=\frac{6.582\times10^{-25}}{4.0\times10^{-13}}
\simeq1.65\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm s.
\]
Thus
\[
L=\beta\gamma c\tau_0
=3(2.998\times10^8)(1.65\times10^{-12})\ \mathrm m
\simeq1.48\ \mathrm{mm}.
\]





8.10 Exercise 10 — Event yield
A process has \(\sigma=2.5\ \mathrm{pb}\) and is studied with \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{int}}=140\ \mathrm{fb}^{-1}\). The selected decay has branching fraction \(0.12\) and efficiency \(0.35\).

Calculate the number produced before decays and selection.
Calculate the expected observed yield.







NoteSolution





Since \(1\ \mathrm{fb}^{-1}=10^3\ \mathrm{pb}^{-1}\),
\[
N_{\mathrm{prod}}=(2.5)(140\times10^3)=3.50\times10^5.
\]
After branching fraction and efficiency,
\[
N_{\mathrm{obs}}
=(3.50\times10^5)(0.12)(0.35)
=1.47\times10^4.
\]





8.11 Exercise 11 — Deep-inelastic variables
An electron of energy \(E=20\ \mathrm{GeV}\) scatters from a proton at rest. The final electron has \(E'=12\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and scattering angle \(\theta=20^\circ\). Use \(M_p=0.938\ \mathrm{GeV}\).

Calculate \(Q^2\) and \(y\).
Calculate \(x\).
Calculate \(W\) and check that the event is inelastic.







NoteSolution





From Equation 28,
\[
Q^2=4(20)(12)\sin^2(10^\circ)
\simeq28.95\ \mathrm{GeV}^2.
\]
In the proton rest frame,
\[
y=1-\frac{E'}E=0.40.
\]
Since \(2P\cdot q=2M_p(E-E')\),
\[
x=\frac{Q^2}{2M_p(E-E')}
\simeq\frac{28.95}{2(0.938)(8)}
\simeq1.93.
\]
This is outside the physical range \(x\le1\). The stated values cannot describe scattering from a free proton at rest. Equivalently,
\[
W^2=M_p^2+2M_p(E-E')-Q^2<0.
\]
The contradiction is useful: measured energies and angles must satisfy the invariant kinematic constraints. For example, at the same energies the angle must be smaller than about \(14.4^\circ\) to keep \(x\le1\).





8.12 Exercise 12 — Physical DIS event
Repeat Exercise 11 with \(\theta=10^\circ\).

Find \(Q^2\), \(y\), \(x\) and \(W\).
Explain separately what \(Q^2\), \(x\) and \(W\) describe.







NoteSolution





The inelasticity is unchanged: \(y=0.40\). Now
\[
Q^2=4(20)(12)\sin^2(5^\circ)
\simeq7.29\ \mathrm{GeV}^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
x=\frac{7.29}{2(0.938)(8)}\simeq0.486.
\]
Finally,
\[
W^2=M_p^2+2M_p(8)-7.29\simeq8.60\ \mathrm{GeV}^2,
\]
so \(W\simeq2.93\ \mathrm{GeV}>M_p\). The event is inelastic. The value \(Q^2\) sets the resolution scale, \(x\) labels the longitudinal momentum fraction in the parton-model interpretation, and \(W\) is the invariant mass produced in the hadronic system.

title: Special relativity and particle kinematics
text:
9 Problems

9.1 Problem 1 — Formation and decay of a resonance
An electron and positron collide head-on with equal beam energies \(E\). They form a resonance \(R\) of mass \(M_R\), which decays as \(R\to\mu^+\mu^-\). Neglect the electron mass.

Find \(s\) and the beam energy required to produce \(R\) at rest.
Find the muon energy and momentum in the resonance rest frame.
Show that the reconstructed dimuon invariant mass is \(M_R\).
If the beams instead have unequal energies \(E_+\) and \(E_-\), find the velocity of the produced resonance in the laboratory.







NoteSolution





For opposite massless beams,
\[
p_-=(E,0,0,E),
\qquad
p_+=(E,0,0,-E).
\]
Their sum is \((2E,\mathbf0)\), so \(s=4E^2\). Resonant production at rest requires
\[
E=\frac{M_R}{2}.
\]
The two muons have equal masses and are back-to-back. Hence
\[
E_\mu^*=\frac{M_R}{2},
\qquad
p_\mu^*=\frac12\sqrt{M_R^2-4m_\mu^2}.
\]
Their total four-momentum is the resonance momentum, so
\[
M_{\mu\mu}^2=(p_{\mu^+}+p_{\mu^-})^2=P_R^2=M_R^2.
\]
For unequal beams,
\[
P_R=(E_-+E_+,0,0,E_--E_+),
\]
therefore
\[
\beta_R=\frac{E_--E_+}{E_-+E_+}.
\]





9.2 Problem 2 — Missing-mass reconstruction
A particle \(A\) of known four-momentum decays as \(A\to B+X\). Only \(B\) is detected.

Express the missing mass \(M_X\) in terms of \(P_A\) and \(p_B\).
In the rest frame of \(A\), express \(M_X^2\) using \(M_A\), \(m_B\) and \(E_B^*\).
Suppose \(M_A=5.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\), \(m_B=1.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\) and \(E_B^*=2.2\ \mathrm{GeV}\). Find \(M_X\).
Explain why the result does not depend on the frame used for the measurement.







NoteSolution





Four-momentum conservation gives \(p_X=P_A-p_B\). Thus
\[
M_X^2=(P_A-p_B)^2.
\]
In the rest frame of \(A\), \(P_A=(M_A,\mathbf0)\), so
\[
M_X^2=M_A^2+m_B^2-2M_AE_B^*.
\]
With the given values,
\[
M_X^2=25+1-2(5)(2.2)=4\ \mathrm{GeV}^2,
\]
and \(M_X=2.0\ \mathrm{GeV}\). The result is frame-independent because it is the Minkowski square of a four-vector.





9.3 Problem 3 — From a cross section to a displaced signal
A particle \(X\) is produced with cross section \(0.80\ \mathrm{pb}\) in a dataset of \(300\ \mathrm{fb}^{-1}\). It decays to the selected channel with branching fraction \(0.05\). The selection efficiency, excluding the decay-position requirement, is \(0.40\). Each accepted particle has approximately \(\beta\gamma=2.5\) and proper lifetime \(\tau_0=0.50\ \mathrm{ns}\).

Find the mean laboratory decay length.
Assuming an exponential decay law, find the probability that \(X\) decays between \(1\ \mathrm{cm}\) and \(20\ \mathrm{cm}\) from the production point.
Find the expected number of selected events in this interval.







NoteSolution





The mean decay length is
\[
L=\beta\gamma c\tau_0
=2.5(2.998\times10^8)(0.50\times10^{-9})\ \mathrm m
\simeq0.375\ \mathrm m.
\]
For an exponential distribution in distance,
\[
P(\ell_1<\ell<\ell_2)
=e^{-\ell_1/L}-e^{-\ell_2/L}.
\]
With \(\ell_1=0.01\ \mathrm m\) and \(\ell_2=0.20\ \mathrm m\),
\[
P\simeq e^{-0.01/0.375}-e^{-0.20/0.375}
\simeq0.387.
\]
The number produced is
\[
N_{\mathrm{prod}}=(0.80)(300\times10^3)=2.40\times10^5.
\]
The expected selected yield is
\[
N_{\mathrm{obs}}
=(2.40\times10^5)(0.05)(0.40)(0.387)
\simeq1.86\times10^3.
\]

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
1 Why symmetries matter
A symmetry is a transformation that changes the mathematical description of a system without changing its physical laws. For example, an isolated experiment gives the same result if it is performed one hour later or if the whole apparatus is rotated. These two observations are related to the conservation of energy and angular momentum.
The relation between symmetry and conservation is not an extra rule added to mechanics. It follows from the action principle. This chapter first derives this connection, then introduces the group language used to describe continuous symmetries. The last sections explain how space-time symmetries define mass and spin, while internal symmetries organise electric charge, isospin and colour.
We use natural units,
\[
\hbar=c=1,
\]
and the Minkowski metric
\[
\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
\]
Greek indices label space-time components. Repeated indices are summed.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
2 The action and field equations
For a mechanical system with coordinates \(q_i(t)\), the action is
\[
S[q_i]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q_i,\dot q_i,t)\,dt.
\]
In field theory, the dynamical variables are fields \(\phi_a(x)\) defined at every point of space-time. The action becomes
\[
S[\phi]=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a,x),
\tag{1}\]
where \(\mathcal L\) is the Lagrangian density. Consider a small variation \(\phi_a\to\phi_a+\delta\phi_a\) which vanishes on the boundary. At first order,
\[
\delta S=\int d^4x\left[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}\delta\phi_a
+\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}
\partial_\mu\delta\phi_a
\right].
\]
Integrating the second term by parts gives
\[
\delta S=\int d^4x\left[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}
-\partial_\mu\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}
\right]\delta\phi_a,
\]
because the surface term vanishes. The variations are arbitrary inside the integration region, so a physical field satisfies
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}
-\partial_\mu\left[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}
\right]=0.}
\tag{2}\]
These are the Euler–Lagrange equations for fields.
For a real scalar field,
\[
\mathcal L=\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi
-\frac12m^2\phi^2.
\tag{3}\]
We have
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi}=-m^2\phi,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}=\partial^\mu\phi.
\]
Equation Equation 2 therefore gives
\[
(\Box+m^2)\phi=0,
\qquad
\Box=\partial_\mu\partial^\mu.
\tag{4}\]
The action, rather than the precise form of \(\mathcal L\), is the important object. Adding a total divergence,
\[
\mathcal L' = \mathcal L+\partial_\mu F^\mu,
\]
changes the action only by a boundary term. Under the usual boundary conditions, \(\mathcal L\) and \(\mathcal L'\) give the same field equations.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
3 Noether’s theorem

3.1 Internal transformations
Consider a continuous transformation which does not move the space-time point:
\[
\phi_a(x)\longrightarrow \phi'_a(x)
=\phi_a(x)+\varepsilon R_a(\phi,x)+O(\varepsilon^2),
\tag{5}\]
where \(\varepsilon\) is a small constant. The variation of the Lagrangian density can always be rearranged as
\[
\delta\mathcal L
=\left[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}
-\partial_\mu\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}
\right]\delta\phi_a
+\partial_\mu\left[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}\delta\phi_a
\right].
\tag{6}\]
On a solution of the field equations, the first term vanishes. If the transformation is a symmetry, the remaining variation is at most a total divergence,
\[
\delta\mathcal L=\varepsilon\,\partial_\mu K^\mu.
\]
Using \(\delta\phi_a=\varepsilon R_a\) in Equation 6 gives
\[
\boxed{
j^\mu=
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}R_a-K^\mu,
\qquad
\partial_\mu j^\mu=0.}
\tag{7}\]
This is the first Noether theorem: every continuous global symmetry of the action produces a conserved current.
Writing the conservation equation as
\[
\partial_tj^0+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0
\]
and integrating over space gives
\[
\frac{dQ}{dt}
=-\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf j\cdot d\mathbf S,
\qquad
Q=\int_V d^3\mathbf x\,j^0.
\]
If the flux through the boundary vanishes, \(Q\) is conserved.






NoteEmmy Noether





In 1918, Emmy Noether showed that continuous symmetries of the action lead to conservation laws and that local symmetries lead to identities between field equations. Her result gave a common origin to conservation laws which had previously been treated separately.





3.2 Example: a complex scalar field
Let
\[
\mathcal L=\partial_\mu\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-m^2\phi^*\phi.
\tag{8}\]
It is invariant under the global phase transformation
\[
\phi\to e^{-iq\alpha}\phi,
\qquad
\phi^*\to e^{iq\alpha}\phi^*,
\tag{9}\]
where \(\alpha\) is constant. At first order,
\[
\delta\phi=-iq\alpha\phi,
\qquad
\delta\phi^*=iq\alpha\phi^*.
\]
Treating \(\phi\) and \(\phi^*\) as independent fields, Equation 7 gives
\[
\boxed{
j^\mu=iq\left(
\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-\phi\partial^\mu\phi^*
\right).}
\tag{10}\]
Its divergence is
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu
=iq(\phi^*\Box\phi-\phi\Box\phi^*).
\]
The field equations \(\Box\phi=-m^2\phi\) and \(\Box\phi^*=-m^2\phi^*\) make this expression zero. After quantisation, the associated charge counts particles and antiparticles with opposite signs.


3.3 Translations and energy-momentum
Space-time transformations also produce Noether currents. Under a translation
\[
x^\mu\to x'^\mu=x^\mu+\varepsilon^\mu,
\]
a scalar field varies at a fixed point as
\[
\delta\phi=-\varepsilon^\nu\partial_\nu\phi.
\]
If \(\mathcal L\) has no explicit dependence on \(x\), the associated current contains the canonical energy-momentum tensor
\[
\boxed{
T^\mu{}_{\nu}
=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}
\partial_\nu\phi_a
-\delta^\mu{}_{\nu}\mathcal L,
\qquad
\partial_\mu T^\mu{}_{\nu}=0.}
\tag{11}\]
The conserved four-momentum is
\[
P_\nu=\int d^3\mathbf x\,T^0{}_{\nu}.
\]
Time translations give energy conservation and spatial translations give momentum conservation. For the real scalar field in Equation 3,
\[
T^{00}=\frac12\dot\phi^2
+\frac12(\boldsymbol\nabla\phi)^2
+\frac12m^2\phi^2.
\]
This expression is the energy density stored in the field.
An infinitesimal Lorentz transformation has the form
\[
\delta x^\mu=\omega^\mu{}_{\nu}x^\nu,
\qquad
\omega_{\mu\nu}=-\omega_{\nu\mu}.
\]
The antisymmetric tensor \(\omega_{\mu\nu}\) contains three rotations and three boosts. The corresponding current is
\[
J^{\lambda\mu\nu}
=x^\mu T^{\lambda\nu}-x^\nu T^{\lambda\mu}
+S^{\lambda\mu\nu}.
\tag{12}\]
The first two terms describe orbital angular momentum. The last term depends on how the field components transform and gives the intrinsic spin part. It vanishes for a scalar field.


3.4 Global and local symmetries
In a global symmetry, the transformation parameter is constant. The corresponding Noether charge generally acts on physical states. In a local symmetry, the parameter may depend on space-time. Such a transformation often expresses a redundancy in the description.
For electromagnetism,
\[
A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha(x)
\]
does not change
\[
F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu.
\]
The local symmetry implies an identity between the equations of motion. If
\[
\mathcal E_A^\mu=\frac{\delta S}{\delta A_\mu},
\]
then gauge invariance gives
\[
0=\delta S
=\int d^4x\,\mathcal E_A^\mu\partial_\mu\alpha
=-\int d^4x\,\alpha\,\partial_\mu\mathcal E_A^\mu.
\]
Since \(\alpha(x)\) is arbitrary,
\[
\partial_\mu\mathcal E_A^\mu\equiv0.
\tag{13}\]
This is a simple form of Noether’s second theorem. It does not provide one independent physical charge at every point; instead, it shows that some field equations are not independent.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
4 Groups and Lie algebras
A set \(G\) is a group if it has an associative product, an identity, an inverse for every element and closure under the product. A symmetry transformation must be reversible, and two successive symmetry transformations must still be a symmetry. This is why groups appear naturally.
A Lie group is also a smooth manifold. Its elements near the identity can be written
\[
U(\boldsymbol\alpha)
=\exp(-i\alpha^aT^a),
\tag{14}\]
where the Hermitian operators \(T^a\) are generators. For small parameters,
\[
U(\boldsymbol\alpha)=1-i\alpha^aT^a+O(\alpha^2).
\]
The generators satisfy commutation relations
\[
\boxed{[T^a,T^b]=if^{ab}{}_cT^c,}
\tag{15}\]
where \(f^{ab}{}_c\) are the structure constants. They describe the Lie algebra of the group.
For an abelian group, all generators commute. For a non-abelian group, the order of two transformations matters. The Jacobi identity,
\[
[T^a,[T^b,T^c]]+[T^b,[T^c,T^a]]+[T^c,[T^a,T^b]]=0,
\]
imposes a consistency condition on the structure constants.






NoteSophus Lie





Sophus Lie introduced continuous transformation groups in the nineteenth century while studying differential equations. The passage from a group to its generators turns a nonlinear composition law into the linear algebra of commutators.




4.1 Representations
An abstract group becomes useful in physics through a representation. A representation assigns a matrix or an operator \(D(g)\) to each group element such that
\[
D(g_1g_2)=D(g_1)D(g_2).
\]
Different objects may transform in different representations of the same group. Under rotations, a scalar has one component, a vector has three components and a spinor has two complex components. The group is the same, but its representations are different.
A representation is reducible if its vector space contains a proper invariant subspace. Otherwise it is irreducible. Irreducible representations are the basic blocks used to classify states.
An operator \(C\) which commutes with every generator,
\[
[C,T^a]=0,
\]
is called a Casimir operator. By Schur’s lemma, a Casimir is proportional to the identity inside an irreducible representation. Its eigenvalue can therefore label that representation.
For \(SU(2)\), the quadratic Casimir is
\[
\mathbf T^2=T_1^2+T_2^2+T_3^2,
\]
with eigenvalue \(j(j+1)\) in the spin-\(j\) representation.


4.2 Tensor products
If one state transforms in \(R_1\) and another in \(R_2\), their combined state transforms in the tensor product \(R_1\otimes R_2\). This product is usually reducible. For two \(SU(2)\) doublets,
\[
\mathbf2\otimes\mathbf2=\mathbf3\oplus\mathbf1.
\tag{16}\]
The singlet is invariant under the group. In quantum mechanics it is the antisymmetric combination
\[
|0,0\rangle
=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle).
\]
The three symmetric states form the triplet.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
5 The Poincaré group
The Poincaré group contains translations and Lorentz transformations. Its generators are the four-momentum \(P^\mu\) and the antisymmetric Lorentz generators \(M^{\mu\nu}=-M^{\nu\mu}\). Their algebra is
\[
[P^\mu,P^\nu]=0,
\]
\[
[M^{\mu\nu},P^\rho]
=i(\eta^{\mu\rho}P^\nu-\eta^{\nu\rho}P^\mu),
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
[M^{\mu\nu},M^{\rho\sigma}]
=i(&\eta^{\mu\rho}M^{\nu\sigma}
-\eta^{\mu\sigma}M^{\nu\rho}\\
&-\eta^{\nu\rho}M^{\mu\sigma}
+\eta^{\nu\sigma}M^{\mu\rho}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}\]
The first Casimir is
\[
P^2=P_\mu P^\mu.
\]
For a one-particle state, its eigenvalue is \(m^2\). Mass is therefore not just a parameter in an equation: it labels an irreducible representation of the space-time symmetry group.
The second Casimir is built from the Pauli–Lubanski vector
\[
W^\mu=\frac12\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}
P_\nu M_{\rho\sigma}.
\tag{18}\]
For a massive particle, we may work in its rest frame, \(P^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\). Then
\[
W^0=0,
\qquad
\mathbf W=m\mathbf J,
\]
and
\[
W^2=-m^2s(s+1).
\tag{19}\]
The states are labelled by mass \(m\) and spin \(s\), with \(2s+1\) spin projections.
For a massless particle there is no rest frame. Physical states are instead labelled by helicity,
\[
h=\frac{\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf p}{|\mathbf p|}.
\]
A photon has two physical helicities, \(h=+1\) and \(h=-1\). This does not mean that a four-vector field has only two components. Field components, constraints, gauge freedom and physical particle states are different things.






NoteWigner’s classification





Eugene Wigner classified elementary particles through the unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group. In this view, mass and spin are the invariant labels of a particle, not properties added after the theory has been built.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
6 Internal symmetries
Internal symmetries act on field components without moving the space-time point. They organise particles into multiplets and determine which interactions are allowed.

6.1 The group \(U(1)\)
\(U(1)\) contains complex phases
\[
U(\alpha)=e^{-iq\alpha}.
\]
It is one-dimensional and abelian. A field of charge \(q\) transforms as in Equation 9. Products with zero total charge are invariant. For example, \(\phi^*\phi\) is invariant, while \(\phi^2\) is not invariant unless \(q=0\).
If the phase becomes local, \(\alpha\to\alpha(x)\), an ordinary derivative produces an extra term:
\[
\partial_\mu\phi
\to e^{-iq\alpha}
(\partial_\mu\phi-iq\,\partial_\mu\alpha\,\phi).
\]
Introduce a gauge field \(A_\mu\) and the covariant derivative
\[
D_\mu=\partial_\mu+iqA_\mu.
\]
If
\[
A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha,
\]
then
\[
D_\mu\phi\to e^{-iq\alpha}D_\mu\phi.
\]
The kinetic term \(|D_\mu\phi|^2\) is locally invariant. The interaction with the gauge field is therefore required by local phase invariance.


6.2 The group \(SU(2)\)
\(SU(2)\) is the group of unitary \(2\times2\) matrices with determinant one. In its fundamental representation, the generators are
\[
T^a=\frac{\sigma^a}{2},
\]
where \(\sigma^a\) are the Pauli matrices. They satisfy
\[
[T^a,T^b]=i\varepsilon^{abc}T^c.
\tag{20}\]
A doublet
\[
\Psi=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1\\\psi_2\end{pmatrix}
\]
transforms as
\[
\Psi\to U\Psi,
\qquad
U=\exp\left(-i\alpha^a\frac{\sigma^a}{2}\right).
\]
Because \(U^\dagger U=1\), the quantity \(\Psi^\dagger\Psi\) is invariant. The irreducible representations are labelled by \(j=0,\frac12,1,\ldots\) and have dimension \(2j+1\).
Historically, the proton and neutron were treated as an approximate isospin doublet,
\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}p\\n\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The strong interaction is nearly invariant under rotations in this internal space. Electromagnetic effects and the difference between the up- and down-quark masses break the symmetry, which is why the proton and neutron masses are close but not equal.


6.3 The group \(SU(3)\)
\(SU(3)\) is the group of unitary \(3\times3\) matrices with determinant one. It has eight generators,
\[
T^a=\frac{\lambda^a}{2},
\qquad a=1,\ldots,8,
\]
where \(\lambda^a\) are the Gell-Mann matrices. Their commutators are
\[
[T^a,T^b]=if^{abc}T^c.
\]
Quark colours form the fundamental triplet,
\[
q=\begin{pmatrix}q_r\\q_g\\q_b\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The eight gluons transform in the adjoint representation, which also has dimension eight. The tensor products
\[
\mathbf3\otimes\overline{\mathbf3}
=\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf8,
\]
and
\[
\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3
=\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf8\oplus\mathbf8\oplus\mathbf{10}
\]
show how colour singlets can be formed from a quark-antiquark pair or from three quarks. Observed hadrons are colour singlets.
For a local non-abelian symmetry, the covariant derivative is
\[
D_\mu=\partial_\mu+igA_\mu^aT^a.
\]
The field strength is
\[
F_{\mu\nu}^a
=\partial_\mu A_\nu^a-\partial_\nu A_\mu^a
-gf^{abc}A_\mu^bA_\nu^c.
\tag{21}\]
The last term is absent in electromagnetism. It produces direct interactions between gauge bosons. This difference follows from the non-commuting generators, not from an extra choice made later.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
7 Exact, broken and anomalous symmetries
An exact symmetry leaves the action invariant and is also respected by the physical state under consideration. Its charge is conserved and states can be arranged into exact multiplets.
An explicit breaking occurs when a term in the Lagrangian is not invariant. The current then satisfies
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu=\Delta,
\]
where \(\Delta\) measures the breaking. If \(\Delta\) is small, the symmetry remains a useful approximation.
In spontaneous breaking, the action is symmetric but the lowest-energy state is not. Consider
\[
V(\phi)=-\mu^2|\phi|^2+\lambda|\phi|^4,
\qquad \mu^2,\lambda>0.
\]
The minima satisfy
\[
|\phi|=\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{2\lambda}}.
\]
All phases have the same energy, but a particular vacuum chooses one phase. For a global continuous symmetry this produces a massless Goldstone mode. For a gauge symmetry, the corresponding degree of freedom becomes part of a massive gauge field through the Higgs mechanism.
Finally, an anomaly is a symmetry of the classical action which is not preserved after quantisation. Anomalies of global symmetries can have physical effects. An anomaly in a gauge symmetry would make the theory inconsistent, so the particle content must make gauge anomalies cancel.
These cases should not be confused: explicit breaking changes the action, spontaneous breaking changes the vacuum, and an anomaly appears during quantisation.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
8 Exercises

8.1 Exercise 1 — Klein–Gordon equation
Starting from Equation 3, derive the Euler–Lagrange equation. Then write it explicitly in terms of time and spatial derivatives.






NoteSolution





The derivatives of the Lagrangian density are
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi}=-m^2\phi,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}=\partial^\mu\phi.
\]
Therefore
\[
(\Box+m^2)\phi=0.
\]
With the chosen metric, \(\Box=\partial_t^2-\nabla^2\), so
\[
\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\phi+m^2\phi=0.
\]





8.2 Exercise 2 — A shift symmetry
Consider a real massless scalar field,
\[
\mathcal L=\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi.
\]
Show that it is invariant under \(\phi\to\phi+\varepsilon\), find the Noether current and explain what changes when a mass term is added.






NoteSolution





The Lagrangian contains only derivatives, so a constant shift does not change it. Here \(R=1\) and \(K^\mu=0\). Thus
\[
j^\mu=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}
=\partial^\mu\phi.
\]
Its conservation, \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=\Box\phi=0\), is the field equation. A mass term \(-m^2\phi^2/2\) changes under the shift and explicitly breaks the symmetry.





8.3 Exercise 3 — Current of a complex field
Derive Equation 10 from the global transformation Equation 9. Verify its conservation directly with the field equations.






NoteSolution





The infinitesimal variations are
\[
\frac{\delta\phi}{\alpha}=-iq\phi,
\qquad
\frac{\delta\phi^*}{\alpha}=iq\phi^*.
\]
Noether’s formula gives
\[
j^\mu
=\partial^\mu\phi^*(-iq\phi)
+\partial^\mu\phi(iq\phi^*)
=iq(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-\phi\partial^\mu\phi^*).
\]
Taking the divergence gives
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu=iq(\phi^*\Box\phi-\phi\Box\phi^*)=0,
\]
because both fields satisfy the Klein–Gordon equation.





8.4 Exercise 4 — Energy of a scalar field
Use Equation 11 to calculate \(T^{00}\) for the real scalar field. Why is each contribution to the total energy non-negative?






NoteSolution





For this field,
\[
T^{\mu\nu}=\partial^\mu\phi\partial^\nu\phi
-\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal L.
\]
Since
\[
\mathcal L=\frac12\dot\phi^2
-\frac12(\boldsymbol\nabla\phi)^2-\frac12m^2\phi^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
T^{00}=\frac12\dot\phi^2
+\frac12(\boldsymbol\nabla\phi)^2+\frac12m^2\phi^2.
\]
For real \(\phi\) and \(m^2\geq0\), every term is a square multiplied by a non-negative coefficient.





8.5 Exercise 5 — The Lie algebra of \(SU(2)\)
Using the Pauli matrices, verify
\[
\left[\frac{\sigma_i}{2},\frac{\sigma_j}{2}\right]
=i\varepsilon_{ijk}\frac{\sigma_k}{2}.
\]
Then calculate the quadratic Casimir in the fundamental representation.






NoteSolution





The Pauli matrices obey
\[
[\sigma_i,\sigma_j]=2i\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k.
\]
Dividing by four gives the required relation. Since \(\sigma_i^2=I\),
\[
\mathbf T^2=\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\sigma_i^2}{4}
=\frac34I.
\]
This is \(j(j+1)\) with \(j=1/2\).





8.6 Exercise 6 — Two spin-\(1/2\) states
Show that the singlet state in Equation 16 is annihilated by the total generators
\[
T_i^{\mathrm{tot}}=T_i\otimes I+I\otimes T_i.
\]
Why does this prove that the state is invariant under \(SU(2)\)?






NoteSolution





For \(T_3^{\mathrm{tot}}\), the two terms in the singlet each have total magnetic number zero. For the raising operator,
\[
T_+^{\mathrm{tot}}|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle
=|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle,
\qquad
T_+^{\mathrm{tot}}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle
=|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle,
\]
so the difference is annihilated. The same holds for \(T_-^{\mathrm{tot}}\). All three generators therefore vanish on the singlet. Exponentiating them leaves the state unchanged.





8.7 Exercise 7 — Abelian and non-abelian transformations
Take two infinitesimal transformations
\[
U_a=1-i\alpha T^a,
\qquad
U_b=1-i\beta T^b.
\]
Calculate \(U_aU_b-U_bU_a\) to the first non-zero order. Interpret the result for \(U(1)\) and \(SU(2)\).






NoteSolution





Terms linear in the parameters cancel, leaving
\[
U_aU_b-U_bU_a=-\alpha\beta[T^a,T^b]+O(\alpha^2,\beta^2).
\]
\(U(1)\) has one generator, so the commutator vanishes. In \(SU(2)\), different generators do not commute; successive rotations around different internal axes depend on their order.





8.8 Exercise 8 — Mass and spin from Poincaré symmetry
For a massive particle in its rest frame, use Equation 18 to show that \(W^0=0\) and \(\mathbf W=m\mathbf J\). Deduce Equation 19.






NoteSolution





With \(P^\mu=(m,\mathbf0)\), the time component contains only spatial components of \(P\) and is zero. The spatial components reduce to
\[
W^i=\frac m2\varepsilon^{i0jk}M_{jk}=mJ^i.
\]
Therefore
\[
W^2=-\mathbf W^2=-m^2\mathbf J^2.
\]
In the spin-\(s\) representation, \(\mathbf J^2=s(s+1)\), hence
\[
W^2=-m^2s(s+1).
\]





8.9 Exercise 9 — Selection rule
Let \(Q\) be a conserved charge with \([Q,S]=0\), where \(S\) is the scattering operator. If
\[
Q|i\rangle=q_i|i\rangle,
\qquad
Q|f\rangle=q_f|f\rangle,
\]
show that \((q_f-q_i)\langle f|S|i\rangle=0\).






NoteSolution





Insert the commutator between the two states:
\[
0=\langle f|[Q,S]|i\rangle
=(q_f-q_i)\langle f|S|i\rangle.
\]
If \(q_f\neq q_i\), the transition amplitude must vanish. Conservation laws therefore appear as selection rules.





8.10 Exercise 10 — Building \(U(1)\) invariants
A complex field transforms as \(\phi\to e^{-iq\alpha}\phi\). Decide which expressions are invariant: \(\phi\), \(\phi^2\), \(\phi^*\phi\), \((\phi^*\phi)^2\) and \(\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi\).






NoteSolution





\(\phi\) has charge \(q\) and \(\phi^2\) has charge \(2q\), so neither is invariant for \(q\neq0\). The products \(\phi^*\phi\) and \((\phi^*\phi)^2\) have total charge zero and are invariant. For a global transformation, \(\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi\) is also invariant because the phase is constant. Under a local transformation, it gains an extra term and must be replaced by \(\phi^*D_\mu\phi\).





8.11 Exercise 11 — Colour singlets
Under \(SU(3)\), a quark transforms as \(q_i\to U_i{}^j q_j\) and an antiquark as \(\bar q^i\to\bar q^j(U^\dagger)_j{}^i\). Show that \(\bar q^iq_i\) is a singlet. Then explain why \(\varepsilon^{ijk}q_iq_jq_k\) is also invariant.






NoteSolution





For the quark-antiquark combination,
\[
\bar q^i q_i
\to \bar q^j(U^\dagger)_j{}^iU_i{}^kq_k
=\bar q^jq_j.
\]
For three quarks,
\[
\varepsilon^{ijk}U_i{}^aU_j{}^bU_k{}^c
=(\det U)\varepsilon^{abc}.
\]
Since \(\det U=1\) in \(SU(3)\), the antisymmetric three-quark combination is invariant.





8.12 Exercise 12 — Explicit or spontaneous breaking?
For a complex scalar field, compare the two potentials
\[
V_1=m^2|\phi|^2+\lambda|\phi|^4+\epsilon(\phi+\phi^*)
\]
and
\[
V_2=-\mu^2|\phi|^2+\lambda|\phi|^4,
\]
with positive \(\lambda\), \(\mu^2\) and non-zero \(\epsilon\). Identify the type of symmetry breaking in each case.






NoteSolution





The term \(\epsilon(\phi+\phi^*)\) changes under a phase rotation, so \(V_1\) explicitly breaks \(U(1)\). The potential \(V_2\) is invariant, but its minima have non-zero magnitude and arbitrary phase. Choosing one minimum breaks the symmetry spontaneously.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
9 Problems

9.1 Problem 1 — Noether theorem in an internal plane
Consider two real scalar fields with
\[
\mathcal L
=\frac12\partial_\mu\phi_1\partial^\mu\phi_1
+\frac12\partial_\mu\phi_2\partial^\mu\phi_2
-\frac12m^2(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2).
\]

Show that the action is invariant under rotations of \((\phi_1,\phi_2)\).
Find the infinitesimal variations.
Derive the conserved current.
Define \(\Phi=(\phi_1+i\phi_2)/\sqrt2\) and relate the result to the \(U(1)\) current.







NoteSolution





The finite transformation is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\phi_1'\\\phi_2'\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\
\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\phi_1\\\phi_2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both \(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\) and the corresponding kinetic term are invariant. At first order,
\[
\delta\phi_1=-\alpha\phi_2,
\qquad
\delta\phi_2=\alpha\phi_1.
\]
Dividing out \(\alpha\), Noether’s formula gives
\[
j^\mu
=-\partial^\mu\phi_1\,\phi_2
+\partial^\mu\phi_2\,\phi_1.
\]
With \(\Phi=(\phi_1+i\phi_2)/\sqrt2\), the rotation becomes \(\Phi\to e^{i\alpha}\Phi\). Apart from the sign convention chosen for the charge, the current is
\[
j^\mu=i(\Phi^*\partial^\mu\Phi-\Phi\partial^\mu\Phi^*).
\]





9.2 Problem 2 — From a global phase to an interaction
Let a complex scalar field transform locally as
\[
\phi(x)\to e^{-iq\alpha(x)}\phi(x).
\]

Show why \(\partial_\mu\phi\) does not transform like \(\phi\).
Find the transformation of \(A_\mu\) that makes \(D_\mu\phi=(\partial_\mu+iqA_\mu)\phi\) covariant.
Expand \((D_\mu\phi)^*D^\mu\phi\) and identify the interaction terms.
Explain why the electromagnetic field strength is invariant.







NoteSolution





Differentiating the transformed field gives
\[
\partial_\mu\phi'
=e^{-iq\alpha}
(\partial_\mu\phi-iq\,\partial_\mu\alpha\,\phi).
\]
The extra term is cancelled if
\[
A_\mu' = A_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha.
\]
Then \(D_\mu'\phi'=e^{-iq\alpha}D_\mu\phi\). Expanding the kinetic term gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(D_\mu\phi)^*D^\mu\phi
={}&\partial_\mu\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi
+iqA^\mu(\phi\partial_\mu\phi^*-\phi^*\partial_\mu\phi)\\
&+q^2A_\mu A^\mu\phi^*\phi.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last two terms describe interactions. Finally,
\[
F_{\mu\nu}'
=\partial_\mu A_\nu'-\partial_\nu A_\mu'
=F_{\mu\nu},
\]
because mixed derivatives commute.





9.3 Problem 3 — Why non-abelian gauge bosons interact
Take
\[
D_\mu=\partial_\mu+igA_\mu,
\qquad
A_\mu=A_\mu^aT^a.
\]

Calculate \([D_\mu,D_\nu]\).
Show that it can be written as \(igF_{\mu\nu}\).
Recover Equation 21.
Explain the physical difference with \(U(1)\).







NoteSolution





Acting on a field,
\[
[D_\mu,D_\nu]
=ig(\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu)
-g^2[A_\mu,A_\nu].
\]
Using
\[
[A_\mu,A_\nu]
=A_\mu^aA_\nu^b[T^a,T^b]
=if^{abc}A_\mu^aA_\nu^bT^c,
\]
we find
\[
[D_\mu,D_\nu]=igF_{\mu\nu}^aT^a,
\]
with
\[
F_{\mu\nu}^a
=\partial_\mu A_\nu^a-\partial_\nu A_\mu^a
-gf^{abc}A_\mu^bA_\nu^c,
\]
which agrees with Equation 21. For \(U(1)\), the generators commute and the last term vanishes. In a non-abelian theory it remains, so the gauge field itself carries the group charge and interacts with other gauge fields.

title: Symmetries, groups and conservation laws
text:
10 Further reading
For a first approach, see D. Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles. More complete discussions can be found in M. Schwartz, Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model, and M. Srednicki, Quantum Field Theory.

title: Theoretical electro­magnetism
text:
Magnetic flux is measured through a surface, while electric charge is measured in a volume. A circulation is measured along a curve. Differential forms describe these integrals and keep track of their orientations.
We will use this language to combine the electric and magnetic fields into one field on spacetime. We first need the wedge product and the exterior derivative. The metric will then enter through the Hodge operator.
We use Heaviside–Lorentz units with \(c=\varepsilon_0=\mu_0=1\), coordinates \((t,x,y,z)\), and the conventions
\[
\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,+1,+1,+1),
\qquad
\operatorname{vol}=dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
\]
Greek indices run from \(0\) to \(3\) and spatial indices from \(1\) to \(3\). An index repeated once above and once below is summed. The fields are assumed smooth in the region under study.

title: Theoretical electro­magnetism
text:
1 Exterior algebra

1.1 Vectors and covectors
Let \(V\) be an \(n\)-dimensional real vector space. A covector is a linear map \(\alpha:V\to\mathbb R\): it takes a vector as input and returns a number. Covectors form the dual space \(V^\ast\).
If \((e_1,\ldots,e_n)\) is a basis of \(V\), the dual basis satisfies
\[
e^i(e_j)=\delta^i{}_j.
\]
For \(v=v^ie_i\) and \(\alpha=\alpha_ie^i\), this gives
\[
\alpha(v)=\alpha_iv^i.
\]
Vectors and covectors have different roles. A displacement is a vector; the differential of a function takes a displacement and gives its first-order change. For example, \(df(v)\) is the directional derivative of \(f\) along \(v\).
A non-degenerate metric \(g\) gives a map between the two spaces:
\[
v^\flat=g(v,\cdot),
\qquad
(v^\flat)_i=g_{ij}v^j,
\qquad
(\alpha^\sharp)^i=g^{ij}\alpha_j.
\]
Here \(\flat\) lowers an index and \(\sharp\) raises it. These maps depend on the metric; the pairing \(\alpha(v)\) does not.


1.2 Alternating forms and the wedge product
A \(p\)-form is a multilinear map from \(p\) vectors to a number. It is alternating, which means that exchanging two arguments changes its sign:
\[
\omega(\ldots,u,\ldots,v,\ldots)
=-\omega(\ldots,v,\ldots,u,\ldots).
\]
It therefore vanishes when two arguments are equal. The space of these forms is \(\Lambda^p(V^\ast)\). A 0-form is a scalar and a 1-form is a covector.
The wedge product combines a \(p\)-form and a \(q\)-form into a \((p+q)\)-form. For two covectors,
\[
(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)
=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u).
\]
In coordinates,
\[
\alpha\wedge\beta
=\sum_{i<j}(\alpha_i\beta_j-\alpha_j\beta_i)e^i\wedge e^j.
\]
For example,
\[
(dx\wedge dy)(u,v)=u_xv_y-u_yv_x.
\]
This determinant is the signed area of the two vectors projected onto the coordinate plane. Exchanging \(u\) and \(v\) reverses the orientation and hence the sign.
For general degrees, the product is defined by antisymmetrizing the tensor product:
\[
(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{i_1\ldots i_{p+q}}
=\frac{(p+q)!}{p!\,q!}
\alpha_{[i_1\ldots i_p}\beta_{i_{p+1}\ldots i_{p+q}]}.
\]
Square brackets mean the signed average over permutations; for example, \(T_{[ij]}=(T_{ij}-T_{ji})/2\). The wedge product is bilinear and associative. It obeys
\[
\alpha\wedge\beta=(-1)^{pq}\beta\wedge\alpha.
\]
To exchange the two groups, each of the \(p\) factors must pass the \(q\) factors in the other group, giving \(pq\) sign changes. This rule is called graded commutativity.
If \(\omega\) has odd degree, then \(\omega\wedge\omega=-\omega\wedge\omega\), so its square is zero. This need not hold for even degree. In four dimensions, for example,
\[
\omega=e^1\wedge e^2+e^3\wedge e^4
\]
gives
\[
\omega\wedge\omega=2e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3\wedge e^4.
\]
The individual squares vanish because of repeated factors. The two cross terms are equal because 2-forms commute.


1.3 The Grassmann algebra
A basis of \(\Lambda^p(V^\ast)\) consists of
\[
e^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e^{i_p},
\qquad
1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_p\leq n.
\]
Choosing \(p\) distinct indices gives
\[
\dim\Lambda^p(V^\ast)=\binom np.
\]
For \(p>n\), every \(p\)-form vanishes. The direct sum of all degrees, with the wedge product, is the exterior algebra, also called the Grassmann algebra:
\[
\Lambda(V^\ast)=\bigoplus_{p=0}^n\Lambda^p(V^\ast),
\qquad
\dim\Lambda(V^\ast)=\sum_{p=0}^n\binom np=2^n.
\]
Writing the degree-one generators as \(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n\) and omitting the wedge symbol gives
\[
\theta^i\theta^j=-\theta^j\theta^i,
\qquad
(\theta^i)^2=0.
\]
Thus every element is a finite sum,
\[
f=f_0+f_i\theta^i+\frac1{2!}f_{ij}\theta^i\theta^j
+\cdots+f_{12\ldots n}\theta^1\cdots\theta^n,
\]
with antisymmetric coefficients. For differential forms, the coordinate differentials \(dx^i\) play the role of these generators.






NoteGrassmann and Cartan





Grassmann developed exterior algebra in the nineteenth century. Cartan later used differential forms to study geometry. Their algebra is useful here because an oriented surface or volume changes sign when its orientation is reversed.

title: Theoretical electro­magnetism
text:
2 Differential forms

2.1 Forms that vary with position
On a smooth manifold \(M\), a differential \(p\)-form assigns a \(p\)-form to the tangent space at each point. Its coefficients vary smoothly. In coordinates,
\[
\omega=\frac1{p!}\omega_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x)
\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}.
\]
The coefficients are antisymmetric. The factor \(1/p!\) removes repeated copies when all index orders are summed. If we sum only over \(i_1<\cdots<i_p\), this factor is omitted.
